3---  # Basics: Functional Programming in Lean
4-
5---  This chapter introduces some of Lean's most essential features for
6---  writing functional programs and proving things about how they behave.
7-
8---  ## Introduction
9-
10---  The *functional style* of programming is founded on simple mathematical
11---  intuitions: a program is essentially a concrete means for computing a
12---  mathematical function, which just maps inputs to outputs. (Even
13---  programs with side effects like reading and writing files or network
14---  packets can be presented in this way, using ideas like *monads*.) This
15---  connection between programs and mathematical functions makes it
16---  possible to reason both precisely and formally about a program's
17---  behavior, i.e., to *prove properties* about programs.
18---
19---  This functional style is one sense of the word "functional" in
20---  "functional programming." The other sense is that it emphasizes the use
21---  of functions as *first-class* values — i.e., values that can be passed
22---  as arguments to other functions, returned as results, included in data
23---  structures, etc. The recognition that functions can be treated as data
24---  gives rise to a host of useful and powerful programming idioms.
25---
26---  Other common features of functional languages include *algebraic data
27---  types* and *pattern matching*, which make it easy to construct and
28---  manipulate rich data structures, and *polymorphic types* supporting
29---  abstraction and code reuse. Lean offers all of these features, and we
30---  will see them often in this book.
31---
32---  The first part of this chapter introduces some key elements of Lean's
33---  functional programming language. The second part shows how to use
34---  *tactics* to prove properties about programs.
35-
36---  ## Data and Functions
37-
38---  Lean's set of primitives is extremely small. For example, instead of
39---  providing the usual palette of *atomic datatypes* — booleans, integers,
40---  strings, and so on — Lean's standard library *defines* them, along with
41---  an extensive collection of other common data structures — lists, hash
42---  tables, etc., etc. It does so with a single powerful and general
43---  mechanism: *inductive definitions*. A type introduced with an inductive
44---  definition is called an *inductive type*, and the word "inductive"
45---  hints at the use of mathematical induction to reason about its values
46---  (as we will see in the next chapter).
47---
48---  To demonstrate how inductive definitions work and illustrate their
49---  expressive power, we will start by defining most of the datatypes we
50---  use in this course from scratch, rather than importing the ones in the
51---  standard library. (We will later switch over to the library versions to
52---  take advantage of all the properties that have already been proved
53---  about them.)
54-
55---  ### Days of the Week (Enumerated Types)
56-
57---  Let's start with a very simple example. The following declaration tells
58---  Lean to give a name to a set of data values, i.e., to define a *type*.
59-
60-inductive Day : Type where
61-  | monday
62-  | tuesday
63-  | wednesday
64-  | thursday
65-  | friday
66-  | saturday
67-  | sunday
68-
69---  The new type is called `Day`, and its members are `monday`, `tuesday`,
70---  etc. These are also called the *constructors* of the `Day` type. We
71---  often call this sort of inductive type an *enumerated type* since the
72---  values belonging to the type are explicitly enumerated in its
73---  definition.
74---
75---  Having defined `Day`, we can write Lean functions that operate on days.
76-
77-def nextWorkingDay (d : Day) : Day :=
78-  match d with
79-  | Day.monday    => Day.tuesday
80-  | Day.tuesday   => Day.wednesday
81-  | Day.wednesday => Day.thursday
82-  | Day.thursday  => Day.friday
83-  | Day.friday    => Day.monday
84-  | Day.saturday  => Day.monday
85-  | Day.sunday    => Day.monday
86-
87---  Note that the argument and result types of this function are explicitly
88---  declared on its first line. As in most functional programming
89---  languages, Lean can often figure out these types for itself when they
90---  are not given explicitly — i.e., it can do *type inference* — but we'll
91---  generally include them to make reading easier.
92---
93---  The `match` on the second line is Lean's keyword for *pattern
94---  matching*, the functional programming way of examining and making
95---  decisions on data. To evaluate `match d with...`, Lean will examine the
96---  structure of `d` to see which case to execute; if `d` is `Day.monday`,
97---  for example, it will evaluate the first case of the `match` statement;
98---  if `d` is `Day.friday`, it will evaluate the fifth case. (There is much
99---  more to say about pattern matching! We'll introduce more of its
100---  features as the need arises.)
101---
102---  You may notice that we *qualified* `Day`'s constructors when using
103---  them, writing `Day.monday` instead of just `monday`, for example. Lean
104---  places all constructors into a *namespace* associated with their type,
105---  and generally requires those constructors to be prefixed with their
106---  namespace when they are used, though we will see later that this
107---  requirement can sometimes be relaxed.
108---
109---  If you ever need to know the type of *any* pattern, object, or
110---  function, you can hover over it with your mouse, either in VS Code or
111---  in the HTML version of the chapter.
112-
113---  Having defined a function, we should check that it works on some
114---  examples. There are a few different ways to do this in Lean. One is to
115---  use the `#eval` command to evaluate a compound expression involving
116---  `nextWorkingDay`.
117-
118-#eval nextWorkingDay Day.friday
119-
120---  Output:
121---    Day.monday
122-
123-#eval nextWorkingDay (nextWorkingDay Day.saturday)
124-
125---  Output:
126---    Day.tuesday
127-
128---  We can also record what we *expect* the result of calling a function to
129---  be in the form of a Lean `example`:
130-
131-example : nextWorkingDay (nextWorkingDay Day.saturday) = Day.tuesday := by
132-  rfl
133-
134---  This declaration asserts that the second working day after `saturday`
135---  is `tuesday`. Having made the assertion, we can also ask Lean to
136---  *verify* it. The `by rfl` can be read as "The assertion we've just made
137---  can be proved by observing that both sides of the equality evaluate to
138---  the same term."
139---
140---  Here, `rfl` is pronounced "reflexivity," the principle that any value
141---  is equal to itself. After evaluation, both sides of the equality are
142---  the same value, so the assertion is true by reflexivity. If we had made
143---  a different assertion, such as
144-
145-sf_expect_failure_in
146-  example : nextWorkingDay (nextWorkingDay Day.saturday) = Day.monday := by rfl
147-
148---  then Lean would not be able to verify it and would instead signal an
149---  error.
150---
151---  (The `sf_expect_failure_in` annotation tells Lean that there is
152---  intended to be an error in the following expression and it should not
153---  mark the whole file as broken.)
154-
155---  ### Aside: Using the VS Code Lean Extension
156-
157---  If you have not already done so, this would be an excellent moment to
158---  fire up VS Code with the [Lean
159---  Extension](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=leanprover.lean4)
160---  and load this file, `Basics.lean`, from the book's Lean sources. Locate
161---  the above example and observe its result in the Lean InfoView panel.
162---
163---  This panel displays the results of commands like `#eval` (click on a
164---  particular `#eval` to see), as well as the current goal state when you
165---  are working on proofs. The InfoView content always follows your cursor.
166---
167---  On Windows and Linux, Ctrl-click a type or variable name to navigate to
168---  its definition. On macOS, Command-click instead. Try this with the
169---  mention of `nextWorkingDay` in the above `#eval`.
170---
171---  You can also hover over expressions in the source code to see their
172---  types. Try this with mentions of `nextWorkingDay` and `Day.saturday` in
173---  the above `#eval`. If you hover over the `#eval` command itself, you
174---  will see the popup that contains its output (at the top). Sometimes we
175---  show Lean's responses to commands in the text below them; by hovering
176---  over the command, you can check against that text.
177---
178---  Experiment with adding your own `#eval` commands to test other inputs.
179---  Lean typechecks the file as you edit it, so you can see the results of
180---  your changes immediately.
181-
182---  ### Booleans
183-
184---  Following the pattern of the days of the week above, we can define the
185---  standard type `Bool` of booleans by enumerating its members `true` and
186---  `false`. We define our own `MyBool` to teach the concept of building
187---  booleans from scratch. Our definition of `MyBool` is equivalent to
188---  Lean's built-in `Bool`, which we'll switch to later. We call it
189---  `MyBool` to avoid clashing with the built-in name. Later in the
190---  chapter, we will show a different way of avoiding such clashes: we will
191---  place our custom natural numbers in a fresh `NatPlayground` namespace,
192---  where they can be called `Nat` without clashing with Lean's built-in
193---  `Nat`.
194-
195-inductive MyBool : Type where
196-  | true
197-  | false
198-
199---  We next invoke a couple of Lean directives to help control formatting.
200---  Exactly what these directives mean is not important for present
201---  purposes — you can understand everything in the rest of the book
202---  without knowing — so we will mark these commands — and similar bits
203---  later on — with `THE FOLLOWING DETAILS CAN BE SKIPPED` comments in
204---  `.lean` files, and with folded-up segments in the HTML presentation.
205---  Feel free to have a peek if you want (click on the triangle in the HTML
206---  to unfold it), or just jump down to the following material and keep
207---  going.
208-
209---  THE FOLLOWING DETAILS CAN BE SKIPPED
210-variable (b : MyBool) (n m : Nat)
211-set_option pp.fieldNotation false
212---  END DETAILS
213-
214---  The next command opens the namespace associated with the `MyBool` type,
215---  so subsequent definitions will be part of the `MyBool` namespace. In
216---  Lean, functions on a type are typically defined in that type's
217---  namespace, which avoids name clashes with functions of the same name
218---  elsewhere (e.g., functions on the built-in `Bool` type). We give a full
219---  treatment of namespaces below.
220-
221-namespace MyBool
222-
223---  Functions over booleans can be defined in the same way as functions
224---  over days of the week.
225-
226-def not (b : MyBool) : MyBool :=
227-  match b with
228-  | MyBool.true => MyBool.false
229-  | MyBool.false => MyBool.true
230-
231-def and (b1 : MyBool) (b2 : MyBool) : MyBool :=
232-  match b1 with
233-  | MyBool.true => b2
234-  | MyBool.false => MyBool.false
235-
236-def or (b1 : MyBool) (b2 : MyBool) : MyBool :=
237-  match b1 with
238-  | MyBool.true => MyBool.true
239-  | MyBool.false => b2
240-
241---  The `and` and `or` definitions illustrate Lean's syntax for
242---  multi-argument functions. The corresponding multi-argument
243---  function-application syntax is illustrated by the following tests,
244---  which effectively constitute a complete specification — a truth table —
245---  for the `or` function:
246-
247-example : or MyBool.true  MyBool.false = MyBool.true  := by rfl
248-example : or MyBool.false MyBool.false = MyBool.false := by rfl
249-example : or MyBool.false MyBool.true  = MyBool.true  := by rfl
250-example : or MyBool.true  MyBool.true  = MyBool.true  := by rfl
251-
252---  Lean also allows us to define symbolic notations for these functions.
253-
254-local prefix:40 (priority := high) "!" => not
255-local infixl:35 (priority := high) " && " => and
256-local infixl:30 (priority := high) " || " => or
257-
258-example :
259-    (MyBool.false || MyBool.false || MyBool.true) = MyBool.true := by rfl
260-
261-example : (!MyBool.false) = MyBool.true := by rfl
262-
263---  The technical details of how these symbolic notations work are not
264---  something you need to understand until quite a bit later in your Lean
265---  journey.
266-
267---  THE FOLLOWING DETAILS CAN BE SKIPPED
268---  Lean has a very flexible notation system. Operators like `||` and `&&`
269---  are defined with specified precedence and associativity. For example,
270---  the `infixl` directive above states that `&&` is an infix operator, has
271---  precedence 35, and is left-associative, while `||` is also infix and
272---  left-associative and has precedence 30. This means that
273---  `MyBool.true || MyBool.false && MyBool.false` is parsed as
274---  `MyBool.true || (MyBool.false && MyBool.false)`.
275---
276---  Custom notations are defined using the `notation`, `infixl`, `infixr`,
277---  `prefix`, and `postfix` commands, some of which we will see (again, in
278---  skippable sections) later on.
279---  END DETAILS
280-
281---  ### Exercise (1 star): nand ⭐
282-
283---  The `sorry` keyword is a placeholder for an incomplete proof or
284---  definition. We use it in exercises to indicate the parts that we're
285---  leaving for you — i.e., your job is to replace `sorry` with real
286---  definitions and proofs.
287---
288---  Remove `sorry` below and complete the definition of the function. The
289---  function should return `MyBool.true` if either or both of its inputs
290---  are `MyBool.false`. Make sure that the `example` assertions below can
291---  be verified by Lean.
292-
293-def nand (b1 : MyBool) (b2 : MyBool) : MyBool
294-  := sorry
295-
296-theorem nand_test1 : nand MyBool.true  MyBool.false = MyBool.true  := sorry
297-theorem nand_test2 : nand MyBool.false MyBool.false = MyBool.true  := sorry
298-theorem nand_test3 : nand MyBool.false MyBool.true  = MyBool.true  := sorry
299-theorem nand_test4 : nand MyBool.true  MyBool.true  = MyBool.false := sorry
300-
301---  ### Exercise (1 star): and3 ⭐
302-
303---  Do the same for the `and3` function below. This function should return
304---  `MyBool.true` when all of its inputs are `MyBool.true`, and
305---  `MyBool.false` otherwise.
306-
307-def and3 (b1 : MyBool) (b2 : MyBool) (b3 : MyBool) : MyBool
308-  := sorry
309-
310-theorem and3_test1 : and3 MyBool.true  MyBool.true  MyBool.true  = MyBool.true  := sorry
311-theorem and3_test2 : and3 MyBool.false MyBool.true  MyBool.true  = MyBool.false := sorry
312-theorem and3_test3 : and3 MyBool.true  MyBool.false MyBool.true  = MyBool.false := sorry
313-theorem and3_test4 : and3 MyBool.true  MyBool.true  MyBool.false = MyBool.false := sorry
314-
315---  ## A First Taste of Proofs
316-
317---  Now that we've defined some basic functions on booleans, let's see how
318---  to *prove* some simple properties of those functions. Here is a simple
319---  rule about `&&`:
320---
321---      For any boolean value b, (MyBool.true && b) = b
322---
323---  This is an example of a *proposition*, a logical claim that we can try
324---  to prove. It says that `MyBool.true && b` is equal to `b` for every
325---  `MyBool` `b`.
326---
327---  How do we write this proposition in Lean? Like this:
328---
329---      theorem true_and : ∀ (b : MyBool), (MyBool.true && b) = b
330---
331---  The keyword `theorem` indicates that we are stating (and eventually
332---  proving) a proposition; the text after the first `:` is the proposition
333---  we want to prove.
334---
335---  You'll notice that this proposition looks a lot like the informal one
336---  we began with, with some additional symbols in front. The `∀` symbol,
337---  pronounced "forall," is a *universal quantifier*: it "quantifies" the
338---  variable `b` that appears in the proposition. Quantifying a variable
339---  with a `∀` means that the proposition applies to all possible values of
340---  its type; we annotate `b` with the type `MyBool` to signify that the
341---  proposition holds for all `b`s of type `MyBool`.
342---
343---  Now that we've stated the theorem we'd like to prove, let's see the
344---  proof.
345-
346-theorem true_and : ∀ (b : MyBool), (MyBool.true && b) = b := by
347-  intro b
348-  rfl
349-
350---  What does this mean?
351---
352---  First, the `by` keyword signals that what follows is a sequence of
353---  *tactics*. The `intro b` and `rfl` after the `by` are examples of
354---  tactics. If you hover over a tactic's name, Lean shows its
355---  documentation.
356---
357---  Tactics manipulate the *proof state*, which you can see in the Lean
358---  InfoView panel. The proof state is divided by the symbol ⊢, pronounced
359---  *turnstile*. The part before the turnstile is the *context*; the part
360---  after it is the *goal*. The context records what we know — the current
361---  assumptions — at some given point in the proof; the goal is what we are
362---  trying to prove at that point.
363---
364---  Each tactic manipulates the goal, the context, or both to move things
365---  toward a configuration that is closer to being "solved." A tactic can
366---  also *close* (solve) the current goal, finishing its proof.
367---
368---  Let's walk through the example above with this terminology in mind.
369-
370-theorem true_and_explained : ∀ (b : MyBool), (MyBool.true && b) = b := by
371-  /- Move your cursor (click) here to see the initial proof state in
372-     the InfoView. If you are viewing the book online,
373-     click instead on the white button after `by`.
374-     The context (before the ⊢) is empty.
375-     The goal is `∀ (b : MyBool), (MyBool.true && b) = b`. -/
376-  intro b
377-  /- Now click here (or the white button after `intro b`)
378-     to see the new proof state that results from the
379-     tactic. Notice how `intro b` has changed the _context_: it now
380-     contains `b : MyBool`.
381-
382-    The `intro` tactic is used to name variables quantified by a `∀`.
383-    Since we are trying to prove a property of all `MyBool`s, we
384-    proceed by introducing an unknown `MyBool` `b` and proving
385-    the property holds for this particular `b`.  Informally,
386-    this move can be read, "We want to prove <some property> for all
387-    `MyBool`s `b`. So suppose `b` is some arbitrary `MyBool`...
388-    <and then go on to prove the property for this particular `b`>..."
389-    Since `b` was chosen arbitrarily, we've now proved the property
390-    for all `b`.
391-
392-    A proof of a theorem beginning with a ∀ will typically start with
393-    an `intro`.
394-
395-    As in the `example`s above, we can use the `rfl` tactic,
396-    which closes goals about equality where both sides are equal to
397-    one another according to the principle of reflexivity. Now,
398-    inspecting our goal will show that it is `(MyBool.true && b) = b`,
399-    which may not appear to be "true by reflexivity", since the two
400-    sides of the equality are not textually identical. However, the tactic
401-    _evaluates_ both sides of the equality before comparing them. In
402-    this case, if we look at the definition of `and`, we can see that,
403-    when its first argument is `MyBool.true`, the result is its second
404-    argument. So the two terms `MyBool.true && b` and `b` are in fact
405-    equal because one evaluates to the other.
406-  -/
407-  rfl
408-  /- The proof is now done! The Lean InfoView tells us there are "No goals". -/
409-
410---  Like some other well-known languages (Python, Haskell, etc.), Lean is
411---  *whitespace-sensitive*. That is, the indentation in proofs is
412---  important, and changing it can change the meaning of the proof, usually
413---  causing it to break.
414---
415---  If we had written the following, we'd see an error:
416-
417-sf_expect_failure_in
418-  theorem true_and_wrong : ∀ (b : MyBool), (MyBool.true && b) = b := by
419-    intro b
420-      rfl
421-
422---  To see the error message in the Lean file, change
423---  `sf_expect_failure_in` to `sf_expect_failure_in?` temporarily. You
424---  should see the following message.
425-
426---  Output:
427---    Tactic `introN` failed: There are no additional binders or `let` bindings in the goal to introduce
428---
429---    b : MyBool
430---    ⊢ (true && b) = b
431-
432---  Lean complains because the `rfl` is not at the same level of
433---  indentation as the `intro b`, so it does not recognize these two
434---  tactics as being sequential in the way they should be.
435---
436---  In general, sequential tactics applied to the same goal must either be
437---  on subsequent lines at the same level of indentation or else be
438---  separated on the same line by a `;` like so:
439-
440-theorem true_and' : ∀ (b : MyBool), (MyBool.true && b) = b := by
441-  intro b; rfl
442-
443---  ### Exercise (1 star): false_or_exercise ⭐
444-
445---  Here's a simple proof for you to try. Remove `sorry` and fill in the
446---  proof.
447-
448-theorem false_or : ∀ (b : MyBool), (MyBool.false || b) = b := by
449-  sorry
450-
451---  In this book we often use `sorry` as a placeholder for you to replace
452---  with an actual proof. This tells Lean that we want to skip trying to
453---  prove the theorem and just accept it as a given. This can be useful for
454---  developing longer proofs.
455---
456---  Be careful, though: every time you say `sorry` you are leaving a door
457---  open for total nonsense to enter Lean's safe, formally checked world!
458-
459-sf_experiment
460-  theorem really_bad : MyBool.true = MyBool.false := by sorry
461-
462---  The facts we've seen so far about booleans are quite simple, so the
463---  tactics we need to prove them are also quite simple. Over the course of
464---  this book, we are going to introduce new tactics and proof techniques
465---  gradually, enriching the propositions we can prove along the way.
466---
467---  Now that we've seen how to define our own booleans and prove some basic
468---  properties about them, let's switch over to Lean's built-in `Bool`
469---  type, which has the same structure but comes with a lot of useful
470---  functions and lemmas.
471-
472-end MyBool
473-
474---  ### Aside: Unicode in Lean
475-
476---  Note that `∀` and `⊢` are Unicode symbols, not plain ASCII characters.
477---  The Lean Extension for VS Code provides convenient shortcuts for
478---  entering such symbols. Simply type `\` (backslash) followed by the name
479---  of the symbol (its "shortcode"), and the extension will automatically
480---  replace it with the actual symbol. For example, typing either `\all` or
481---  `\forall` will produce `∀`, and `\->` or `\to` will produce `→`. To
482---  find out what backslash sequence produces a Unicode symbol that you can
483---  see on the screen, just hover over it. To see a list of all of the
484---  Unicode shortcodes, open the Command Palette (Ctrl+Shift+P on
485---  Windows/Linux or Cmd+Shift+P on macOS), type "Lean 4: Show Unicode
486---  Input Abbreviations", and press Enter.
487-
488---  ### Types
489-
490---  Every expression in Lean has a type describing what sort of value it
491---  computes. The `#check` command asks Lean to print the type of an
492---  expression.
493-
494-#check Bool.true
495-
496---  Output:
497---    Bool.true : Bool
498-
499---  If the expression after `#check` is followed by a colon and a type,
500---  Lean will verify that the type of the expression matches the given type
501---  and signal an error if not.
502-
503-#check (Bool.true : Bool)
504-#check (Bool.not Bool.true : Bool)
505-
506---  Output:
507---    true : Bool
508-
509---  Output:
510---    !true : Bool
511-
512---  Functions like `Bool.not` are themselves ordinary values, just like
513---  `Bool.true` and `Bool.false`. Their types are called *function types*,
514---  and they are written with arrows.
515-
516-#check Bool.not
517-
518---  The type of `Bool.not`, written `Bool → Bool` and pronounced "`Bool`
519---  arrow `Bool`," can be read, "Given an input of type `Bool`, this
520---  function produces an output of type `Bool`." Similarly, the type of
521---  `Bool.and`, written `Bool → Bool → Bool`, can be read, "Given two
522---  inputs, each of type `Bool`, this function produces an output of type
523---  `Bool`."
524-
525---  ### New Types from Old
526-
527---  The enumerated types we have seen so far are so named because their
528---  definitions explicitly enumerate a finite set of elements: their
529---  constructors. Here is a more interesting inductive type definition,
530---  `Color`, where one of the constructors takes an argument:
531-
532-inductive RGB : Type where
533-  | red
534-  | green
535-  | blue
536-
537-inductive Color : Type where
538-  | black
539-  | white
540-  | primary (p : RGB)
541-
542---  *Constructor expressions* are formed by applying a constructor to zero
543---  or more other constructors or constructor expressions, obeying the
544---  declared number and types of the constructor arguments. E.g., these are
545---  valid constructor expressions...
546---
547---  - `RGB.red`
548---  - `Bool.true`
549---  - `Color.primary` `RGB.red`
550---
551---  ...but these are not:
552---
553---  - `RGB.red Color.primary`
554---  - `Bool.true RGB.red`
555---  - `Color.primary (Color.primary RGB.red)`
556-
557---  We can define functions on colors using pattern matching, just as we
558---  did for `Day` and `MyBool`.
559-
560-def monochrome (c : Color) : Bool :=
561-  match c with
562-  | Color.black => Bool.true
563-  | Color.white => Bool.true
564-  | Color.primary p => Bool.false
565-
566---  Since the `primary` constructor takes an argument, a pattern that
567---  matches `.primary` should include a variable, a constant of appropriate
568---  type, or `_`. Lean's convention is to use a `_` (called a *wildcard*)
569---  when the argument to a constructor doesn't matter. In the definition of
570---  `monochrome`, we don't use the argument to `Color.primary`, so a more
571---  idiomatic definition would be:
572-
573-def monochrome' (c : Color) : Bool :=
574-  match c with
575-  | Color.black => Bool.true
576-  | Color.white => Bool.true
577-  | Color.primary _ => Bool.false
578-
579---  We can use a constant argument to `Color.primary` to match a specific
580---  primary color:
581-
582-def isRed (c : Color) : Bool :=
583-  match c with
584-  | Color.black => Bool.false
585-  | Color.white => Bool.false
586-  | Color.primary RGB.red => Bool.true
587-  | Color.primary _ => Bool.false
588-
589---  The pattern `Color.primary RGB.red` will match only when `c` is
590---  `Color.primary` with the argument `RGB.red`. The pattern
591---  `Color.primary _` matches every `Color.primary` color, but because
592---  patterns are checked in order, the `Color.primary _` case will never be
593---  reached if the color is `RGB.red`.
594-
595---  An alternative way to write the same function would be to explicitly
596---  nest match statements:
597-
598-def isRed' (c : Color) : Bool :=
599-  match c with
600-  | Color.black => Bool.false
601-  | Color.white => Bool.false
602-  | Color.primary r =>
603-    match r with
604-    | RGB.red => Bool.true
605-    | _ => Bool.false
606-
607---  This `isRed'` function produces the same result as `isRed`. It also
608---  illustrates the *use* of a pattern variable in the corresponding
609---  branch.
610-
611---  The `Color.primary r` pattern stores the `RGB` argument into variable
612---  `r`, and then pattern matches on that argument to produce the final
613---  result.
614-
615---  ### Exercise (1 star): is_weekend ⭐
616-
617---  Define a function that takes a `Day` and returns `true` iff the day is
618---  a weekend.
619---
620---  Then fill in the right-hand sides of the `example` blocks below. If
621---  you've done both correctly, the blocks will produce no errors and
622---  contain no uses of `sorry`.
623---
624---  Hint: You could write this function by pattern matching on each
625---  possible day of the week, or you could try to come up with a shorter
626---  solution...
627-
628-def is_weekend (d : Day) : Bool
629-  := sorry
630-
631-theorem is_weekend_test1 : is_weekend Day.sunday = true := sorry
632-theorem is_weekend_test2 : is_weekend Day.friday = false := sorry
633-
634---  ### Exercise (1 star): isInversion ⭐
635-
636---  Define a function that takes two colors and returns `true` if the
637---  second color is an *inversion* of the first, and `false` otherwise.
638---
639---  Inversion is defined by cases: Black is an inversion of white and vice
640---  versa. Red is an inversion of blue and vice versa. Green is not an
641---  inversion of anything.
642---
643---  As before, write the right-hand sides of the `example` blocks to ensure
644---  they pass with no `sorry`.
645-
646-def isInversion (c1 c2 : Color) : Bool
647-  := sorry
648-
649-theorem isInversion_test1 : isInversion Color.black Color.white = true := sorry
650-theorem isInversion_test2 : isInversion Color.white Color.black = Bool.true := sorry
651-theorem isInversion_test3 : isInversion (Color.primary RGB.red) (Color.primary RGB.blue) = Bool.true :=
652-  sorry
653-theorem isInversion_test4 : isInversion (Color.primary RGB.green) (Color.primary RGB.red) = Bool.false :=
654-  sorry
655-
656---  ### Namespaces
657-
658---  This chapter has already used Lean's system of *namespaces* for
659---  managing potentially conflicting names in a few places. Now we have
660---  seen enough that we can look more closely at how it works.
661---
662---  When we enclose a collection of declarations in
663---  `namespace X ... end X`, references from outside this collection to
664---  names declared within it are referred to with prefix `X.`, like `X.foo`
665---  instead of just `foo`. In large Lean developments, namespaces are used
666---  to organize definitions and theorems similarly to how modules are used
667---  in other programming languages.
668-
669-def myFoo : Bool := true
670-namespace Playground
671-def myFoo : RGB := RGB.blue
672-end Playground
673-
674-#check myFoo
675-#check Playground.myFoo
676-
677---  Output:
678---    myFoo : Bool
679-
680---  Output:
681---    Playground.myFoo : RGB
682-
683---  Namespaces can be closed and later reopened, as often as you like, to
684---  add new definitions and access old ones more conveniently. When inside
685---  a `namespace`, definitions from that namespace can be referenced
686---  without prefixes.
687-
688-namespace Playground
689-def myBar : RGB := myFoo
690-end Playground
691-
692-#check Playground.myBar
693-
694---  Output:
695---    Playground.myBar : RGB
696-
697---  Lean gives each constructor of an inductive type a name prefixed by the
698---  type's name, such as `RGB.blue`. When we enter the `RGB` `namespace`,
699---  we can use its constructors without the `RGB` prefix. For example, we
700---  can write just `blue` below.
701-
702-namespace RGB
703-def myBlue : RGB := blue
704-end RGB
705-
706---  Top-level definitions can also be prefixed by a namespace, which opens
707---  the namespace temporarily for the body of the definition.
708-
709--- The following works because the definition is qualified by `RGB.`
710-def RGB.myOtherBlue : RGB := myBlue
711-
712-#check RGB.myBlue
713-#check RGB.myOtherBlue
714-
715---  Output:
716---    RGB.myBlue : RGB
717-
718---  Output:
719---    RGB.myOtherBlue : RGB
720-
721-sf_expect_failure_in
722-  -- This doesn't work: the identifier is undefined
723-  #check myBlue
724-
725---  Output:
726---    Unknown identifier `myBlue`
727-
728---  Similarly, we could rewrite the definition of `nextWorkingDay` inside
729---  the `Day` namespace like so:
730-
731-def Day.nextWorkingDay' (d : Day) : Day :=
732-  match d with
733-  | monday    => tuesday
734-  | tuesday   => wednesday
735-  | wednesday => thursday
736-  | thursday  => friday
737-  | friday    => monday
738-  | saturday  => monday
739-  | sunday    => monday
740-
741---  We can also use `open` to bring the definitions of a namespace into the
742---  current scope; after that, we can refer to any of the namespace's
743---  definitions without a prefix.
744-
745-namespace MyNamespace
746-def myDef : Bool := Bool.true
747-end MyNamespace
748-
749-open MyNamespace
750-
751-#check myDef
752-
753---  Output:
754---    MyNamespace.myDef : Bool
755-
756---  If we only want to bring *some*, rather than all, of the definitions of
757---  a namespace into the current scope, we can use the `open (...)` form:
758-
759-namespace MyOtherNamespace
760-def myHiddenDef : Bool := Bool.true
761-def myVisibleDef : Bool := Bool.false
762-end MyOtherNamespace
763-
764-open MyOtherNamespace (myVisibleDef)
765-
766--- `myVisibleDef` is now usable without qualification:
767-#check myVisibleDef
768-
769---  Output:
770---    MyOtherNamespace.myVisibleDef : Bool
771-
772---  But `myHiddenDef`, which we did not include in the `open`, still needs
773---  to be qualified:
774-
775-sf_expect_failure_in
776-  #check myHiddenDef
777-
778---  Output:
779---    Unknown identifier `myHiddenDef`
780-
781---  You might be wondering why we can use constructors like `true` and
782---  `false` and functions like `not` without qualifying them with `Bool`,
783---  and without explicitly `open`ing the `Bool` `namespace`. Lean provides
784---  a way to *export* unprefixed names from a `namespace`, with the same
785---  effect as selectively `open`ing that `namespace` downstream, and the
786---  Lean prelude does that for commonly used names from the standard
787---  library. We don't explain this mechanism here because it's rarely used.
788-
789-#check Bool.true
790-#check true
791-
792---  Output:
793---    Bool.true : Bool
794-
795---  Output:
796---    Bool.true : Bool
797-
798---  Finally, Lean can often use an expression's expected type to fill in
799---  the missing prefix of a name that begins with `.`. So, instead of the
800---  fully qualified style `Day.monday`, we can write just `.monday`.
801---
802---  For example, when the expected type is `Day`, Lean interprets `.monday`
803---  as `Day.monday`. If the context does not determine an expected type,
804---  Lean reports an error.
805---
806---  So, for example, we can also write `nextWorkingDay` like this, using
807---  the shorter style for both the value being matched and the value being
808---  returned:
809-
810-def nextWorkingDay' (d : Day) : Day :=
811-  match d with
812-  | .monday    => .tuesday
813-  | .tuesday   => .wednesday
814-  | .wednesday => .thursday
815-  | .thursday  => .friday
816-  | .friday    => .monday
817-  | .saturday  => .monday
818-  | .sunday    => .monday
819-
820---  Here, both the type of `d` and the return type of the function are
821---  declared to be `Day`s. When we use the `.monday` style in the function
822---  body, Lean can figure out that we must mean `Day.monday`. However, in
823---  the example below, there is no expected type, so Lean cannot determine
824---  which declaration named `.true` is intended. In this case, it raises an
825---  error:
826-
827-sf_expect_failure_in
828-  #check .true
829-
830---  Output:
831---    Invalid dotted identifier notation: The expected type of `.true` could not be determined
832---
833---    Hint: Using one of these would be unambiguous:
834---      [apply] `true`
835---      [apply] `MyBool.true`
836---      [apply] `Lake.Toml.true`
837---      [apply] `Lean.LBool.true`
838---      [apply] `Std.Do.ExceptConds.true`
839---      [apply] `Lean.Meta.Grind.Filter.true`
840-
841---  But in the following example, because `Bool.not` takes a `Bool`
842---  argument, Lean knows that `.true` must here be a `Bool`:
843-
844-#check (Bool.not .true)
845-
846---  Output:
847---    !true : Bool
848-
849---  ### Exercise (1 star): custom_namespace_checks ⭐
850-
851---  Predict the output of each of the statements below. Would their results
852---  change depending on which namespace the statements appear in? How?
853-
854---  #check .black           -- Write your prediction here.
855---  #check Color.black      -- Write your prediction here.
856---  #check RGB              -- Write your prediction here.
857---  #check Playground.myFoo -- Write your prediction here.
858-
859---  Once you have written your predictions, copy the lines from the comment
860---  into an active section of the book to evaluate them.
861-
862---  ### Constructors with Multiple Parameters (Tuple Types)
863-
864-namespace Playground
865-
866---  A constructor of an inductive type can have multiple parameters, not
867---  just zero or one. This feature lets us define *tuple types* in Lean.
868---
869---  As an example, consider representing the four bits in a nibble (half a
870---  byte). We first define a datatype `Bit` that resembles `Bool` (using
871---  the constructors `b1` and `b0` for the two possible bit values) and
872---  then define the datatype `Nibble`, which is a tuple of four bits.
873-
874-inductive Bit : Type where
875-  | b1
876-  | b0
877-
878-inductive Nibble : Type where
879-  | bits (x0 x1 x2 x3 : Bit)
880-
881-#check Nibble.bits .b1 .b0 .b1 .b0
882-
883---  Output:
884---    Nibble.bits Bit.b1 Bit.b0 Bit.b1 Bit.b0 : Nibble
885-
886---  The `bits` constructor illustrates a convenience feature of
887---  multi-parameter declarations, both for constructors and for functions:
888---  instead of writing `(x0 : Bit) (x1 : Bit) ...`, we write
889---  `(x0 x1 ... : Bit)` since all of the variables have the same type. We
890---  could have done the same with the function definition `MyBool.or`
891---  above, writing `or (b1 b2 : MyBool)` rather than
892---  `or (b1 : MyBool) (b2 : MyBool)`.
893---
894---  The `bits` constructor acts as a wrapper for its contents. Unwrapping
895---  happens during pattern matching, as in the `allZero` function below,
896---  which tests a `Nibble` to see if all its bits are `b0`.
897-
898-def allZero (nb : Nibble) : Bool :=
899-  match nb with
900-  | .bits .b0 .b0 .b0 .b0 => true
901-  | .bits _   _   _   _   => false
902-
903-example : allZero (.bits .b1 .b0 .b1 .b0) = false := by rfl
904-example : allZero (.bits .b0 .b0 .b0 .b0) = true  := by rfl
905-
906-end Playground
907-
908---  #### Structures
909-
910---  An inductive type with just one constructor can alternatively be
911---  defined as a `structure`, an analog of a record type in other
912---  programming languages.
913-
914-structure NibbleStruct : Type where
915-  x0 : Playground.Bit
916-  x1 : Playground.Bit
917-  x2 : Playground.Bit
918-  x3 : Playground.Bit
919-
920---  Rather than construct an instance of this type as
921---  `.bits .b0 .b0 .b0 .b0`, we write it like this:
922-
923-#check NibbleStruct.mk .b0 .b0 .b0 .b0
924-
925---  Output:
926---    { x0 := Playground.Bit.b0, x1 := Playground.Bit.b0, x2 := Playground.Bit.b0, x3 := Playground.Bit.b0 } : NibbleStruct
927-
928---  The `.mk` constructor is created for us.
929-
930---  A nicer way to build structure values is to assign values to their
931---  fields by name.
932-
933-def zeroNibble : NibbleStruct := {
934-    x0 := .b0
935-    x1 := .b0
936-    x2 := .b0
937-    x3 := .b0
938-  }
939-
940---  Since the result type is declared to be `NibbleStruct`, Lean knows
941---  which structure and fields we mean. Unlike `NibbleStruct.mk`, this
942---  construction syntax doesn't depend on the order of fields.
943---
944---  Besides constructing structures from scratch, we can also "update" an
945---  existing structure — i.e., construct a new structure while reusing some
946---  of the old fields.
947-
948-def setFirstTwoBits (old : NibbleStruct)
949-    (newX0 : Playground.Bit)
950-    (newX1 : Playground.Bit) : NibbleStruct :=
951-  { old with x0 := newX0, x1 := newX1 }
952-
953---  The expression `{ old with ... }` constructs a new `NibbleStruct` whose
954---  `x0` and `x1` have the given values and whose other fields are copied
955---  from `old`. Keep in mind that `old` was not modified — we constructed a
956---  new structure starting from the old one.
957-
958-def makeNibbleStruct (x0 x1 x2 x3 : Playground.Bit) : NibbleStruct :=
959-  { x0, x1, x2, x3 }
960-
961---  When a field and the variable supplying its value have the same name,
962---  Lean lets us write just the name. Thus `{ x0, x1, x2, x3 }` is a
963---  shorthand for `{ x0 := x0, x1 := x1, x2 := x2, x3 := x3 }`. This is
964---  called *field abbreviation*.
965-
966---  ### Natural Numbers
967-
968---  We put this portion of the chapter in a namespace so that our
969---  definition of numbers does not interfere with the one from the standard
970---  library. Our definition matches the standard one, which we will use in
971---  the rest of the book.
972-
973-namespace NatPlayground
974-
975---  All the types we have defined so far — both enumerated types such as
976---  `Day`, `MyBool`, and `Playground.Bit`, and tuple types such as
977---  `Playground.Nibble` built from them — are finite. The natural numbers,
978---  on the other hand, are an infinite set, so we'll need to use a slightly
979---  richer form of inductive type declaration to represent them:
980---  *recursive* inductive types.
981---
982---  While the need for recursion is unequivocal, there are many recursively
983---  defined representations of numbers to choose from. You are certainly
984---  familiar with decimal notation (base 10), using the digits 0 through 9,
985---  for example, to form the number 123. You have likely also encountered
986---  hexadecimal notation (base 16), in which the same number is represented
987---  as 7B, or octal (base 8), where it is 173, or binary (base 2), where it
988---  is 1111011. Using an enumerated type to represent digits, we could use
989---  any of these as our representation of natural numbers.
990---
991---  There are circumstances in which each of these choices is useful. The
992---  binary representation is valuable in computer hardware because the
993---  digits can be represented with just two distinct voltage levels,
994---  resulting in simple circuitry.
995---
996---  Here we choose an even simpler *unary* (base 1) representation, for the
997---  sake of streamlining proofs. As a Lean datatype, it uses two
998---  constructors. The `zero` constructor represents the number zero. The
999---  `succ` constructor can be applied to the representation of the natural
1000---  number `n`, yielding the representation of `n + 1`, where `succ` stands
1001---  for "successor." The number `n` is then represented by `n` applications
1002---  of `succ` to `zero`.
1003---
1004---  Here is the complete datatype definition:
1005-
1006-inductive Nat : Type where
1007-  | zero
1008-  | succ (n : Nat)
1009-
1010---  With a little Lean magic, we can also arrange that ordinary numerals
1011---  such as 0, 1, and 2 will be interpreted as values of our new `Nat` type
1012---  whenever this is sensible in context. The technical details are not
1013---  important.
1014-
1015---  THE FOLLOWING DETAILS CAN BE SKIPPED (Library Nat to SFL Nat coercion)
1016-def ofNat : _root_.Nat → Nat
1017-  | .zero => .zero
1018-  | .succ n => .succ (ofNat n)
1019-
1020-instance (n : _root_.Nat) : OfNat Nat n := ⟨ofNat n⟩
1021-attribute [pp_nodot] Nat.succ
1022---  END DETAILS
1023-
1024---  We'll define some shorthands for numbers, putting them in the `Nat`
1025---  namespace so we don't need to use `.` notation everywhere.
1026-
1027-namespace Nat
1028-
1029-def one   : Nat := succ zero
1030-def two   : Nat := succ one
1031-def three : Nat := succ two
1032-def four  : Nat := succ three
1033-
1034---  We can also write functions on `Nat`.
1035-
1036-def pred (n : Nat) : Nat :=
1037-  match n with
1038-  | zero => zero
1039-  | succ n' => n'
1040-
1041-def minusTwo (n : Nat) : Nat :=
1042-  match n with
1043-  | zero => zero
1044-  | succ (zero) => zero
1045-  | succ (succ n') => n'
1046-
1047-#eval minusTwo four
1048-
1049---  Look at the types of `succ`, `pred`, and `minusTwo`:
1050-
1051-#check (succ)
1052-#check (pred)
1053-#check (minusTwo)
1054-
1055---  Output:
1056---    succ : Nat → Nat
1057-
1058---  Output:
1059---    pred : Nat → Nat
1060-
1061---  Output:
1062---    minusTwo : Nat → Nat
1063-
1064---  These are all things that can be applied to a number to yield a number.
1065---  But there is a difference between `succ` and the other two.
1066-
1067---  Functions like `pred` and `minusTwo` are defined by giving *computation
1068---  rules* — e.g., the definition of `pred` says that
1069---  `pred (succ (succ zero))` can be simplified to `succ zero` — while the
1070---  definition of `succ` has no such behavior attached. Although it is like
1071---  a function in the sense that it can be applied to an argument, it does
1072---  not *do* anything at all! It is just the way we write down numbers.
1073-
1074---  We can also define *recursive functions*: functions that call
1075---  themselves repeatedly down to a base case. Recursion is the essence of
1076---  repeated computation in functional programming; in this course, we will
1077---  make extensive use of recursive functions.
1078---
1079---  We first define a simple recursive function, `even`, then a slightly
1080---  more sophisticated recursive function, `add`.
1081-
1082-def even (n : Nat) : Bool :=
1083-  match n with
1084-  | zero => true
1085-  | succ (zero) => false
1086-  | succ (succ n') => even n'
1087-
1088-example : even one = false := by rfl
1089-example : even four = true := by rfl
1090-
1091---  We could define `odd` by a similar recursive declaration, but here is a
1092---  simpler way:
1093-
1094-def odd (n : Nat) : Bool :=
1095-  not (even n)
1096-
1097-example : odd one = true := by rfl
1098-example : odd four = false := by rfl

1103-  match m with
1104-  | zero => n

1121---  ## Proof by Rewriting
1122-
1123---  ### Proving Properties about Functions in Lean
1124-
1125---  Being recursive on a `Nat` and returning a `Nat` as well, `add` is the
1126---  first example of a more sophisticated class of functions. In this
1127---  chapter and beyond, we will *prove* properties about recursive
1128---  functions like `add` over inductive datatypes like `Nat`, using
1129---  *simplification rules*, also known as *characterizing lemmas*, about
1130---  their behavior.
1131---
1132---  Here is a simplification rule about `add`:
1133---
1134---  - `n + zero = n`
1135---
1136---  In Lean, this rule looks like this:
1137-
1138-theorem add_zero : ∀ n : Nat, n + zero = n := by
1139-  intro n
1140-  rfl
1141-
1142-#check add_zero
1143-
1144---  Output:
1145---    NatPlayground.Nat.add_zero (n : Nat) : n + zero = n
1146-
1147---  Using our simplification rule `add_zero`, we can carry out a simple
1148---  proof about natural numbers.
1149-
1150-theorem add_zero_zero : ∀ n : Nat, n + zero + zero = n := by
1151-  intro n
1152-  rewrite [add_zero]
1153-  rewrite [add_zero]
1154-  rfl
1155-
1156---  We'll walk through this proof in the next section.
1157-
1158---  ### Proof State and Tactics
1159-
1160---  The `rewrite` tactic in the proof of `add_zero_zero` is used to
1161---  transform the goal of the proof according to an equality. The
1162---  `add_zero` in brackets is an *argument* to the `rewrite` tactic.
1163---
1164---  Let's walk through the theorem again in detail.
1165-
1166-theorem add_zero_zero_explained : ∀ n : Nat, n + zero + zero = n := by
1167-  intro n
1168-  /- After introducing `n`, our goal is `n + zero + zero = n`.
1169-     What can we do to simplify this expression? If you hover
1170-     your cursor over the `add_zero` in the rewrite below, you
1171-     can see its type: `n + zero = n`. So, we can use that
1172-     simplification rule to transform an appearance of `n + zero`
1173-     in the goal to `n`. -/
1174-  rewrite [add_zero]
1175-  /- Now click here to see the new proof state that results
1176-     from the tactic. Notice how `n + zero + zero` changes to
1177-     `n + zero` in the goal. -/
1178-  rewrite [add_zero]
1179-  /- Again the goal changes, from `n + zero` to `n`. Now the
1180-     proof state is an equality with both sides equal, so it
1181-     can be closed by the tactic `rfl`. -/
1182-  rfl
1183-  /- The proof is now done! The Lean InfoView tells us there are
1184-     "No goals". -/
1185-
1186---  Give this proof a try (it's similar):
1187-
1188-theorem add_zero_zero_zero : ∀ n : Nat, n + zero + zero + zero = n := by
1189-  intro n
1190-  rewrite [add_zero]
1191-  rewrite [add_zero]
1192-  rewrite [add_zero]
1193-  rfl
1194-
1195---  ### The `rewrite` tactic
1196-
1197---  The `rewrite` tactic tells Lean to rewrite (part of) a goal or
1198---  hypothesis based on a rule (or rules), given in square brackets. For
1199---  example, given the rule `add_zero`, which states that `n + zero` is
1200---  equal to `n` for any `n`, we can replace any `n + zero` in our proof
1201---  with `n` via `rewrite [add_zero]`.
1202-
1203---  ### The `rfl` tactic
1204-
1205---  The `rfl` tactic closes a goal of the shape `a = a`, for any `a`. It
1206---  checks that both sides of the equality are *definitionally equal* —
1207---  that is, that they reduce to the same term. (So, in particular, a term
1208---  is always definitionally equal to itself.)
1209-
1210---  ### A New `add` Rule
1211-
1212---  Here is another fundamental rule about addition:
1213---
1214---  `n + (succ m) = succ (n + m)`.
1215---
1216---  This is the rule we need to push `succ` around.
1217---
1218---  Here it is in Lean:
1219-
1220-theorem add_succ : ∀ n m : Nat, n + (succ m) = succ (n + m) := by
1221-  intro n m
1222-  rfl
1223-
1224---  Now, let's use `add_succ` in a proof:
1225-
1226-theorem add_one (n : Nat) : n + (succ zero) = succ n + zero := by
1227-  rewrite [add_succ]
1228-  rewrite [add_zero]
1229-  rewrite [add_zero]
1230-  rfl
1231-
1232---  We recommend stepping through these proofs in VS Code — that is, moving
1233---  past each tactic with your cursor to see how it changes the proof state
1234---  and hovering over each argument to `rewrite` to see its type.
1235-
1236---  ### Irreducibility, Rewriting, and Proof Engineering
1237-
1238---  Lean, like any other programming language, has conventions and best
1239---  practices for writing good software. Lean takes inspiration from
1240---  object-oriented programming in favoring the use of *encapsulation*. In
1241---  OOP, it is considered poor style to expose the fields of an object in
1242---  its interface; instead, those fields should be accessible only by an
1243---  object's methods (like getters and setters). Doing so hides the
1244---  object's definition, so that, if its fields or implementation ever
1245---  change, the interface it exposes to the outside world remains the same.
1246---  In simple examples, such conventions may seem overly pedantic; in
1247---  complex codebases, they are the only way to maintain crucial invariants
1248---  that prevent a system from becoming unmaintainable.
1249---
1250---  The same principle applies to programs and proofs in Lean. In this
1251---  chapter, we will be proving facts about functions entirely through
1252---  their simplification rules, rather than using `rfl` to unfold their
1253---  implementations invisibly. This makes every computation step visible
1254---  and lets a proof rely on a function's interface rather than its
1255---  definition.
1256---
1257---  We can do this because the foundational theorems `add_zero` and
1258---  `add_succ` provide a characterization of the behavior of `add` that
1259---  makes using `rfl` to simplify expressions unnecessary; instead, we can
1260---  rewrite by these theorems anywhere we want to describe how `add`
1261---  evaluates. In real-world Lean developments, the style of writing proofs
1262---  using simplification rules is both standard and expected.
1263---
1264---  For the next few chapters, we mark definitions with
1265---  `attribute [irreducible]` to prevent this kind of unfolding. This means
1266---  that `rfl` cannot unfold these definitions behind the scenes: after
1267---  rewriting by their simplification rules, it closes only the remaining
1268---  straightforward equality. We use `attribute [irreducible]` for now to
1269---  enforce the style of using simplification rules, so that it is natural
1270---  to you moving forward. We will relax this discipline in later chapters.
1271-
1272-attribute [irreducible] add
1273-
1274---  These simplification rules also follow a particular pattern. Let's look
1275---  again at the definition of `add`, without the `+` notation for maximum
1276---  clarity:
1277-
1278-namespace AddPlayground
1279-
1280-def add (n : Nat) (m : Nat) : Nat :=
1281-  match m with
1282-  | zero => n
1283-  | succ m' => succ (add n m')
1284-
1285-theorem add_zero : ∀ (n : Nat), add n zero = n := by
1286-  intro n
1287-  rfl
1288-
1289-theorem add_succ : ∀ (n m : Nat), add n (succ m) = succ (add n m) := by
1290-  intro n m
1291-  rfl
1292-
1293-end AddPlayground
1294-
1295---  Each of `add_zero` and `add_succ` corresponds to one branch of the
1296---  `match` statement defining `add` and describes how the evaluation of
1297---  `add` proceeds in that case. The `add_zero` theorem describes how
1298---  `add n zero` evaluates, while `add_succ` describes (symbolically) how
1299---  `add n (succ m)` evaluates.
1300---
1301---  These are instances of a general pattern: for each definition that
1302---  pattern matches on an inductive type, we will provide one
1303---  simplification rule for each branch of control flow through the
1304---  function.
1305---
1306---  So, for example, we need two simplification rules for the definition of
1307---  `pred`:
1308-
1309-theorem pred_zero : pred zero = zero := by rfl
1310-theorem pred_succ (n : Nat) : pred (succ n) = n := by rfl
1311-
1312---  Now that we have defined and proved `pred`'s simplification rules, we
1313---  can mark it `irreducible` to enforce rewriting by these lemmas.
1314-
1315-attribute [irreducible] pred
1316-
1317---  Similarly, for each of the three branches of the definition of `even`,
1318---  we need one simplification rule:
1319-
1320-theorem even_zero : even zero = true := rfl
1321-theorem even_one : even (succ zero) = false := rfl
1322-theorem even_succ_succ (n : Nat) : even (succ (succ n)) = even n := rfl
1323-
1324-attribute [irreducible] even odd
1325-
1326---  In the remainder of this textbook, we will pair definitions with
1327---  simplification rules. After proving these rules, instead of using `rfl`
1328---  to peek through the definitions, we will `rewrite` using the rules.
1329---
1330---  Eventually, we will introduce a way to *automatically* apply these
1331---  simplification rules. Real-world Lean developments use automation
1332---  extensively, and you will learn to do so gradually throughout this
1333---  book. For the moment, it is important that you work through these early
1334---  concepts by hand, without automation. By the time the more powerful
1335---  tools are introduced, you will have the foundational understanding to
1336---  use them with precision and skill.
1337-
1338---  ### Working with Numerals
1339-
1340---  We know from our definitions above that `one` is just `succ zero`,
1341---  `two` is `succ one`, and so on. We can write rules for these equalities
1342---  too:
1343-
1344-theorem one_eq_succ_zero : one = succ zero := by rfl
1345-theorem two_eq_succ_one : two = succ one := by rfl
1346-theorem three_eq_succ_two : three = succ two := by rfl
1347-theorem four_eq_succ_three : four = succ three := by rfl
1348-
1349---  We can rewrite with these rules to expand numerals into their
1350---  definitions, which allows us to use our `add` rules. Here's an example
1351---  of how to start a proof this way.
1352-
1353---  ### Exercise (1 star): nat_eq_rules ⭐
1354-
1355---  Finish the proof using the `add` rules:
1356-
1357-theorem one_plus_one_eq_two : one + one = two := by
1358-  rewrite [one_eq_succ_zero]
1359-  sorry
1360-
1361---  Try the same for `two + two = four`.
1362-
1363-theorem two_plus_two_eq_four : two + two = four := by
1364-  sorry

1366---  #### Multiplication
1367-
1368---  Now that we know how addition is defined, we can use it to define
1369---  multiplication:
1370-
1371-def mul (n m : Nat) : Nat :=
1372-  match m with
1373-  | zero => zero
1374-  | succ m' => (mul n m') + n
1375-
1376-scoped infixl:70 " * " => mul
1377-

1382---

1386-
1387-theorem mul_zero : ∀ n : Nat, n * zero = zero := by
1388-  sorry

1398-  rewrite [one_eq_succ_zero]

1400-  rfl
1401-

1403---  with all of the simplification rules at once, for example.
1404---

1406---  immediately after a rule to see how the goal is changing. This happens

1408---  `rewrite` blocks with multiple rules.

1428---  #### Equality and Ordering
1429-
1430---  When we say that Lean relies on almost nothing that's truly built-in,
1431---  we really mean it: even testing equality is not a primitive operation,
1432---  but an ordinary function that we could reimplement ourselves as users.
1433-
1434---  Here is a function `beq` that tests natural numbers for equality,
1435---  yielding a boolean.
1436-
1437-def beq (n m : Nat) : Bool :=
1438-  match n with
1439-  | zero => match m with
1440-            | zero => true
1441-            | succ _ => false
1442-  | succ n' => match m with
1443-               | zero => false
1444-               | succ m' => beq n' m'
1445-
1446---  We could also write this by pattern matching on both `n` and `m` at the
1447---  same time:
1448-
1449-def beq' (n m : Nat) : Bool :=
1450-  match n, m with
1451-  | zero, zero => true
1452-  | zero, succ _ => false
1453-  | succ _, zero => false
1454-  | succ n', succ m' => beq n' m'
1455-
1456---  The definitions of `beq` and `beq'` are equivalent.
1457---
1458---  Similarly, the `ble` function tests whether its first argument is less
1459---  than or equal to its second argument, yielding a boolean.
1460-
1461-def ble (n m : Nat) : Bool :=
1462-  match n with
1463-  | zero => true
1464-  | succ n' =>
1465-      match m with
1466-      | zero => false
1467-      | succ m' => ble n' m'
1468-
1469-theorem zero_ble (n : Nat) : ble zero n = true := by rfl
1470-theorem succ_ble_zero (n : Nat) : ble (succ n) zero = false := by rfl
1471-theorem succ_ble_succ (n m : Nat) : ble (succ n) (succ m) = ble n m := by rfl
1472-
1473-example : ble two two = true  := by rfl
1474-example : ble two four = true := by rfl
1475-example : ble four two = false := by rfl
1476-

1478-

1480-

1482-

1484-example : blt two four = true  := sorry
1485-theorem blt_test3 : blt four two = false := sorry
1486-
1487-attribute [irreducible] blt ble
1488-
1489---  We'll be using `beq` a lot, so let's give it an infix notation.
1490-
1491-scoped infixl:30 " == " => beq
1492-
1493---  We now have seen two symbols that both look like equality: `=` and
1494---  `==`. We'll have much more to say about their differences and
1495---  similarities later. For now, notice that `x = y` is a logical *claim* —
1496---  a "proposition" — that we can try to prove, while `x == y` is a boolean
1497---  *expression* whose value (either `true` or `false`) Lean can compute.
1498-
1499---  We can also now define the simplification rules for `beq` with our new
1500---  notation, one for each of the four cases of control flow through the
1501---  function.
1502-
1503-theorem zero_beq_zero : (zero == zero) = true := by rfl
1504-theorem zero_beq_succ (n : Nat) : (zero == (succ n)) = false := by rfl
1505-theorem succ_beq_zero (n : Nat) : ((succ n) == zero) = false := by rfl
1506-theorem succ_beq_succ (n m : Nat) : ((succ n) == (succ m)) = (n == m) := by rfl
1507-
1508-attribute [irreducible] beq
1509-
1510---  Aside: Our naming convention for simplification rules encodes their
1511---  meaning. For `add_zero` and `add_succ`, notice that the `zero` and
1512---  `succ` come after the `add`; this is because they depend on `add`'s
1513---  *second* argument and do not care about its first.
1514---
1515---  Also, in the `beq` rules above, we write `zero_beq_zero` and
1516---  `zero_beq_succ` because the rules apply to both the first and second
1517---  arguments of `beq`. We put `beq` between the arguments because it is
1518---  usually written in infix notation. There are no strict style
1519---  conventions for naming theorems like this in Lean, but many developers
1520---  follow this approach.
1521-
1522---  ### General Proofs about Natural Numbers
1523-
1524---  We now begin to make claims about *general* natural numbers.
1525---
1526---  We begin by making a universal claim about all numbers `n` and `m` that
1527---  are equal to each other (`n = m`). The arrow symbol is pronounced
1528---  "implies." Enter it with `\to` or `\->` or `\r`.
1529---
1530---  The `intro` tactic moves the universally quantified variables and the
1531---  hypothesis into the context, giving them names. The goal is now to
1532---  prove `n + n = m + m` under the assumption `h : n = m`.
1533---
1534---  The tactic that tells Lean to perform replacement is one we have seen
1535---  before: `rewrite`. It can take a hypothesis from the context as an
1536---  argument, just like it can take a previously proved theorem. In this
1537---  case, we want to rewrite with the hypothesis `h`, which says that `n`
1538---  and `m` are equal, so that we can replace `n` with `m` in the goal.
1539---
1540---  After the rewrite, the goal is `m + m = m + m`, which can be closed by
1541---  `rfl`.
1542-
1543-theorem add_id_example : ∀ n m : Nat,
1544-    n = m → n + n = m + m := by
1545-  intro n m
1546-  intro h
1547-  rewrite [h]
1548-  rfl
1549-
1550---  ### Exercise (1 star): add_id_exercise ⭐
1551-
1552---  Remove `sorry` and fill in the proof.
1553-
1554-theorem add_id_exercise : ∀ n m o : Nat,
1555-    n = m → m = o → n + m = m + o := by
1556-  sorry
1557-
1558---  #### Displaying Theorem Statements
1559-
1560---  The `#check` command can also be used to examine the statements of
1561---  previously declared lemmas and theorems.
1562-
1563-#check mul_zero
1564-#check mul_succ
1565-
1566---  Output:
1567---    NatPlayground.Nat.mul_zero (n : Nat) : n * zero = zero
1568-
1569---  Output:
1570---    NatPlayground.Nat.mul_succ (n m : Nat) : n * succ m = n * m + n
1571-
1572---  Note that you may see a slight discrepancy in the output: `#check`
1573---  shows the theorem differently from the way it was introduced earlier.
1574---
1575---  First, Lean may print the theorem's fully qualified name
1576---  `NatPlayground.Nat.mul_zero`. The qualification identifies the
1577---  namespace containing the theorem, though the shorter name `mul_zero` is
1578---  usually sufficient when Lean can determine which declaration we mean.
1579---
1580---  Second, Lean displays the theorem's arguments before the colon, as in
1581---  `mul_zero (n : Nat) : n * zero = zero`. Writing arguments as binders
1582---  before the colon is called *declaration-header style*. The same
1583---  statement can be written using an explicit universal quantifier, as we
1584---  have seen before:
1585---
1586---      mul_zero : ∀ (n : Nat), n * zero = zero
1587---
1588---  Writing statements in declaration-header style shortens proofs because
1589---  Lean automatically adds declared variables to the context, rather than
1590---  requiring them to be added with `intro`. The declaration-header style
1591---  is conventional in Lean, and we will generally use it from now on.
1592-
1593---  ## Proof by Case Analysis
1594-
1595---  Of course, not everything can be proved by simple calculation and
1596---  rewriting: in general, the presence of unknown, hypothetical values
1597---  (arbitrary numbers, booleans, etc.) can block a proof.
1598-
1599-sf_expect_failure_in
1600-  example (n : Nat) : (succ zero + n == zero) = false := by
1601-    /-
1602-      We can't rewrite by any lemmas here: `add`'s definition matches on its
1603-      *second* argument, and here that argument is the unknown `n`!
1604-    -/
1605-
1606---  The tactic that tells Lean to consider separate cases is called
1607---  `cases`.
1608-
1609-theorem add_one_neb_zero (n : Nat) : (succ zero + n == zero) = false := by
1610-  cases n with
1611-  | zero =>
1612-    rewrite [add_zero, succ_beq_zero]
1613-    rfl
1614-  | succ n' =>
1615-    rewrite [add_succ, succ_beq_zero]
1616-    rfl
1617-
1618---  The `cases` tactic generates *two* subgoals, which we must prove
1619---  separately in order to get Lean to accept the theorem. The generated
1620---  subgoals are tagged by the names of the constructors. `| zero =>` and
1621---  `| succ n' =>` select which subgoal to work on next and introduce
1622---  variable names. Note also that when we enter a subcase, we increase the
1623---  level of indentation at which we are working by two spaces.
1624---
1625---  The `cases` tactic can be used with any inductively defined datatype.
1626---  For example, we use it next to prove that boolean negation is
1627---  involutive (that is, that negation is its own inverse).
1628-
1629-theorem not_involutive (b : Bool) : (!!b) = b := by
1630-  cases b with
1631-  | false =>
1632-    rewrite [Bool.not_false, Bool.not_true]
1633-    rfl
1634-  | true =>
1635-    rewrite [Bool.not_true, Bool.not_false]
1636-    rfl
1637-
1638---  The proof above uses some simplification rules that we didn't prove
1639---  previously. These come from Lean's standard library, in particular from
1640---  the section about booleans. In the UsingLean chapter we will discuss
1641---  how to search through the standard library for theorems like these. For
1642---  now, note that, if you hover over the names of these theorems in VS
1643---  Code, the Lean extension will show you what the theorem proves.
1644-
1645---  We can also have nested case analysis:
1646-
1647-theorem and_commutative (b c : Bool) :
1648-    (b && c) = (c && b) := by
1649-  cases b with
1650-  | true =>
1651-    cases c with
1652-    | true =>
1653-      rewrite [Bool.and_self]
1654-      rfl
1655-    | false =>
1656-      rewrite [Bool.and_false, Bool.and_true]
1657-      rfl
1658-  | false =>
1659-    cases c with
1660-    | true =>
1661-      rewrite [Bool.and_true, Bool.and_false]
1662-      rfl
1663-    | false =>
1664-      rewrite [Bool.and_self]
1665-      rfl
1666-
1667-theorem and3_exchange (b c d : Bool) :

1707---  As you can see, proofs by cases can become very verbose. We will
1708---  introduce some tactics for writing shorter proofs by case analysis in
1709---  the Tactics chapter.
1710-
1711---  ### New Tactics: `rewrite ... at` and `exact`
1712-
1713---  Some new tactics will be useful for the exercises ahead.
1714---
1715---  The `rewrite ... at` tactic can be used to rewrite in a hypothesis
1716---  instead of the goal. For example, if `hp : p` is in the context and we
1717---  have a rule `r : p = q`, then `rewrite [r] at hp` changes the
1718---  hypothesis to `hp : q`.
1719---
1720---  The `exact` tactic closes a goal by providing the exact proof of the
1721---  goal. For example, if `hp : p` is in the context and the goal is `p`,
1722---  then `exact hp` closes the goal. You can also transform `hp` slightly
1723---  when using `exact`, and we will explain how when we get to an example
1724---  that needs it.
1725-
1726---  ### Exercise (2 stars): or_false_true ⭐⭐
1727-
1728---  Prove the following claim.
1729---
1730---  Tip: the simplification rule for `(b || false)` is called
1731---  `Bool.or_false`.
1732-
1733-theorem or_false_true (b : Bool) (h : (b || false) = true) :
1734-  b = true := by
1735-  sorry
1736-
1737---  ### Exercise (1 star): zero_neb_add_one ⭐
1738-
1739-theorem zero_neb_add_one (n : Nat) :
1740-  (zero == (succ zero + n)) = false := by
1741-  sorry
1742-
1743---  ### Structural Recursion (Optional)
1744-
1745---  Here is a copy of the definition of `even`:
1746-
1747-def even' (n : Nat) : Bool :=
1748-  match n with
1749-  | zero => true
1750-  | succ (zero) => false
1751-  | succ (succ n') => even' n'
1752-
1753---  When Lean checks this definition, it verifies that the recursion
1754---  terminates. Specifically, it checks that the recursive argument is
1755---  *structurally decreasing* — each recursive call made in the body of the
1756---  definition is made on an argument that is smaller than the original
1757---  input. In the `even'` example above, the argument to the recursive call
1758---  to `even'` is the variable `n'`. Because of our pattern match, we know
1759---  that `n` is equal to `succ (succ n')`, and therefore that `n'` is
1760---  smaller than `n`. This makes `n'` an acceptable argument to `even'` for
1761---  Lean's termination checker, and so this recursive definition is
1762---  accepted.
1763---
1764---  This requirement is a fundamental feature of Lean's design: it
1765---  guarantees that every ordinary recursive definition accepted into
1766---  Lean's logic terminates on all inputs. However, because Lean's
1767---  termination analysis is not always able to figure things out
1768---  automatically, it is sometimes necessary to provide hints or write
1769---  functions in slightly different ways.
1770-
1771---  ### Exercise (2 stars): decreasing (Optional, Manually graded) ⭐⭐
1772-
1773---  To get a concrete sense of how termination checking works in Lean, find
1774---  a way to write a sensible recursive definition (of a simple function on
1775---  numbers, say) that does actually terminate on all inputs, but that Lean
1776---  will reject because it cannot automatically prove termination.
1777-
1778---  ### Binary Numerals
1779-
1780---  ### Exercise (3 stars): binary ⭐⭐⭐
1781-
1782---  We can generalize our unary representation of natural numbers to the
1783---  more efficient binary representation by treating a binary number as a
1784---  sequence of constructors `b0` and `b1` (representing 0s and 1s),
1785---  terminated by a `z`.
1786---
1787---  For example:
1788-
1789---  decimal                binary   unary
1790---        0                     z   zero
1791---        1                  b1 z   succ zero
1792---        2             b0 (b1 z)   succ (succ zero)
1793---        3             b1 (b1 z)   succ (succ (succ zero))
1794---        4        b0 (b0 (b1 z))   succ (succ (succ (succ zero)))
1795---        5        b1 (b0 (b1 z))   succ (succ (succ (succ (succ zero))))
1796---        6        b0 (b1 (b1 z))   succ (succ (succ (succ (succ (succ zero)))))
1797---        7        b1 (b1 (b1 z))   succ (succ (succ (succ (succ (succ (succ zero))))))
1798---        8   b0 (b0 (b0 (b1 z)))   succ (succ (succ (succ (succ (succ (succ (succ zero)))))))
1799-
1800---  Note that the low-order bit is on the left and the high-order bit is on
1801---  the right — the opposite of the way binary numbers are usually written.
1802---  This choice makes them easier to manipulate.
1803---
1804---  (Comprehension check: What unary numeral does `b0 z` represent?)
1805-
1806-inductive Bin : Type where
1807-  | z
1808-  | b0 (n : Bin)
1809-  | b1 (n : Bin)
1810-
1811---  THE FOLLOWING DETAILS CAN BE SKIPPED
1812-attribute [pp_nodot] Bin.b1 Bin.b0
1813---  END DETAILS

1816-  := sorry
1817-
1818-def binToNat (m : Bin) : Nat
1819-  := sorry

1822-theorem incr_test2 : incr (.b0 (.b1 .z)) = .b1 (.b1 .z) := sorry
1823-theorem incr_test3 : incr (.b1 (.b1 .z)) = .b0 (.b0 (.b1 .z)) := sorry
1824-
1825-theorem incr_z : incr .z = .b1 .z := sorry
