1879---  ### Airport Exercise
1880-
1881---  Now that we have learned some basic features of Lean, let's close the
1882---  chapter with an exercise that brings them together.
1883---
1884---  In this exercise, we will model part of a database storing information
1885---  about travelers passing through an airport. The database contains one
1886---  entry per traveler, recording information about where the traveler is
1887---  in the airport process and the contents of their current carry-on bag.
1888---
1889---  We will implement several operations on these entries, state intended
1890---  properties of the database's behavior, and prove that the
1891---  implementation satisfies them.
1892-
1893-namespace Airport
1894-
1895---  For simplicity, a carry-on bag either contains a prohibited item, such
1896---  as a liquid that exceeds the allowed limit, causing it to fail
1897---  inspection, or contains only ordinary items.
1898-
1899-inductive BagContent : Type where
1900-  | prohibited
1901-  | ordinary
1902-
1903---  After a traveler checks in, the database also records the result of the
1904---  most recent security screening of their carry-on bag.
1905-
1906-inductive ScreeningStatus : Type where
1907-  | notScreened
1908-  | cleared
1909-  | blocked
1910-
1911---  Next, we define the possible stages of the airport process a traveler
1912---  can inhabit:
1913---
1914---  - they have not yet purchased a ticket;
1915---
1916---  - they have a ticket but have not yet checked in;
1917---
1918---  - they have checked in, in which case the database also stores the
1919---    screening status of their carry-on bag.
1920---
1921---  We can represent these possible database entries directly with an
1922---  inductive type.
1923-
1924-inductive Traveler : Type where
1925-  | noTicket  (bagContent : BagContent)
1926-  | ticketed  (bagContent : BagContent)
1927-  | checkedIn (bagContent : BagContent) (screeningStatus : ScreeningStatus)
1928-
1929---  Buying a ticket changes a traveler with no ticket into a ticketed
1930---  traveler. If the traveler already has a ticket or has already checked
1931---  in, nothing changes.
1932-
1933---  ### Exercise (1 star): buyTicket ⭐
1934-
1935-def buyTicket (t : Traveler) : Traveler := sorry
1936-theorem buyTicket_test1 : buyTicket (.noTicket .ordinary) = .ticketed .ordinary := sorry
1937-theorem buyTicket_test2 : buyTicket (.checkedIn .prohibited .blocked) = .checkedIn .prohibited .blocked := sorry
1938-
1939---  Here are the simplification rules for `buyTicket`:
1940-
1941-theorem buyTicket_noTicket (bagContent : BagContent) :
1942-    buyTicket (.noTicket bagContent) = .ticketed bagContent := sorry
1943-
1944-theorem buyTicket_ticketed (bagContent : BagContent) :
1945-    buyTicket (.ticketed bagContent) = .ticketed bagContent := sorry
1946-
1947-theorem buyTicket_checkedIn (bagContent : BagContent)
1948-    (screeningStatus : ScreeningStatus) :
1949-    buyTicket (.checkedIn bagContent screeningStatus) = .checkedIn bagContent screeningStatus := sorry
1950-
1951-attribute [irreducible] buyTicket
1952-
1953---  The first property we will prove about our system is that purchasing a
1954---  ticket is an *idempotent* operation (i.e., performing it twice has the
1955---  same effect as performing it once).
1956-
1957---  ### Exercise (2 stars): buyTicket_idempotent ⭐⭐
1958-
1959-theorem buyTicket_idempotent (t : Traveler) :
1960-    buyTicket (buyTicket t) = buyTicket t := by
1961-  sorry
1962-
1963---  A traveler can check in only after buying a ticket. Checking in records
1964---  that their carry-on bag still needs to be inspected. Calling `checkIn`
1965---  before buying a ticket or after already checking in does nothing.
1966-
1967---  ### Exercise (1 star): checkIn ⭐
1968-
1969-def checkIn (t : Traveler) : Traveler := sorry
1970-
1971-theorem checkIn_test1 : checkIn (.noTicket .ordinary) = .noTicket .ordinary := sorry
1972-theorem checkIn_test2 : checkIn (.ticketed .prohibited) = .checkedIn .prohibited .notScreened := sorry
1973-theorem checkIn_test3 : checkIn (.checkedIn .ordinary .cleared) = .checkedIn .ordinary .cleared := sorry
1974-
1975---  Again, we record one simplification rule for each case:
1976-
1977-theorem checkIn_noTicket (bagContent : BagContent) :
1978-    checkIn (.noTicket bagContent) = .noTicket bagContent := sorry
1979-
1980-theorem checkIn_ticketed (bagContent : BagContent) :
1981-    checkIn (.ticketed bagContent) = .checkedIn bagContent .notScreened := sorry
1982-
1983-theorem checkIn_checkedIn (bagContent : BagContent)
1984-    (screeningStatus : ScreeningStatus) :
1985-    checkIn (.checkedIn bagContent screeningStatus) = .checkedIn bagContent screeningStatus := sorry
1986-
1987-attribute [irreducible] checkIn
1988-
1989---  A traveler who does not yet have a ticket can buy one and then check
1990---  in. After this, the traveler is checked in and their carry-on bag needs
1991---  to be screened.
1992-
1993---  ### Exercise (1 star): buyTicket_then_checkIn ⭐
1994-
1995-theorem buyTicket_then_checkIn (bagContent : BagContent) :
1996-    checkIn (buyTicket (.noTicket bagContent)) = .checkedIn bagContent .notScreened := by
1997-  sorry
1998-
1999---  Carry-on inspection happens only after check-in. A bag containing only
2000---  ordinary items is cleared, while a bag containing a prohibited item is
2001---  blocked. If the traveler has not checked in, `inspectBag` does nothing.
2002-
2003---  ### Exercise (1 star): inspectBag ⭐
2004-
2005---  Define `inspectBag`.
2006-
2007-def inspectBag (t : Traveler) : Traveler := sorry
2008-
2009-theorem inspectBag_test1 : inspectBag (.ticketed .prohibited) = .ticketed .prohibited := sorry
2010-theorem inspectBag_test2 : inspectBag (.checkedIn .ordinary .notScreened) = .checkedIn .ordinary .cleared := sorry
2011-theorem inspectBag_test3 : inspectBag (.checkedIn .prohibited .notScreened) = .checkedIn .prohibited .blocked := sorry
2012-
2013---  Again, we record one characterization lemma for each case.
2014-
2015-theorem inspectBag_noTicket (bagContent : BagContent) :
2016-    inspectBag (.noTicket bagContent) = .noTicket bagContent := sorry
2017-
2018-theorem inspectBag_ticketed (bagContent : BagContent) :
2019-    inspectBag (.ticketed bagContent) = .ticketed bagContent := sorry
2020-
2021-theorem inspectBag_ordinary (screeningStatus : ScreeningStatus) :
2022-    inspectBag (.checkedIn .ordinary screeningStatus) = .checkedIn .ordinary .cleared := sorry
2023-
2024-theorem inspectBag_prohibited (screeningStatus : ScreeningStatus) :
2025-    inspectBag (.checkedIn .prohibited screeningStatus) = .checkedIn .prohibited .blocked := sorry
2026-
2027-attribute [irreducible] inspectBag
2028-
2029---  ### Exercise (2 stars): inspectBag_idempotent ⭐⭐
2030-
2031---  Show that inspecting the same unchanged carry-on bag twice has the same
2032---  effect as inspecting it once.
2033-
2034-theorem inspectBag_idempotent (t : Traveler) : inspectBag (inspectBag t) = inspectBag t := by
2035-  sorry
2036-
2037---  A traveler may leave the screened area and return with a different
2038---  carry-on bag. Since the previous screening result applied to the old
2039---  bag, a new carry-on must be screened again before the traveler can
2040---  re-enter.
2041-
2042---  ### Exercise (1 star): changeBag ⭐
2043-
2044---  Define `changeBag`.
2045-
2046-def changeBag (newContent : BagContent) (t : Traveler) : Traveler := sorry
2047-
2048-theorem changeBag_test1 : changeBag .prohibited (.ticketed .ordinary) = .ticketed .prohibited := sorry
2049-theorem changeBag_test2 : changeBag .prohibited (.checkedIn .ordinary .cleared) = .checkedIn .prohibited .notScreened := sorry
2050-
2051---  As before, we record one simplification rule for each case.
2052-
2053-theorem changeBag_noTicket (newContent oldContent : BagContent) :
2054-    changeBag newContent (.noTicket oldContent) = .noTicket newContent := sorry
2055-
2056-theorem changeBag_ticketed (newContent oldContent : BagContent) :
2057-    changeBag newContent (.ticketed oldContent) = .ticketed newContent := sorry
2058-
2059-theorem changeBag_checkedIn (newContent oldContent : BagContent)
2060-    (screeningStatus : ScreeningStatus) :
2061-    changeBag newContent (.checkedIn oldContent screeningStatus) =
2062-    .checkedIn newContent .notScreened := sorry
2063-
2064-attribute [irreducible] changeBag
2065-
2066---  It is easy to see that replacing a bag after it has been inspected
2067---  resets its screening status. In other words, `inspectBag` and
2068---  `changeBag` do not, in general, commute: the order in which the two
2069---  operations are performed can affect the result.
2070---
2071---  However, if the traveler has not checked in, `inspectBag` does nothing,
2072---  so changing and inspecting the carry-on can be performed in either
2073---  order. There are two such cases: the traveler may not yet have a
2074---  ticket, or may have a ticket but not yet be checked in.
2075-
2076---  ### Exercise (2 stars): inspectBag_changeBag_comm ⭐⭐
2077-
2078-theorem inspectBag_changeBag_comm_noTicket
2079-    (oldContent newContent : BagContent) :
2080-    inspectBag (changeBag newContent (.noTicket oldContent)) =
2081-    changeBag newContent (inspectBag (.noTicket oldContent)) := by
2082-  sorry
2083-
2084-theorem inspectBag_changeBag_comm_ticketed
2085-    (oldContent newContent : BagContent) :
2086-    inspectBag (changeBag newContent (.ticketed oldContent)) =
2087-    changeBag newContent (inspectBag (.ticketed oldContent)) := by
2088-  sorry
2089-
2090-end Airport
2091-end NatPlayground

10-namespace Lean.Parser

13-/-- Internal syntactic representation of a single inversion alternative. -/
14-declare_syntax_cat invAlt
15-syntax " | " caseArg " => " tacticSeq : invAlt
16-
17-/-- An inversion alternative matching one or more goal tags,
18-  expanding to multiple single [invAlt]s. -/
19-declare_syntax_cat invAlts
20-syntax (" | " caseArg)+ " => " tacticSeq : invAlts
21-
22-/--
23-  `inversion h` behaves like `cases h` except that where `cases` would fail with
24-  > "Dependent elimination failed: Failed to solve equation ...",
25-
26-  `inversion` instead leaves behind those unsolveable equations in the context.
27-  These equations arise from generalizing the indices of `h`'s type.
28-  In such cases, `h` itself is generalized with a heterogenenous equality `heq`
29-  to the corresponding constructor in each branch.
30-
31-  For instance, given a hypothesis `h : f n ≤ 0`,
32-  `inversion h` will produce one goal for the case `Nat.le.refl {n} : n ≤ n`
33-  with the equations `eq : f n = 0` and `heq : h ≍ Nat.le.refl`,
34-  rather than failing to solve `f n = 0`.
35-
36-  * If `inversion +clear h` is set, then `heq` will be `clear`ed from the context if present,
37-    along with `h` if there are no dependencies on it.
38-    This is the usual behavior of `cases`.
39-  * The form `inversion t with (tac ...) | tag₁ x ... => tac ... | ... | tagₙ z ... => tac ...`
40-    is supported, similar to that of `cases` and `induction`.
41--/
42-syntax (name := inversion)
43-  "inversion " optConfig ident (" with " (tacticSeq)? (colGe invAlts)*)? : tactic
44-
45-end Lean.Parser
46-
47-namespace Lean.Meta
48-
49-/-- Get the user-facing name for the given metavariable. -/
50-def _root_.Lean.MVarId.getUserName (mvarId : MVarId) : MetaM Name := do
51-  let decl ← mvarId.getDecl
52-  return decl.userName
53-
54-/-- Get the string suffix of a name as a name -/
55-def _root_.Lean.Name.getSuffix : Name → Name
56-| .anonymous => .anonymous
57-| .str _ s => .str .anonymous s
58-| .num n _ => n.getSuffix
59-
60-/--
61-  This function is similar to `forallMetaTelescopeReducing`: Given `e` of the
62-  form `forall ..xs, A`, this combinator will create a new metavariable for
63-  each `x` in `xs` until it reaches an `x` whose type is defeq to `t`,
64-  and instantiate `A` with these, while also reducing `A` if needed.
65-  It uses `forallMetaTelescopeReducing`.
66-
67-  This function returns a triple `(mvs, bis, out)` where
68-  - `mvs` is an array containing the new metavariables.
69-  - `bis` is an array containing the binder infos for the `mvs`.
70-  - `out` is `e` but instantiated with the `mvs`.
71-
72-  Lifted from [https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/master/Mathlib/Lean/Meta/Basic.lean#L41].
73--/
74-def forallMetaTelescopeReducingUntilDefEq
75-    (e t : Expr) (kind : MetavarKind := MetavarKind.natural) :
76-    MetaM (Array Expr × Array BinderInfo × Expr) := do
77-  let (ms, bs, tp) ← forallMetaTelescopeReducing e (some 1) kind
78-  unless ms.size == 1 do
79-    if ms.size == 0 then throwError m!"Failed: {← ppExpr e} is not the type of a function."
80-    else throwError m!"Failed"
81-  let mut mvs := ms
82-  let mut bis := bs
83-  let mut out : Expr := tp
84-  while !(← isDefEq (← inferType mvs.toList.getLast!) t) do
85-    let (ms, bs, tp) ← forallMetaTelescopeReducing out (some 1) kind
86-    unless ms.size == 1 do
87-      throwError m!"Failed to find {← ppExpr t} as the type of a parameter of {← ppExpr e}."
88-    mvs := mvs ++ ms
89-    bis := bis ++ bs
90-    out := tp
91-  return (mvs, bis, out)
92-
93-/-- Given equations `eqs` in the local context of `mvarId`,
94-  unify them using [Lean.Meta.unifyEq?],
95-  but if unification fails, leave the equation in the context.
96-  This means we should never get a "Dependent elimination failed" error.
97-  While marked partial, this _should_ always terminate,
98-  decreasing on the sum of the sizes of the terms of each equation.
99-
100-  Lifted from [Lean.Meta.Cases.unifyEqs]. -/
101-partial def unifyEqs (eqs : List FVarId) (mvarId : MVarId) (subst : FVarSubst) (caseName? : Option Name) : MetaM (MVarId × FVarSubst) := withIncRecDepth do
102-  match eqs with
103-  | [] => return (mvarId, subst)
104-  | eq :: eqs =>
105-    let some { mvarId, subst, numNewEqs } ← Option.join <$> (observing? $ unifyEq? mvarId eq subst MVarId.acyclic caseName?)
106-      | unifyEqs eqs mvarId subst caseName?
107-    let (newEqs, mvarId) ← mvarId.introN numNewEqs
108-    let eqs := eqs.map (Expr.fvarId! ∘ subst.get)
109-    unifyEqs (newEqs.toList ++ eqs) mvarId subst caseName?
110-
111-/-- Lifted from [Lean.Meta.Cases.unifyCasesEqs]. -/
112-def unifyCasesEqs (eqs : List FVarId) (subgoals : Array CasesSubgoal) : MetaM (Array CasesSubgoal) :=
113-  subgoals.filterMapM fun s => do
114-    let eqs := eqs.filterMap (Expr.fvarId? ∘ s.subst.get)
115-    let (mvarId, subst) ← unifyEqs eqs s.mvarId s.subst s.ctorName
116-    if (← mvarId.isAssignedOrDelayedAssigned) then return none
117-    else return some { s with
118-      mvarId := mvarId,
119-      subst  := subst,
120-      fields := s.fields.map (subst.apply ·)
121-    }
122-
123-/-- Try to clear the given fvars from the local context of each subgoal,
124-  using the subgoals' substitution mappings to find the fvars.
125-
126-  As with [MVarId.tryClearMany], the fvars must be in the order they appear in the context.  -/
127-def casesClearMany (subgoals : Array CasesSubgoal) (fvarIds : Array FVarId) : MetaM (Array CasesSubgoal) :=
128-  subgoals.mapM fun s => do
129-    let fvarIds := fvarIds.filterMap (Expr.fvarId? ∘ s.subst.get)
130-    let mvarId ← s.mvarId.tryClearMany fvarIds
131-    return { s with mvarId }
132-
133-end Lean.Meta

135-namespace Lean.Elab.Tactic
136-open Meta Term
137-
138--- [https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/master/Mathlib/Tactic/Lemma.lean]
139--- [https://github.com/leanprover-community/batteries/blob/main/Batteries/Tactic/Lemma.lean]
140-/-- Synonym for `theorem`. -/
141-macro "lemma " thm:declId sig:declSig val:declVal : command => `(theorem $thm $sig $val)
142-
143-/--
144-  `apply t at i` uses forward reasoning with `t` at the hypothesis `i`.
145-  Explicitly, if `t : α₁ → ⋯ → αᵢ → ⋯ → αₙ` and `i` has type `αᵢ`, then this tactic adds
146-  metavariables/goals for any terms of `αⱼ` for `j = 1, …, i-1`,
147-  then replaces the type of `i` with `αᵢ₊₁ → ⋯ → αₙ` by applying those metavariables and the
148-  original `i`.
149-
150-  Lifted from [https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/master/Mathlib/Tactic/ApplyAt.lean].
151--/
152-elab "apply " t:term " at " i:ident : tactic => withSynthesize <| withMainContext do
153-  let f ← elabTermForApply t
154-  let some ldecl := (← getLCtx).findFromUserName? i.getId
155-    | throwErrorAt i m!"Identifier {i} not found"
156-  let (mvs, bis, _) ← forallMetaTelescopeReducingUntilDefEq (← inferType f) ldecl.type
157-  for (m, b) in mvs.zip bis do
158-    if b.isInstImplicit && !(← m.mvarId!.isAssigned) then
159-      try m.mvarId!.inferInstance
160-      catch _ => continue
161-  let (_, mainGoal) ← (← getMainGoal).note ldecl.userName
162-    (← mkAppOptM' f (mvs.pop.push ldecl.toExpr |>.map some))
163-  let mainGoal ← mainGoal.tryClear ldecl.fvarId
164-  replaceMainGoal <| [mainGoal] ++ mvs.pop.toList.map (·.mvarId!)
165-
166-structure InversionConfig where
167-  clear : Bool := false
168-
169-declare_config_elab elabInversionConfig InversionConfig
170-
171-open Cases in
172-/-- Perform inversion on the given variable in the context of the given goal.
173-  Behaves like [Lean.Meta.Cases.cases] and generalizes indices if they aren't independent,
174-  except instead of calling [Lean.Meta.Cases.unifyEqs], which may fail
175-  if the generalizing equations can't all be destructed and substituted away,
176-  it calls our [unifyCasesEqs] above, which keeps unsolvable equations in the context. -/
177-def _root_.Lean.MVarId.inversion (mvarId : MVarId) (h : FVarId) (config : InversionConfig)
178-    (givenNames : Array AltVarNames := #[]) (interestingCtors? : Option (Array Name) := none) :
179-    TacticM (Array CasesSubgoal) := mvarId.withContext do
180-  let goal ← getMainGoal
181-  goal.withContext do
182-    let some ctx ← mkCasesContext? h
183-    | throwTacticEx `inversion goal "Target {Expr.fvar h} does not belong to an inductive type"
184-    -- If the target's type isn't a predicate with indices, behave like `cases`
185-    if ← hasIndepIndices ctx then
186-      let subgoals ← inductionCasesOn goal h givenNames ctx (interestingCtors? := interestingCtors?)
187-      let subgoals ← if config.clear
188-        then casesClearMany subgoals #[h]
189-        else pure subgoals
190-      return subgoals
191-    -- Otherwise, use custom [unifyEqs] to not fail on unifying HEqs
192-    else
193-      let gis@⟨newGoal, _, newTarget, numEqs⟩ ← generalizeIndices goal h
194-      let (newEqs, newGoal) ← newGoal.introN numEqs
195-      let some targetEq := newEqs.back?
196-      | throwTacticEx `inversion newGoal "Failed to generalize target"
197-      let subgoals ← inductionCasesOn newGoal newTarget givenNames ctx (interestingCtors? := interestingCtors?)
198-      let subgoals ← elimAuxIndices gis subgoals
199-      let subgoals ← unifyCasesEqs newEqs.toList subgoals
200-      let subgoals ← if config.clear
201-        then casesClearMany subgoals #[h, targetEq]
202-        else pure subgoals
203-      return subgoals
204-
205-/-- Given an inversion alternative and a list of goals,
206-  solve the tagged goal with the provided tactics,
207-  throwing an error if the goal cannot be found or solved. -/
208-def evalInvAlt (goals : List MVarId) (alt : TSyntax `invAlt) : TacticM (List MVarId) :=
209-  match alt with
210-  | `(invAlt| | $tag:ident $vars:binderIdent* => $tactics:tacticSeq) => do
211-    if let some goal ← goals.findM? (matchTag tag.getId <$> ·.getUserName) then
212-      return [← trySolveGoal vars tactics goal]
213-    else throwError m!"Invalid alternative name `{tag.getId}`: {← errorMsg}"
214-  | `(invAlt| | _ $vars:binderIdent* => $tactics:tacticSeq) => do
215-    if !goals.isEmpty then
216-      goals.mapM (trySolveGoal vars tactics)
217-    else throwErrorAt alt m!"Invalid wildcard alternative: {← errorMsg}"
218-  | _ => throwErrorAt alt "Could not parse inversion alternative"
219-where
220-  matchTag tag name : Bool :=
221-    tag == name || tag.isPrefixOf name || tag.isSuffixOf name
222-  trySolveGoal vars tactics goal : TacticM MVarId := do
223-    let goals ← renameInaccessibles goal vars >>= evalTacticAt tactics
224-    unless goals.isEmpty do
225-      reportUnsolvedGoals goals
226-    return goal
227-  errorMsg : TacticM MessageData := do
228-    let goalMsgs ← goals.mapM (.ofName <$> ·.getUserName)
229-    return if goals.isEmpty
230-      then m!"There are no unhandled alternatives"
231-      else m!"Expected {.orList goalMsgs}"
232-
233-@[tactic Lean.Parser.inversion, inherit_doc Lean.Parser.inversion]
234-public meta def evalInversion : Tactic
235-  | `(tactic| inversion $config $h:ident $[with $[$tactics?:tacticSeq]? $[$alts?:invAlts]*]?) => do
236-    let casesSubgoals ← (← getMainGoal).inversion (← getFVarId h) (← elabInversionConfig config)
237-    let mut goals ← casesSubgoals.toList.mapM setUserName
238-    if let some tactics := tactics?.join then
239-      let subgoals ← goals.mapM (evalTacticAt tactics)
240-      goals ← subgoals.flatten.filterM (not <$> ·.isAssignedOrDelayedAssigned)
241-    if let some alts := alts? then
242-      let expandedAlts ← Array.flatten <$> alts.mapM expandInvAlts
243-      for alt in expandedAlts do
244-        let solvedGoals ← evalInvAlt goals alt
245-        goals := goals.removeAll solvedGoals
246-      unless goals.isEmpty do
247-        reportUnsolvedGoals goals
248-    replaceMainGoal goals
249-  | stx => throwErrorAt stx "Could not parse inversion tactic"
250-where
251-  setUserName subgoal : TacticM MVarId := do
252-    if let some name := subgoal.ctorName then
253-      subgoal.mvarId.setUserName name.getSuffix
254-    return subgoal.mvarId
255-  expandInvAlts
256-    | `(invAlts| $[| $args:caseArg]* => $tactics:tacticSeq) =>
257-      args.mapM (`(invAlt| | $(·) => $tactics))
258-    | stx => throwErrorAt stx "Could not parse inversion alternatives"
259-
260-end Lean.Elab.Tactic
261-
262-end -- meta section

264-namespace Tests

267-set_option autoImplicit false
268-set_option pp.proofs true

271-/-! # `inversion` tests -/
272-
273-/-- In Lean, "inversion" on `leq : f n ≤ 0`, where `f : Nat → Nat`,
274-  requires `generalizing e : f n = m`, since Lean does not perform
275-  the dependent case analysis automatically. `cases leq` will fail here.
276-  We want to keep the style of reasoning familiar to PL:
277-  "I know `h`; what must have been true for `h` to be true?"
278-  The technicality of needing to generalize hinders teaching and learning
279-  this style of reasoning for audiences new to proof assistants and logic.
280-  To solve this, we introduce and use the `inversion` tactic,
281-  which automatically generalizes varaibles, performs case analysis,
282-  and eliminates impossible subcases. -/
283-example (f : Nat → Nat) (n : Nat) (leq : f n ≤ 0) : 0 = f n := by
284-  -- cases leq /- Dependent elimination failed: Failed to solve equation 0 = f n -/
285-  inversion leq; assumption
286-
287-example (f : Nat → Nat) (n : Nat) (leq : f n ≤ 0) : 0 = f n := by
288-  inversion +clear leq; assumption
289-
290-/-- error: Unknown identifier `leq` -/
291-#guard_msgs(error) in
292-example (f : Nat → Nat) (n : Nat) (leq : f n ≤ 0) : 0 = f n := by
293-  inversion +clear leq
294-  guard_hyp leq
295-
296-example (f : Nat → Nat) (n : Nat) (leq : f n ≤ 0) : 0 = f n := by
297-  inversion leq with
298-  | refl heq eq =>
299-    guard_hyp heq : leq ≍ le.refl
300-    guard_hyp eq : 0 = f n
301-    assumption
302-
303-/-- warning: declaration uses `sorry` -/
304-#guard_msgs(warning) in
305-example (f : Nat → Nat) (n m : Nat) (leq : f n ≤ f m) : f n = 0 := by
306-  inversion leq with
307-  | refl e _ | step k _ e _ =>
308-    try rw [← e]
309-    sorry
310-
311-/-- error: Invalid wildcard alternative: There are no unhandled alternatives -/
312-#guard_msgs(error) in
313-example (f : Nat → Nat) (n m : Nat) (leq : f n ≤ f m) : f n = 0 := by
314-  inversion +clear leq with
315-  | refl e | step k _ e =>
316-    try rw [← e]
317-    sorry
318-  | _ => sorry
319-
320-/-- error: Invalid alternative name `step`: There are no unhandled alternatives -/
321-#guard_msgs(error) in
322-example (f : Nat → Nat) (n m : Nat) (leq : f n ≤ f m) : f n = 0 := by
323-  inversion +clear leq with
324-  | _ e | step k _ e =>
325-    try rw [← e]
326-    sorry
327-
328-inductive The : ∀ {α}, α → Prop where
329-  | mk : The zero
330-
331-/-- sfl#40: Case names should be the constructors' names -/
332-example {x : Nat} (h : The x) : x = zero := by
333-  inversion h with
334-  | mk => rfl
335-
336-example {α} {n m k : α} : [n, m] = [k, k] → [n] = [m] := by
337-  intro h
338-  inversion h; rfl
339-
340-example {n : Nat} : n + 1 = 1 + n := by
341-  induction n with try rfl
342-  | succ => lia
343-
344-inductive NoStutter {α : Type} : List α → Prop where
345-  | nostutter0: NoStutter []
346-  | nostutter1 {n} : NoStutter (n :: [])
347-  | nostutter2 {x y l} (hneq : x ≠ y) (h : NoStutter (y :: l)) : NoStutter (x :: y :: l)
348-
349-/-- The last (only) case name need not be provided -/
350-example : ¬ (NoStutter [3, 1, 1, 4]) := by
351-  intro contra
352-  inversion contra with | _ contra =>
353-  inversion contra with | _ h _ =>
354-  apply h
355-  rfl
356-
357-/-- Inversion may optionally take a sequence of tactics on all goals -/
358-example {α x y} {l : List α} (h : NoStutter l) (hl : l = x :: y :: []) : x ≠ y := by
359-  inversion h with
360-    injections
361-    try subst_vars
362-  | nostutter2 => assumption
363-
364-/-- `with` acts similarly to `<;>` on the optional sequence of tactics -/
365-example {α x y} {l : List α} (h : NoStutter l) (hl : l = x :: y :: []) : x ≠ y := by
366-  inversion h with
367-    injections
368-    try (subst_vars; assumption)
369-
370-example {x y} {l : List Nat} (h : NoStutter l) (hl : l = x :: y :: []) : x ≠ y := by
371-  inversion h with
372-    injections
373-    try cases x
374-  | nostutter2.zero => subst_vars; assumption
375-  | nostutter2.succ => subst_vars; assumption
376-
377-inductive Vec α : Nat → Type where
378-  | nil : Vec α 0
379-  | cons {n} : α → Vec α n → Vec α (n + 1)

381-/-- Inversion should work on indexed `Type`s as well -/
382-example {α} (n : Nat) (v : Vec α (n + 1)) : ∃ hd tl, v = Vec.cons hd tl := by
383-  inversion v with
384-  | cons hd tl => exists hd, tl

387-  | nil : Wec α 0
388-  | cons {n} (f : Nat → Nat) : α → Wec α n → Wec α (f n)
389-
390-/-- warning: declaration uses `sorry` -/
391-#guard_msgs(warning) in
392-example {α} (n : Nat) (v : Wec α (succ n)) :
393-    ∃ hd tl, v = Wec.cons succ hd tl := by
394-  inversion v with
395-  | cons m f hd tl eq heq =>
396-    guard_hyp eq : succ n = f m

398-    sorry
399-
400-inductive EmptyRelation : Nat → Nat → Prop where
401-
402-/-- sfl#52: Inversion should still work on nonindexed `Prop`s -/
403-example n m : ¬ EmptyRelation n m := by
404-  intro contra; inversion contra
405-
406-/-- With `inductive.autoPromoteIndices` true (the default),
407-  this is also a nonindexed `Prop`... -/
408-inductive silly : Nat → Prop where
409-| silly1 n (h : n > 1) : silly n
410-| silly2 n (h : exists m, m * 2 = n) : silly n
411-| silly3 n (h : exists m, n = m + 2) : silly n
412-
413-/-- ...and inversion should continue to work -/
414-example {n} (h : silly n) : n ≠ 1 := by
415-  inversion h <;> omega

418-example (n : Nat) : Nat := by
419-  inversion n with
420-  | zero => exact zero
421-  | succ n' => exact n'

LF/IndProp.lean

1-import LF.Logic
2-import LF.CustomTactics
3-
4-import SFLCompat
5-
6---  # IndProp: Inductively Defined Propositions
7-
8---  ## Inductively Defined Propositions
9-
10---  In the Logic chapter, we looked at several ways of writing
11---  propositions, including conjunction, disjunction, and existential
12---  quantification.
13---
14---  In this chapter, we bring yet another new tool into the mix:
15---  *inductively defined propositions*.
16---
17---  To begin, some examples...
18-
19---  ### Example: The Collatz Conjecture
20-
21---  The *Collatz Conjecture* is a famous open problem in number theory.
22---
23---  Its statement is quite simple. First, we define a function `csf` on
24---  numbers, as follows (where `csf` stands for "Collatz step function"):
25-
26-def div2 (n : Nat) : Nat :=
27-  match n with
28-  | 0      => 0
29-  | 1      => 0
30-  | n' + 2 => div2 n' + 1
31-
32-def csf (n : Nat) : Nat :=
33-  bif n.even then div2 n
34-  else (3 * n) + 1
35-
36---  Next, we look at what happens when we repeatedly apply `csf` to some
37---  given starting number. For example, `csf 12` is `6`, and `csf 6` is
38---  `3`, so by repeatedly applying `csf` we get the sequence
39---  `12, 6, 3, 10, 5, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1`.
40---
41---  Similarly, if we start with `19`, we get the longer sequence
42---  `19,
43---  58, 29, 88, 44, 22, 11, 34, 17, 52, 26, 13, 40, 20, 10, 5, 16, 8,
44---  4, 2, 1`.
45---
46---  Both of these sequences eventually reach `1`. The question posed by
47---  Collatz was: Is the sequence starting from *any* positive natural
48---  number guaranteed to reach `1` eventually?
49---
50---  To formalize this question in Lean, we might try to define a recursive
51---  *function* that calculates the total number of steps that it takes for
52---  such a sequence to reach `1`. You can write this definition in a
53---  standard programming language, but it is rejected by Lean's termination
54---  checker, since the argument to the recursive call, `csf n`, is not
55---  "obviously smaller" than `n`.
56-
57-sf_expect_failure_in
58-  def reaches1In (n : Nat) : Nat :=
59-    bif n == 1 then 0
60-    else 1 + reaches1In (csf n)
61-
62---  Output:
63---    fail to show termination for
64---      reaches1In
65---    with errors
66---    failed to infer structural recursion:
67---    Cannot use parameter n:
68---      failed to eliminate recursive application
69---        reaches1In (csf n)
70---
71---
72---    failed to prove termination, possible solutions:
73---      - Use `have`-expressions to prove the remaining goals
74---      - Use `termination_by` to specify a different well-founded relation
75---      - Use `decreasing_by` to specify your own tactic for discharging this kind of goal
76---    n : Nat
77---    ⊢ csf n < n
78-
79---  Indeed, this isn't just a pointless limitation: functions in Lean are
80---  required to be total, to ensure logical consistency.
81---
82---  Moreover, we can't fix it by devising a more clever termination
83---  checker: deciding whether this particular function is total would be
84---  equivalent to settling the Collatz conjecture!
85---
86---  Another idea could be to express the concept "eventually reaches `1` in
87---  the Collatz sequence" as a *recursively defined property* of numbers
88---  `CollatzHoldsFor : Nat → Prop`. This is also rejected by the
89---  termination checker. In principle, we could convince Lean that `div2 n`
90---  is smaller than `n` by supplying an appropriate proof. However, we
91---  still can't convince it that `(3 * n) + 1` is smaller than `n`!
92-
93-sf_expect_failure_in
94-  def CollatzHoldsFor (n : Nat) : Prop :=
95-    match n with
96-    | 0 => False
97-    | 1 => True
98-    | _ => bif n.even then CollatzHoldsFor (div2 n)
99-                     else CollatzHoldsFor ((3 * n) + 1)
100-
101---  Output:
102---    fail to show termination for
103---      CollatzHoldsFor
104---    with errors
105---    failed to infer structural recursion:
106---    Cannot use parameter n:
107---      failed to eliminate recursive application
108---        CollatzHoldsFor (div2 n)
109---
110---
111---    failed to prove termination, possible solutions:
112---      - Use `have`-expressions to prove the remaining goals
113---      - Use `termination_by` to specify a different well-founded relation
114---      - Use `decreasing_by` to specify your own tactic for discharging this kind of goal
115---    n x✝ : Nat
116---    ⊢ div2 n < x✝
117-
118---  Fortunately, there is another way to do it: We can express the concept
119---  "reaches `1` eventually in the Collatz sequence" as an *inductively
120---  defined property* of numbers. Intuitively, this property is defined by
121---  a set of rules:
122---
123---                    ─────────────────── (chf_one)
124---                     CollatzHoldsFor 1
125---
126---      even n = true     CollatzHoldsFor (div2 n)
127---      ─────────────────────────────────────────── (chf_even)
128---                     CollatzHoldsFor n
129---
130---      even n = false    CollatzHoldsFor ((3 * n) + 1)
131---      ─────────────────────────────────────────────── (chf_odd)
132---                     CollatzHoldsFor n
133---
134---  So there are three ways to prove that a number `n` eventually reaches
135---  `1` in the Collatz sequence:
136---
137---  - `n` is `1`;
138---  - `n` is even and `div2 n` eventually reaches `1`;
139---  - `n` is odd and `(3 * n) + 1` eventually reaches `1`.
140---
141---  We can prove that a number reaches `1` by constructing a (finite)
142---  derivation using these rules. For instance, here is the derivation
143---  proving that `12` reaches `1` (where we leave out the evenness/oddness
144---  premises):
145---
146---      ─────────────────────── (chf_one)
147---        CollatzHoldsFor 1
148---      ─────────────────────── (chf_even)
149---        CollatzHoldsFor 2
150---      ─────────────────────── (chf_even)
151---        CollatzHoldsFor 4
152---      ─────────────────────── (chf_even)
153---        CollatzHoldsFor 8
154---      ─────────────────────── (chf_even)
155---        CollatzHoldsFor 16
156---      ─────────────────────── (chf_odd)
157---        CollatzHoldsFor 5
158---      ─────────────────────── (chf_even)
159---        CollatzHoldsFor 10
160---      ─────────────────────── (chf_odd)
161---        CollatzHoldsFor 3
162---      ─────────────────────── (chf_even)
163---        CollatzHoldsFor 6
164---      ─────────────────────── (chf_even)
165---        CollatzHoldsFor 12
166---
167---  Formally in Lean, the `CollatzHoldsFor` property is *inductively
168---  defined*:
169-
170-inductive CollatzHoldsFor : Nat → Prop where
171-  | chf_one  : CollatzHoldsFor 1
172-  | chf_even {n : Nat} (h₁ : n.even = true)
173-    (h₂ : CollatzHoldsFor (div2 n)) : CollatzHoldsFor n
174-  | chf_odd  {n : Nat} (h₁ : n.even = false)
175-    (h₂ : CollatzHoldsFor ((3 * n) + 1)) : CollatzHoldsFor n
176-
177---  What we've done here is to use Lean's `inductive` definition mechanism
178---  to characterize the property "Collatz holds for..." by stating three
179---  different ways in which it can hold: (1) Collatz holds for `1`, (2) if
180---  Collatz holds for `div2 n` and `n` is even then Collatz holds for `n`,
181---  and (3) if Collatz holds for `(3 * n) + 1` and `n` is odd then Collatz
182---  holds for `n`. This Lean definition directly corresponds to the three
183---  rules we wrote informally above.
184-
185---  For particular numbers, we can now prove that the Collatz sequence
186---  reaches `1` (we'll look more closely at how it works a bit later in the
187---  chapter). Each step applies a rule and discharges the boolean evenness
188---  premise by `rfl`; the recursive premise is then reduced by the kernel
189---  from `CollatzHoldsFor (div2 12)` to `CollatzHoldsFor 6`, etc.
190-
191-example : CollatzHoldsFor 12 := by
192-  apply CollatzHoldsFor.chf_even;  rfl
193-  apply CollatzHoldsFor.chf_even;  rfl
194-  apply CollatzHoldsFor.chf_odd;   rfl
195-  apply CollatzHoldsFor.chf_even;  rfl
196-  apply CollatzHoldsFor.chf_odd;   rfl
197-  apply CollatzHoldsFor.chf_even;  rfl
198-  apply CollatzHoldsFor.chf_even;  rfl
199-  apply CollatzHoldsFor.chf_even;  rfl
200-  apply CollatzHoldsFor.chf_even;  rfl
201-  exact CollatzHoldsFor.chf_one
202-
203---  The Collatz conjecture then states that the sequence beginning from
204---  *any* positive number reaches `1`:
205-
206-def Collatz := ∀ n, n ≠ 0 → CollatzHoldsFor n
207-
208---  If you succeed in proving this conjecture, you've got a bright future
209---  as a number theorist! But don't spend too long on it ─ it's been open
210---  since 1937.
211-
212---  ### Example: Binary Relation for Comparing Numbers
213-
214---  A binary *relation* on a set `α` has Lean type `α → α → Prop`. This is
215---  a family of propositions parameterized by two elements of `α` ─ i.e., a
216---  proposition about pairs of elements of `α`.
217---
218---  For example, one familiar binary relation on `Nat` is
219---  `Le : Nat → Nat → Prop`, the less-than-or-equal-to relation, which can
220---  be inductively defined by the following two rules:
221---
222---        ─────── (le_refl)
223---        Le n n
224---
225---        Le n m
226---      ──────────── (le_step)
227---      Le n (m + 1)
228-
229---  These rules say that there are two ways to show that a number is less
230---  than or equal to another: either observe that they are the same number,
231---  or, if the second has the form `m + 1`, give evidence that the first is
232---  less than or equal to `m`.
233-
234-namespace LePlayground
235-
236-inductive Le : Nat → Nat → Prop where
237-  | refl {n : Nat}                : Le n n
238-  | step {n m : Nat} (h : Le n m) : Le n (m + 1)
239-
240-scoped infix:50 (priority := high) " ≤ " => Le
241-
242---  This definition is a bit simpler and more elegant than the Boolean
243---  function `Nat.ble` we defined in Basics. As usual, `Le` and `Nat.ble`
244---  are equivalent, and there is an exercise about that later.
245-
246-example : 3 ≤ 5 := by
247-  apply Le.step; apply Le.step; exact Le.refl
248-
249-end LePlayground
250-
251---  ### Example: Transitive Closure
252-
253---  Another example: The *transitive closure* of a relation `R` is the
254---  smallest relation that contains `R` and that is transitive. This can be
255---  defined by the following two rules:
256---
257---                    R x y
258---               ─────────────── (t_step)
259---               ClosTrans R x y
260---
261---      ClosTrans R x y    ClosTrans R y z
262---      ──────────────────────────────────── (t_trans)
263---               ClosTrans R x z
264---
265---  In Lean this looks as follows:
266-
267-inductive ClosTrans {α : Type} (R : α → α → Prop) : α → α → Prop where
268-  | t_step {x y : α} (h : R x y) : ClosTrans R x y
269-  | t_trans {x y z : α}
270-    (h₁ : ClosTrans R x y)
271-    (h₂ : ClosTrans R y z) :
272-    ClosTrans R x z
273-
274---  For example, suppose we define a "parent of" relation on a group of
275---  people...
276-
277-inductive Person : Type where
278-  | sage
279-  | cleo
280-  | ridley
281-  | moss
282-
283-inductive ParentOf : Person → Person → Prop where
284-  | po_SC : ParentOf .sage .cleo
285-  | po_SR : ParentOf .sage .ridley
286-  | po_CM : ParentOf .cleo .moss
287-
288---  In this example, `sage` is a parent of both `cleo` and `ridley`; and
289---  `cleo` is a parent of `moss`.
290-
291---  The `ParentOf` relation is not transitive, but we can define an
292---  "ancestor of" relation as its transitive closure:
293-
294-def AncestorOf : Person → Person → Prop := ClosTrans ParentOf
295-
296---  Here is a derivation showing that `sage` is an ancestor of `moss`:
297---
298---       ——————————————————— (po_SC)     ——————————————————— (po_CM)
299---       ParentOf .sage .cleo            ParentOf .cleo .moss
300---      ————————————————————— (t_step)  ————————————————————— (t_step)
301---      AncestorOf .sage .cleo          AncestorOf .cleo .moss
302---      ———————————————————————————————————————————————————— (t_trans)
303---                      AncestorOf .sage .moss
304-
305-example : AncestorOf .sage .moss := by
306-  apply ClosTrans.t_trans
307-  . apply ClosTrans.t_step; apply ParentOf.po_SC
308-  . apply ClosTrans.t_step; apply ParentOf.po_CM
309-
310---  Computing the transitive closure can be undecidable even for a relation
311---  R that is decidable (e.g., the `CMS` relation below), so in general we
312---  can't expect to define transitive closure as a boolean function.
313---  Fortunately, Lean allows us to define transitive closure as an
314---  inductive relation.
315---
316---  The transitive closure of a binary relation cannot, in general, be
317---  expressed in first-order logic. The logic of Lean is, however, much
318---  more powerful, and can easily define such inductive relations.
319-
320---  ### Example: Reflexive and Transitive Closure
321-
322---  As another example, the *reflexive and transitive closure* of a
323---  relation `R` is the smallest relation that contains `R` and that is
324---  reflexive and transitive. This can be defined by the following three
325---  rules (where we added a reflexivity rule to `ClosTrans`):
326---
327---                         R x y
328---               ——————————————————————— (rt_step)
329---                 ClosReflTrans R x y
330---
331---               ——————————————————————— (rt_refl)
332---                 ClosReflTrans R x x
333---
334---         ClosReflTrans R x y    ClosReflTrans R y z
335---      —————————————————————————————————————————————— (rt_trans)
336---                 ClosReflTrans R x z
337-
338-inductive ClosReflTrans {α : Type} (R : α → α → Prop) : α → α → Prop where
339-  | rt_step {x y : α} (h : R x y) : ClosReflTrans R x y
340-  | rt_refl {x : α} : ClosReflTrans R x x
341-  | rt_trans {x y z : α}
342-    (h₁ : ClosReflTrans R x y)
343-    (h₂ : ClosReflTrans R y z) :
344-    ClosReflTrans R x z
345-
346---  For instance, this enables an equivalent definition of the Collatz
347---  conjecture. First we define a binary relation corresponding to the
348---  "Collatz step function" `csf`:
349-
350-def CS (n m : Nat) : Prop := csf n = m
351-
352---  This Collatz step relation can be used in conjunction with the
353---  reflexive and transitive closure operation to define a *Collatz
354---  multi-step* (`CMS`) relation, expressing that a number `n` reaches
355---  another number `m` in zero or more Collatz steps:
356-
357-def CMS (n m : Nat) : Prop := ClosReflTrans CS n m
358-def Collatz' : Prop := ∀ (n : Nat), n ≠ 0 → CMS n 1
359-
360---  This `CMS` relation defined in terms of `ClosReflTrans` allows for more
361---  interesting derivations than the linear ones of the directly-defined
362---  `CollatzHoldsFor` relation:
363---
364---      csf 16 = 8            csf 8 = 4            csf 4 = 2            csf 2 = 1
365---      —————————— (rt_step)  ————————— (rt_step)  ————————— (rt_step)  ————————— (rt_step)
366---      CMS 16 8              CMS 8 4              CMS 4 2              CMS 2 1
367---      ——————————————————————————————— (rt_trans) —————————————————————————————— (rt_trans)
368---                 CMS 16 4                                    CMS 4 1
369---                 ——————————————————————————————————————————————————— (rt_trans)
370---                                       CMS 16 1
371-
372---  ### Exercise (1 star): clos_refl_trans_sym (Optional, Manually graded) ⭐
373-
374---  How would you modify the `ClosReflTrans` definition above so as to
375---  define the reflexive, symmetric, and transitive closure?

379---  ### Example: Permutations
380-
381---  The familiar mathematical concept of *permutation* also has an elegant
382---  formulation as an inductive relation. For simplicity, let's focus on
383---  permutations of lists with exactly three elements.
384---
385---  We can define such permutations by the following rules:
386---
387---         ───────────────────────── (perm3_swap12)
388---         Perm3 [a, b, c] [b, a, c]
389---
390---         ───────────────────────── (perm3_swap23)
391---         Perm3 [a, b, c] [a, c, b]
392---
393---      Perm3 l₁ l₂       Perm3 l₂ l₃
394---      ───────────────────────────── (perm3_trans)
395---               Perm3 l₁ l₃
396---
397---  For instance we can derive `Perm3 [1, 2, 3] [3, 2, 1]` as follows:
398---
399---      ───────────────────────── (perm3_swap12)   ───────────────────────── (perm3_swap23)
400---      Perm3 [1, 2, 3] [2, 1, 3]                  Perm3 [2, 1, 3] [2, 3, 1]
401---      ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── (perm3_trans)   ───────────────────────── (perm3_swap12)
402---      Perm3 [1, 2, 3] [2, 3, 1]                                                            Perm3 [2, 3, 1] [3, 2, 1]
403---      ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── (perm3_trans)
404---      Perm3 [1, 2, 3] [3, 2, 1]
405-
406---  This definition says:
407---
408---  - If `l₂` can be obtained from `l₁` by swapping the first and second
409---    elements, then `l₂` is a permutation of `l₁`.
410---
411---  - If `l₂` can be obtained from `l₁` by swapping the second and third
412---    elements, then `l₂` is a permutation of `l₁`.
413---
414---  - If `l₂` is a permutation of `l₁` and `l₃` is a permutation of`l₂`,
415---    then `l₃` is a permutation of `l₁`.
416-
417---  In Lean, we can define `Perm3` as follows:
418-
419-inductive Perm3 {α : Type} : List α → List α → Prop where
420-  | perm3_swap12 {x y z : α} : Perm3 [x, y, z] [y, x, z]
421-  | perm3_swap23 {x y z : α} : Perm3 [x, y, z] [x, z, y]
422-  | perm3_trans {l₁ l₂ l₃ : List α}
423-    (h₁₂ : Perm3 l₁ l₂)
424-    (h₂₃ : Perm3 l₂ l₃) :
425-    Perm3 l₁ l₃
426-
427---  ### Exercise (1 star): perm (Optional, Manually graded) ⭐
428-
429---  According to this definition, is `[1, 2, 3]` a permutation of itself?
430-
431---  ### Example: Evenness (yet again)
432-
433---  We've already seen two ways of stating a proposition that a number `n`
434---  is even: We can say
435---
436---  (1) `Nat.even n = true` (using the recursive boolean function
437---  `Nat.even`), or
438---
439---  (2) `∃ k, n = Nat.double k` (using an existential quantifier).
440---
441---  A third possibility, which we'll use as a simple running example in
442---  this chapter, is to say that a number is even if we can *establish* its
443---  evenness from the following two rules:
444---
445---          ———— (ev_0)
446---          Ev 0
447---
448---          Ev n
449---      —————————————— (ev_succ_succ)
450---        Ev (n + 2)
451-
452---  Intuitively these rules say that:
453---
454---  - The number `0` is even.
455---  - If `n` is even, then `n + 2` is even.
456---
457---  (Defining evenness in this way may seem a bit confusing, since we have
458---  already seen two perfectly good ways of doing it. It makes a convenient
459---  running example because it is simple and compact, but we will soon
460---  return to the more compelling examples above.)
461-
462---  To illustrate how this new definition of evenness works, let's imagine
463---  using it to show that `4` is even:
464---
465---                    ———— (ev_0)
466---                    Ev 0
467---             ———————————————————— (ev_succ_succ)
468---             Ev (.succ (.succ 0))
469---      ——————————————————————————————————— (ev_succ_succ)
470---      Ev (.succ (.succ (.succ (.succ 0))))
471-
472---  In words, to show that `4` is even, by rule `ev_succ_succ`, it suffices
473---  to show that `2` is even. This, in turn, is again guaranteed by rule
474---  `ev_succ_succ`, as long as we can show that `0` is even. But this last
475---  fact follows directly from the `ev_0` rule.
476-
477---  We can translate the informal definition of evenness from above into a
478---  formal `inductive` declaration, where each "way that a number can be
479---  even" corresponds to a separate constructor:
480-
481-inductive Ev : Nat → Prop where
482-  | ev_0                              : Ev 0
483-  | ev_succ_succ {n : Nat} (h : Ev n) : Ev (n + 2)
484-
485---  Such definitions are interestingly different from previous uses of
486---  `inductive` for defining inductive datatypes like `Nat` or `List`. For
487---  one thing, we are defining not a `Type` (like `Nat`) or a function
488---  yielding a `Type` (like `List`), but rather a function from `Nat` to
489---  `Prop` ─ that is, a property of numbers. But what is really new is
490---  that, because the `Nat` argument of `Ev` appears to the *right* of the
491---  colon on the first line, it is allowed to take *different* values in
492---  the types of different constructors: `0` in the type of `Ev.ev_0` and
493---  `(n + 2)` in the type of `Ev.ev_succ_succ`. Accordingly, the type of
494---  each constructor must be specified explicitly (after a colon), and each
495---  constructor's type must have the form `Ev n` for some natural number
496---  `n`.
497---
498---  In contrast, recall the definition of `List`:
499-
500-sf_expect_failure_in
501-  inductive List (α : Type) : Type where
502-    | nil
503-    | cons (x : α) (l : List α)
504-
505---  or (equivalently but more explicitly):
506-
507-sf_expect_failure_in
508-  inductive List (α : Type) : Type where
509-    | nil                       : List α
510-    | cons (x : α) (l : List α) : List α
511-
512---  This definition introduces the `α` parameter *globally*, to the *left*
513---  of the colon, forcing the result of `List.nil` and `List.cons` to be
514---  the same type (i.e., `List α`). But if we had tried to bring `Nat` to
515---  the left of the colon in defining `Ev`, we would have seen an error:
516-
517-sf_expect_failure_in
518-  inductive WrongEv (n : Nat) : Prop where
519-    | wrong_ev_0 : WrongEv 0
520-    | wrong_ev_succ_succ (h : WrongEv n) : WrongEv (n + 2)
521-
522---  Output:
523---    Mismatched inductive type parameter in
524---      WrongEv 0
525---    The provided argument
526---      0
527---    is not definitionally equal to the expected parameter
528---      n
529---
530---    Note: The value of parameter `n` must be fixed throughout the inductive declaration. Consider making this parameter an index if it must vary.
531-
532---  In an `inductive` definition, an argument to the type constructor on
533---  the left of the colon is called a "parameter", whereas an argument on
534---  the right is called an "index" or "annotation."
535---
536---  For example, in `inductive List (α : Type) ...`, the `α` is a
537---  parameter, while in `inductive Ev : Nat → Prop ...`, the unnamed `Nat`
538---  argument is an index.
539-
540---  We can think of the inductive definition of `Ev` as defining a Lean
541---  property `Ev : Nat → Prop`, together with two "evidence constructors":
542-
543-#check Ev.ev_0         -- Ev 0
544-#check Ev.ev_succ_succ -- ∀ (n : Nat) (h : Ev n) : Ev (n + 2)
545-
546---  Indeed, Lean also accepts the following equivalent definition of `Ev`.
547-
548-namespace EvPlayground
549-
550-inductive Ev : Nat → Prop where
551-  | ev_0 : Ev 0
552-  | ev_succ_succ {n : Nat} (h : Ev n) : Ev (n + 2)
553-
554-end EvPlayground
555-
556---  These evidence constructors can be thought of as "primitive evidence of
557---  evenness", and they can be used later on just like proven theorems. In
558---  particular, we can use Lean's `apply` and `exact` tactics with the
559---  constructor names to obtain evidence for `Ev` of particular numbers...
560-
561-namespace Ev
562-
563-example : Ev 4 := by
564-  apply ev_succ_succ; apply ev_succ_succ; exact ev_0
565-
566---  ... or we can use function application syntax to combine several
567---  constructors:
568-
569-example : Ev 4 := by
570-  exact ev_succ_succ (ev_succ_succ ev_0)
571-
572---  ... or we can also use the `constructor` tactic we saw earlier to
573---  select the appropriate inductive constructor:
574-
575-example : Ev 4 := by
576-  constructor; constructor; constructor
577-
578---  In this way, we can also prove theorems that have hypotheses involving
579---  `Ev`.
580-
581-theorem plus4 (n : Nat) (h : Ev n) : Ev (4 + n) := by
582-  rw [Nat.add_comm]
583-  exact (ev_succ_succ (ev_succ_succ h))
584-
585---  ### Exercise (1 star): ev_double ⭐
586-
587-theorem double (n : Nat) : Ev n.double := by
588-  sorry
589-
590-end Ev
591-
592---  ### Constructing Evidence for Permutations
593-
594---  Similarly we can apply the evidence constructors to obtain evidence of
595---  `Perm3 [1, 2, 3] [3, 2, 1]`:
596-
597-namespace Perm3
598-
599-theorem rev : Perm3 [1, 2, 3] [3, 2, 1] := by
600-  apply perm3_trans (l₂:= [2, 3, 1])
601-  . apply perm3_trans (l₂ := [2, 1, 3])
602-    . apply perm3_swap12
603-    . apply perm3_swap23
604-  . apply perm3_swap12
605-
606---  And again we can equivalently use function application syntax to
607---  combine several constructors. (Note that the Lean type checker can
608---  infer not only types, but also `Nat`s and `List`s, when they are clear
609---  from the context.)
610-
611-theorem rev' : Perm3 [1, 2, 3] [3, 2, 1] := by
612-  exact (perm3_trans
613-          (perm3_trans perm3_swap12 perm3_swap23)
614-          perm3_swap12)
615-
616---  So the informal derivation trees we drew above are not too far from
617---  what's happening formally. Formally we're using the evidence
618---  constructors to build *evidence trees*, similar to the finite trees we
619---  built using the constructors of data types such as `Nat`, `List`,
620---  binary trees, etc.
621-
622---  ### Exercise (1 star): Perm3 ⭐
623-
624-theorem ex1 : Perm3 [1, 2, 3] [2, 3, 1] := by
625-  sorry
626-
627-theorem refl (α : Type) (a b c : α) : Perm3 [a, b, c] [a, b, c] := by
628-  sorry
629-
630-end Perm3
631-
632---  ## Using Evidence in Proofs
633-
634---  Besides *constructing* evidence that numbers are even, we can also
635---  *destruct* such evidence, reasoning about how it could have been built.
636---
637---  Defining `Ev` with an `inductive` declaration tells Lean not only that
638---  the constructors `Ev.ev_0` and `Ev.ev_succ_succ` are valid ways to
639---  build evidence that some number is `Ev`, but also that these two
640---  constructors are the *only* ways to build evidence that numbers are
641---  `Ev`.
642---
643---  In other words, if someone gives us evidence `e` for the proposition
644---  `Ev n`, then we know that `e` must be one of two things:
645---
646---  - `e = ev_0` and `n = 0`, or
647---
648---  - `e = ev_succ_succ n' e'` and `n = n' + 2`, where `e'` is evidence for
649---    `Ev n'`.
650-
651---  This suggests that it should be possible to analyze a hypothesis of the
652---  form `Ev n` much as we do inductively defined data structures; in
653---  particular, it should be possible to argue either by *case analysis* or
654---  by *induction* on such evidence. Let's look at a few examples to see
655---  what this means in practice.
656-
657---  ### Destructing and Inverting Evidence
658-
659---  Suppose we are proving some fact involving a number `n`, and we are
660---  given `Ev n` as a hypothesis. We already know how to perform case
661---  analysis on `n` using `cases` or `induction`, generating separate
662---  subgoals for the case where `n = 0` and the case where `n = n' + 1` for
663---  some `n'`. But for some proofs we may instead want to analyze the
664---  evidence for `Ev n` *directly*.
665---
666---  As a tool for such proofs, we can formalize the intuitive
667---  characterization that we gave above for evidence of `Ev n`, using
668---  `cases`.
669-
670-theorem ev_inversion (n : Nat) (h : Ev n) :
671-    (n = 0) ∨ ∃ n', n = n' + 2 ∧ Ev n' := by
672-  cases h with
673-  | ev_0 => left; rfl
674-  | @ev_succ_succ n h => right; exists n
675-
676---  Facts like this are often called "inversion lemmas" because they allow
677---  us to "invert" some given information to reason about all the different
678---  ways it could have been derived.
679-
680---  Here there are two ways to prove `Ev n`, and the inversion lemma makes
681---  this explicit.
682-
683---  ### Exercise (1 star): le_inversion ⭐
684-
685---  Let's prove a similar inversion lemma for `le`.
686-
687-namespace LePlayground
688-theorem le_inversion (n m : Nat) (h : Le n m) :
689-    (n = m) ∨ (∃ m', m = m' + 1 ∧ Le n m') := by
690-  sorry
691-
692-end LePlayground
693-
694---   ----------------------------------------
695-
696---  _Quiz:_
697-
698---  Which tactics are needed to prove this goal?
699---
700---      ∀ (n : Nat), Ev n → n = 1 → true = false
701---
702---  (A) `cases` (B) `contradiction` (C) Both `cases` and `contradiction`
703---  (D) these tactics are not sufficient to solve the goal.
704-
705---   ----------------------------------------
706-
707---  We can use the inversion lemma that we proved above to help structure
708---  proofs:
709-
710-theorem ev_succ_succ_ev (n : Nat) (h : Ev (n + 2)) : Ev n := by
711-  apply ev_inversion at h
712-  obtain ⟨⟨⟩⟩ | ⟨n', ⟨h₁,  h₂⟩⟩ := h
713-  injections h₁ heq
714-  subst heq
715-  exact h₂
716-
717---  Note how the inversion lemma produces two subgoals, which correspond to
718---  the two ways of proving `Ev`. The first subgoal is a contradiction that
719---  is discharged with `contradiction`. The second subgoal makes use of
720---  `injections` and `subst`. The `subst` tactic takes an equation `x = t`
721---  and replaces `x` by `t` in the context's hypotheses and in the goal,
722---  then removes that equation from the context.
723---
724---  We've defined a handy tactic called `inversion` that factors out this
725---  common pattern, saving us the trouble of explicitly stating and proving
726---  an inversion lemma for every `inductive` definition we make.
727---
728---  Here, the `inversion` tactic can detect (1) that the first case, where
729---  `n = 0`, does not apply and (2) that the `n'` that appears in the
730---  `ev_succ_succ` case must be the same as `n`.
731---
732---  The details of how `inversion` is implemented are beyond the scope of
733---  this course, but suffice to say Lean's metaprogramming capabilities are
734---  such that almost any sequence of reasoning steps can be implemented as
735---  a new tactic.
736-
737-theorem ev_succ_succ_ev' (n : Nat) (h : Ev (n + 2)) : Ev n := by
738-  inversion h; assumption
739-
740---  The `inversion` tactic can apply the principle of explosion to
741---  "obviously contradictory" hypotheses involving inductively defined
742---  properties, something that takes a bit more work using our inversion
743---  lemma. Compare:
744-
745-theorem one_not_even : ¬ Ev 1 := by
746-  intro h; apply ev_inversion at h
747-  obtain ⟨⟨⟩⟩ | ⟨n', ⟨h₁,  h₂⟩⟩ := h
748-  injections
749-
750-theorem one_not_even' : ¬ Ev 1 := by
751-  intro h; inversion h
752-

769---
770---  Note that `inversion` also works on equality propositions.
771-
772-theorem inversion_ex1 (n m o : Nat) (h : [n, m] = [o, o]) : [n] = [m] := by
773-  inversion h; rfl
774-
775-theorem inversion_ex2 n (h : n + 1 = 0) : 2 + 2 = 5 := by
776-  inversion h

778---  Here's how `inversion` works in general.
779---
780---  - Suppose the name `h` refers to an assumption `p` in the current
781---    context, where `p` has been defined by an `inductive` declaration.
782---
783---  - Then, for each of the constructors of `p`, `inversion h` generates a
784---    subgoal in which `h` has been replaced by the specific conditions
785---    under which this constructor could have been used to prove `p`.
786---
787---  - Some of these subgoals will be self-contradictory; `inversion` throws
788---    these away.
789---
790---  - The ones that are left represent the cases that must be proved to
791---    establish the original goal. For those, `inversion` adds to the proof
792---    context all equations that must hold of the arguments given to `p` ─
793---    e.g., `n' = n` in the proof of `ev_succ_succ_ev`.
794-
795---   ----------------------------------------
796-
797---  _Quiz:_
798-
799---  Which tactics are needed to prove this goal, in addition to `apply` or
800---  `exact`?
801---
802---      ∀ n, Ev (2 + n) → Ev n
803---
804---  (A) `inversion` (B) `inversion`, `injections` (C) `inversion`,
805---  `rw [Nat.add_comm]` (D) `inversion`, `rw [Nat.add_comm]`, `injections`
806-
807---   ----------------------------------------
808-
809---  The `Ev.double` exercise above allows us to easily show that our new
810---  notion of evenness is implied by the two earlier ones (since, by
811---  `Nat.even_bool_prop` in the Logic chapter, we already know that those
812---  are equivalent to each other). To show that all three coincide, we just
813---  need the following lemma.
814-
815-sf_expect_failure_in
816-  example (n : Nat) : Ev n → Nat.Even n := by
817-    /- We could try to proceed by case analysis or induction on `n`.  But
818-        since `Ev` is mentioned in a premise, this strategy seems
819-        unpromising, because (as we've noted before) the induction
820-        hypothesis will talk about `n-1` (which is _not_ even!).  Thus, it
821-        seems better to first try `inversion` on the evidence for `Ev`.
822-        Indeed, the first case can be solved trivially. -/
823-    intro h
824-    inversion h with
825-    /- h = ev_0 -/
826-    | ev_0 => exists 0  -- (`0 = double 0` is closed by `exists`'s final `rfl`)
827-    /- h = ev_succ_succ n' h' -/
828-    | ev_succ_succ n' h' =>
829-    /- Unfortunately, the second case is harder.  We need to show
830-      `∃ n₀, n' + 2 = double n₀`, but the only available assumption is
831-      `h'`, which states that `Ev n'` holds.  Since this isn't directly
832-      useful, it seems that we are stuck and that performing case
833-      analysis on `h` was a waste of time.
834-  
835-      If we look more closely at our second goal, however, we can see
836-      that something interesting happened: By performing case analysis
837-      on `h`, we were able to reduce the original result to a similar
838-      one that involves a _different_ piece of evidence for `Ev`: namely
839-      `h'`.  More formally, we could finish our proof if we could show
840-      that
841-      ```
842-      ∃ k', n' = double k',
843-      ```
844-      which is the same as the original statement, but with `n'` instead
845-      of `n`.  Indeed, it is not difficult to convince Lean that this
846-      intermediate result would suffice. -/
847-      have he : (∃ (k' : Nat), n' = k'.double) → (∃ (n₀ : Nat), n' + 2 = n₀.double) := by
848-        intro ⟨k, hk⟩; exists (k + 1); rw [Nat.double_succ, hk]
849-      apply he
850-      /- Unfortunately, now we are stuck: we are trying to prove another instance
851-          of the same theorem we set out to prove -- only here we are
852-          talking about `n'` instead of `n`. -/
853-
854---  ### Induction on Evidence
855-
856---  If this story feels familiar, it is no coincidence: We encountered
857---  similar problems in the Induction chapter, when trying to use case
858---  analysis to prove results that required induction. And once again the
859---  solution is... induction!
860-
861---  The behavior of `induction` on evidence is the same as its behavior on
862---  data: It causes Lean to generate one subgoal for each constructor that
863---  could have been used to build that evidence, while providing an
864---  induction hypothesis for each recursive occurrence of the property in
865---  question.
866---
867---  To prove that a property of `n` holds for all even numbers (i.e., those
868---  for which `Ev n` holds), we can use induction on `Ev n`. This requires
869---  us to prove two things, corresponding to the two ways in which `Ev n`
870---  could have been constructed. If it was constructed by `Ev.ev_0`, then
871---  `n = 0` and the property must hold of `0`. If it was constructed by
872---  `Ev.ev_succ_succ`, then the evidence of `Ev n` is of the form
873---  `Ev.ev_succ_succ n' h'`, where `n = n' + 2` and `h'` is evidence for
874---  `Ev n'`. In this case, the inductive hypothesis says that the property
875---  we are trying to prove holds for `n'`.
876-
877---  Let's try proving that lemma again:
878-
879-theorem Nat.ev_Even (n : Nat) (h : Ev n) : Even n := by
880-  induction h with
881-  -- h = ev_0
882-  | ev_0 => exists 0 -- (`0 = double 0` is closed by `exists`'s final `rfl`)
883-  -- h = ev_succ_succ n' h', with ih : Even n'
884-  | ev_succ_succ h' ih =>
885-    let ⟨k, hk⟩ := ih
886-    exists k + 1; rw [double_succ, hk]
887-
888---  Here, we can see that Lean produced an `ih` that corresponds to `h`,
889---  the single recursive occurrence of `Ev` in its own definition. Since
890---  `h'` mentions `n'`, the induction hypothesis talks about `n'`, as
891---  opposed to `n` or some other number.
892-
893---  The equivalence between the second and third definitions of evenness
894---  now follows.
895-
896-theorem Nat.ev_Even_iff (n : Nat) : Ev n ↔ Even n := by
897-  apply Iff.intro
898-  . intro h; exact Nat.ev_Even _ h
899-  . intro ⟨k, hk⟩; rw [hk]; exact Ev.double k
900-
901---  As we will see in later chapters, induction on evidence is a recurring
902---  technique across many areas ─ in particular for formalizing the
903---  semantics of programming languages.
904---
905---  The following exercises provide simpler examples of this technique, to
906---  help you familiarize yourself with it.

932---  Another example of a proposition that can be characterized both
933---  recursively and inductively is the `List.In` predicate we defined in
934---  the Logic chapter. As a reminder, the recursive definition we saw
935---  looked like this:
936-
937-def In {α : Type} (x : α) (xs : List α) : Prop :=
938-  match xs with
939-  | [] => False
940-  | x' :: xs' => x = x' ∨ In x xs'
941-
942---  We can also write this definition inductively like so:
943-
944-inductive In_Inductive {α : Type} (x : α) : List α → Prop
945-  | head {l : List α} : In_Inductive x (x :: l)
946-  | tail {y : α} {l : List α} (h : In_Inductive x l) : In_Inductive x (y :: l)
947-
948---  In fact, this is exactly how Lean defines this proposition, which it
949---  calls `Membership.mem` and which is written `x ∈ l`. Its negation
950---  `¬ x ∈ l` is also written as `x ∉ l`.
951---
952---  A good exercise to test your understanding of induction on evidence is
953---  to prove the equivalence of these definitions:
954-
955---  ### Exercise (2 stars): in_mem ⭐⭐
956-
957-theorem in_mem {α} (x : α) (l : List α) : List.In x l ↔ x ∈ l := by
958-  sorry

963---  ### Multiple Induction Hypotheses
964-
965---  Recall the definition of the reflexive, transitive, closure of a
966---  relation:
967-
968-namespace ClosReflTransRemainder
969-
970-inductive ClosReflTrans {α : Type} (R : α → α → Prop) : α → α → Prop where
971-  | rt_step {x y : α} (h : R x y) : ClosReflTrans R x y
972-  | rt_refl {x : α} : ClosReflTrans R x x
973-  | rt_trans {x y z : α}
974-    (h₁ : ClosReflTrans R x y)
975-    (h₂ : ClosReflTrans R y z) :
976-    ClosReflTrans R x z
977-end ClosReflTransRemainder
978-
979---  Let's say that a relation on a type `α` is *diagonal* if it refines the
980---  identity relation ─ i.e., if `R x y` implies `x = y`.
981-
982-def Diagonal {α : Type} (R : α → α → Prop) := ∀ {x y}, R x y → x = y
983-
984---  Now consider the following lemma about diagonal relations:
985-
986-theorem closure_of_diagonal_is_diagonal {α} (R : α → α → Prop)
987-    (hDiag : Diagonal R) :
988-    Diagonal (ClosReflTrans R) := by
989-  intro x y h
990-  induction h with
991-  /- The two first cases go as you'd expect... -/
992-  | rt_step hr =>
993-    rw [hDiag hr]
994-  | rt_refl => rfl
995-  /- ...  but something interesting happens here: there are two
996-       induction hypotheses, `ih` and `ih'`! If you think about it, it
997-       is not that weird: we are in the case `rt_trans`, which has
998-       two recursive components, `hxy`, relating `x` to `y` and `hyz`,
999-       relating `y` to `z`. Hence we may want (and will actually need)
1000-       an induction hypothesis for `hxy` and one for `hyz` ─ they are
1001-       called `ihxy` and `ihyz` here. In general, Lean will always
1002-       generate one induction hypothesis per recursive constructor of
1003-       the type being inducted over. -/
1004-  | rt_trans _ _ ihxy ihyz => rw [ihxy, ihyz]
1005-

1075---  ## Exercising with Inductive Relations
1076-
1077---  Just as a single-argument proposition defines a *property*, a
1078---  two-argument proposition defines a *relation*.
1079---
1080---  A proposition parameterized by a number (such as `Ev`) can be thought
1081---  of as a *property* — i.e., it defines a subset of `Nat`, namely those
1082---  numbers for which the proposition is provable. In the same way, a
1083---  two-argument proposition can be thought of as a *relation* — i.e., it
1084---  defines a set of pairs for which the proposition is provable.
1085-
1086-namespace Playground
1087-
1088---  Just like properties, relations can be defined inductively. One useful
1089---  example is the "less than or equal to" relation on numbers that we
1090---  briefly saw above.
1091-
1092-inductive Le : Nat → Nat → Prop where
1093-  | refl {n : Nat}                : Le n n
1094-  | succ {n m : Nat} (h : Le n m) : Le n (m + 1)
1095-
1096---  (We've written the definition a bit differently this time, giving
1097---  explicit names to the arguments to the constructors and moving them to
1098---  the left of the colons.)
1099---
1100---  Proofs of facts about `≤` using the constructors `Nat.le.refl` and
1101---  `Nat.le.step` follow the same patterns as proofs about properties, like
1102---  `Ev` above. We can `apply` the constructors to prove `≤` goals (e.g.,
1103---  to show that `3 ≤ 3` or `3 ≤ 6`), and we can use tactics like
1104---  `inversion` to extract information from `≤` hypotheses in the context
1105---  (e.g., to prove that `(2 ≤ 1) → 2 + 2 = 5`.)
1106---
1107---  Here are some sanity checks on the definition. (Notice that, although
1108---  these are the same kind of simple "unit tests" as we gave for the
1109---  testing functions we wrote in the first few lectures, we must construct
1110---  their proofs explicitly ─ `rw` and `rfl` don't do the job, because the
1111---  proofs aren't just a matter of simplifying computations.)
1112---
1113---  Some sanity checks...
1114-
1115-theorem test_le1 : 3 ≤ 3 := by
1116-  apply Nat.le.refl
1117-
1118-theorem test_le2 : 3 ≤ 6 := by
1119-  apply Nat.le.step; apply Nat.le.step; apply Nat.le.step; apply Nat.le.refl
1120-
1121-theorem test_le3 (h : 2 ≤ 1) : 2 + 2 = 5 := by
1122-  inversion h with
1123-  | step h' => inversion h'
1124-
1125---  The "strictly less than" relation `n < m` can now be defined in terms
1126---  of `Nat.le`.
1127-
1128-def lt (n m : Nat) : Prop := Nat.le (n + 1) m
1129-
1130---  The `≥` operation is defined in terms of `≤`. Lean provides a theorem
1131---  `ge_iff_le` allowing us to rewrite between them.
1132-
1133-def ge (m n : Nat) : Prop := Nat.le n m
1134-
1135-example (m n : Nat) (h : m ≥ n) : n ≤ m := by
1136-  rw [← ge_iff_le]; assumption
1137-
1138-end Playground
1139-
1140---  From the definition of `Nat.le`, we can sketch the behaviors of `cases`
1141---  and `induction` on a hypothesis `h` providing evidence of the form
1142---  `n ≤ m`. Doing `cases h` will generate two cases. In the first case,
1143---  `n = m`, and it will replace instances of `m` with `n` in the goal and
1144---  context. In the second case, `n = m' + 1` for some `m'` for which
1145---  `n ≤ m'` holds, and it will replace instances of `m` with `m' + 1`.
1146---  Doing `inversion h` will remove impossible cases and add generated
1147---  equalities to the context for further use. Doing `induction h` will, in
1148---  the second case, add the induction hypothesis that the goal holds when
1149---  `m` is replaced with `m'`.
1150---

1152---  going to need later in the course. The proofs make good practice
1153---  exercises.

1233-  | c5 {m n k : Nat} (h : R  m       n       k)      : R  n      m       k

1262---  ### Exercise (4 stars): subsequence (Advanced) ⭐⭐⭐⭐
1263-
1264---  A list is a *subsequence* of another list if all of the elements in the
1265---  first list occur in the same order in the second list, possibly with
1266---  some extra elements in between. For example,
1267---
1268---      [1, 2, 3]
1269---
1270---  is a subsequence of each of the lists
1271---
1272---      [1, 2, 3]
1273---      [1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3]
1274---      [1, 2, 7, 3]
1275---      [5, 6, 1, 9, 9, 2, 7, 3, 8]
1276---
1277---  but it is *not* a subsequence of any of the lists
1278---
1279---      [1, 2]
1280---      [1, 3]
1281---      [5, 6, 2, 1, 7, 3, 8].
1282---

1535---  The *pigeonhole principle* states a basic fact about counting: if we
1536---  distribute more than `n` items into `n` pigeonholes, some pigeonhole
1537---  must contain at least two items. As often happens, this apparently
1538---  trivial fact about numbers requires non-trivial machinery to prove, but
1539---  we now have enough...

5---  # Induction: Proof by Induction
6-
7---  This chapter shows how to carry out *proofs by induction*, one of the
8---  most fundamental reasoning tools in computer science and mathematics,
9---  in Lean.
10-
11---  ## Separate Compilation
12-
13---  Before getting started on this chapter, we need to import all of our
14---  definitions from the previous chapter:
15-
16---  For this `import` to work, Lean needs to be able to find a compiled
17---  version of the previous chapter (`Basics.lean`). This compiled version,
18---  called `Basics.olean`, is analogous to the `.class` files compiled from
19---  `.java` source files and the `.o` files compiled from `.c` files.
20---
21---  When using Lake (Lean's build system), the file `lakefile.toml`
22---  specifies dependencies and build configuration. Running `lake build`
23---  will compile all necessary files in the correct order.
24---
25---  If you are using VS Code with the Lean 4 extension, compilation happens
26---  automatically in the background. When you open a file, the extension
27---  compiles its dependencies as needed.
28---
29---  Troubleshooting:
30---
31---  - If you get complaints about missing imports, make sure you have run
32---    `lake build` from the project root directory in a terminal, at least
33---    once.
34---
35---  - If you modify `Basics.lean`, VS Code will automatically recompile it
36---    when you save. You may need to reopen this file or wait for
37---    recompilation to finish.
38---
39---  - If you get errors that seem inconsistent with the source, try running
40---    `lake clean` followed by `lake build` to recompile everything from
41---    scratch.
42---
43---    (If you are using the Lean 4 extension for VS Code, you can also
44---    restart the extension on the current file via the `Restart File`
45---    button in the InfoView. The extension should prompt you to do this if
46---    you change things upstream in the dependency tree.)

166-
167---  ## Proof by Induction
168-
169---  We will introduce proofs by induction on natural numbers, first
170---  motivating why induction is needed, and then explaining what it is and
171---  how you do it in Lean.
172-
173---  ### Motivation
174-
175---  We defined `add` to recurse on its *second* argument:
176-
177-sf_recall
178-  def add (n : Nat) (m : Nat) : Nat :=
179-    match m with
180-    | zero => n
181-    | succ m' => succ (add n m')
182-
183---  For the `add_zero` simplification rule, we were able to prove that
184---  `zero` is a neutral element for `+` on the *right* using just `rfl`.
185-
186---      theorem add_zero : ∀ (n : Nat), n + zero = n := by
187---        intro n
188---        rfl
189---
190---  This worked because `n + zero` reduces to `n` by definition. What if we
191---  wanted to prove a rule that `zero` is also a neutral element on the
192---  *left*? Just applying `rfl` doesn't work, since the `n` in `zero + n`
193---  is an arbitrary unknown number, so the `match` in the definition of `+`
194---  can't be reduced.
195-
196-sf_expect_failure_in
197-  example (n : Nat) : zero + n = n := by
198-    rfl    -- doesn't work here!
199-
200---  Output:
201---    Tactic `rfl` failed: The left-hand side
202---      zero + n
203---    is not definitionally equal to the right-hand side
204---      n
205---
206---    n : Nat
207---    ⊢ zero + n = n
208-
209---  And reasoning by cases using `cases` on `n` doesn't get us much
210---  further: the branch of the case analysis where we assume `n = zero`
211---  goes through just fine, but in the branch where `n = n' + 1` for some
212---  `n'` we get stuck in exactly the same way.
213-
214-sf_expect_failure_in
215-  example (n : Nat) : zero + n = n := by
216-    cases n with
217-    | zero => /- n = zero -/
218-      rewrite [add_zero]
219-      rfl
220-      -- so far so good...
221-    | succ n' =>   /- n = succ n' -/
222-      _     -- ...but we're stuck on zero + n'
223-
224---  Output:
225---    unsolved goals
226---    case succ
227---    n' : Nat
228---    ⊢ zero + succ n' = succ n'
229-
230---  We could use `cases` on `n'` to get a bit further, but, since `n` can
231---  be arbitrarily large, we'll never get all the way there if we just go
232---  on like this.
233-
234---  ### Induction: In Principle and in Lean
235-
236---  To prove interesting facts about numbers, lists, and other inductively
237---  defined sets, we often need a more powerful reasoning principle:
238---  *induction*.
239---
240---  Recall (from a discrete math course, probably) the *principle of
241---  induction over natural numbers*: If `P(n)` is some proposition
242---  involving a natural number `n` and we want to show that `P` holds for
243---  all numbers `n`, we can reason like this:
244---
245---  - show that `P(zero)` holds;
246---  - show that, for any `n'`, if `P(n')` holds, then so does `P(succ n')`;
247---  - conclude that `P(n)` holds for all `n`.
248---
249---  In Lean, the steps are the same: we begin with the goal of proving
250---  `P(n)` for all `n` and use the `induction` tactic to break it down into
251---  two separate subgoals: one where we must show `P(zero)` and another
252---  where we must show `P(n') → P(succ n')`. Here's how this works for the
253---  theorem at hand...
254-
255-theorem zero_add (n : Nat) : zero + n = n := by
256-  induction n with
257-  | zero => /- n = zero -/
258-    rewrite [add_zero]
259-    rfl
260-  | succ n' ih => /- n = succ n' -/
261-    /-
262-      Goal: zero + (succ n') = succ n'
263-      We can rewrite `zero + (succ n')` to `succ (zero + n')`.
264-      Then we can rewrite with the induction hypothesis.
265-    -/
266-    rewrite [add_succ, ih]
267-    rfl
268-
269---  Like `cases`, the `induction` tactic takes a `with` clause that
270---  specifies the names of the variables to be introduced in the subgoals.
271---  Since there are two subgoals (for `zero` and `succ`), the `with` clause
272---  has two branches.
273---
274---  In the first subgoal, `n` is replaced by `zero`. The goal becomes
275---  `zero + zero = zero`, which follows by `rewrite [add_zero]` and `rfl`.
276---
277---  In the second subgoal, `n` is replaced by `succ n'`, and the induction
278---  hypothesis `ih : zero + n' = n'` is added to the context. The goal
279---  becomes `zero + (succ n') = succ n'`. `add_succ` tells us that
280---  `a + (succ b) = succ (a + b)`, so `rewrite [add_succ]` transforms the
281---  goal to `succ (zero + n') = succ n'`. Then `rewrite [ih]` rewrites
282---  `zero + n'` to `n'`, and the goal becomes `succ n' = succ n'`, which
283---  closes with reflexivity.
284-

286---  numbers.

290-  | zero =>
291-    rewrite [zero_beq_zero]
292-    rfl
293-  | succ n' ih =>
294-    rewrite [succ_beq_succ]
295-    exact ih
