1196---  ## Working with Decidable Properties
1197-
1198---  We've seen two different ways of expressing logical claims in Lean:
1199---  with *booleans* (of type `Bool`), and with *propositions* (of type
1200---  `Prop`). Here are the key differences between `Bool` and `Prop`:
1201---
1202---      |                     | `Bool` | `Prop` |
1203---      | ------------------- | ------ | ------ |
1204---      | decidable?          | yes    | no     |
1205---      | useable with match? | yes    | no     |
1206-
1207---  The crucial difference between the two worlds is *decidability*. Every
1208---  (closed) expression of type `Bool` can be simplified in a finite number
1209---  of steps to either `true` or `false` — i.e., there is a terminating
1210---  mechanical procedure for deciding whether or not it is `true`.
1211---
1212---  This means that, for example, the type `Nat → Bool` is inhabited only
1213---  by functions that, given a `Nat`, always yield either `true` or `false`
1214---  in finite time; this, in turn, means (by a standard computability
1215---  argument) that there is *no* function in `Nat → Bool` that checks
1216---  whether a given number is the code of a terminating Turing machine.
1217---
1218---  By contrast, the type `Prop` includes both decidable and undecidable
1219---  mathematical propositions; in particular, the type `Nat → Prop` does
1220---  contain functions representing properties like "the nth Turing machine
1221---  halts."
1222---
1223---  The second table row follows directly from this essential difference.
1224---  To evaluate a pattern match (or conditional) on a boolean, we need to
1225---  know whether the scrutinee evaluates to `true` or `false`; this only
1226---  works for `Bool`, not `Prop`.
1227-
1228---  Since `Prop` includes *both* decidable and undecidable properties, we
1229---  have two options when we want to formalize a property that happens to
1230---  be decidable: we can express it either as a boolean computation, or as
1231---  a function into `Prop`.
1232---
1233---  For instance, to claim that a number `n` is even, we can say either
1234---  that `Nat.even n` evaluates to `true`...
1235-
1236-example : Nat.even 42 = true := rfl
1237-
1238---  ... or that there exists some `k` such that `n = double k`.
1239-
1240-example : Nat.Even 42 := by rw [Nat.Even]; exists 21
1241-
1242---  Of course, it would be deeply strange if these two characterizations of
1243---  evenness did not describe the same set of natural numbers! Fortunately,
1244---  they do!
1245---
1246---  To prove this, we first need two helper lemmas.
1247-
1248-theorem even_double (k : Nat) :
1249-    Nat.even (Nat.double k) = true := by
1250-  induction k with
1251-  | zero => rw [Nat.double_zero]; rfl
1252-  | succ k' ih => rw [Nat.double_succ]; exact ih
1253-
1254-theorem even_double_conv (n : Nat) : ∃ k : Nat,
1255-    n = bif Nat.even n then Nat.double k else Nat.double k + 1 := by
1256-  sorry
1257-
1258---  Now the main theorem:
1259-
1260-theorem Nat.even_bool_prop (n : Nat) : Nat.even n = true ↔ Even n := by
1261-  constructor
1262-  · intro h
1263-    obtain ⟨k, hk⟩ := even_double_conv n
1264-    rw [h] at hk; rw [cond_true] at hk; rw [Even]; exists k
1265-  · intro ⟨k, hk⟩; rw [hk]; apply even_double
1266-
1267---  In view of this theorem, we can say that the boolean computation
1268---  `Nat.even n` is *reflected* in the truth of the proposition
1269---  `∃ k, n = Nat.double k`.
1270-
1271---  Similarly, to state that two numbers `n` and `m` are equal, we can say
1272---  either
1273---
1274---  1. that `n == m` returns `true`, or
1275---  2. that `n = m`.
1276---
1277---  Again, these two notions are equivalent:
1278---
1279---  (For the reverse direction we need the simple fact that `==` is
1280---  reflexive.)
1281---
1282---  Don't worry too much about `Nat.beq_eq_true_eq` yet, we need this from
1283---  Lean because `n == m` is a wrapper of `DecidableEq Nat`. We will go
1284---  over this in the Typeclasses chapter.
1285-
1286-theorem beq_eq_true (n m : Nat) :
1287-    (n == m) = true ↔ n = m := by
1288-  rw [Nat.beq_eq_true_eq]
1289-
1290---  So what should we do in situations where some claim could be formalized
1291---  as either a proposition or a boolean computation? Which should we
1292---  choose?
1293---
1294---  In general, *both* can be useful. For example, booleans are more useful
1295---  for defining functions, since we can test whether they are true using
1296---  conditional expressions.
1297-
1298-def is_even_prime (n : Nat) : Bool :=
1299-  bif n == 2 then true else false
1300-
1301---  Beyond the fact that non-computable properties are possible in general
1302---  to phrase as boolean computations, even many *computable* properties
1303---  are easier to express using `Prop` than `Bool`, since recursive
1304---  function definitions are subject to significant restrictions. For
1305---  instance, the next chapter shows how to define the property that a
1306---  regular expression matches a given string using `Prop`. Doing the same
1307---  with `Bool` would amount to writing a regular expression matching
1308---  algorithm, which would be more complicated, harder to understand, and
1309---  harder to reason about than a simple (non-algorithmic) definition of
1310---  this property.
1311---
1312---  Conversely, an important side benefit of stating facts using booleans
1313---  is enabling some proof automation through computation with terms, a
1314---  technique known as *proof by reflection*.
1315---
1316---  Consider the following statement:
1317-
1318---  The most direct way to prove this is to give the value of `k`
1319---  explicitly.
1320-
1321-example : Nat.Even 100 := by
1322-  exists 50
1323-
1324---  The proof of the corresponding boolean statement is simpler, because we
1325---  don't have to invent the witness `50`: computation does it for us!
1326-
1327-example : Nat.even 100 = true := rfl
1328-
1329---  Now, the useful observation is that, since the two notions are
1330---  equivalent, we can use the boolean formulation to prove the other one
1331---  without mentioning the value 50 explicitly:
1332-
1333-example : Nat.Even 100 := by
1334-  obtain ⟨h, _⟩ := Nat.even_bool_prop 100
1335-  apply h; rfl
1336-
1337---  Although we haven't gained much in terms of proof-script simplicity in
1338---  this case, larger proofs can often be made considerably simpler by the
1339---  use of reflection.
1340---
1341---  As an extreme example, a famous mechanized proof of the even more
1342---  famous *four colour theorem* uses reflection to reduce the analysis of
1343---  hundreds of different cases to a boolean computation.
1344---
1345---  Another advantage of booleans is that the *negation* of a claim about
1346---  booleans is straightforward to state and (when true) to prove: simply
1347---  flip the expected boolean result.
1348-
1349-example : Nat.even 101 = false := rfl
1350-
1351---  In contrast, propositional negation can be difficult to work with
1352---  directly. For example, suppose we state the nonevenness of `101`
1353---  propositionally:
1354---
1355---  Proving this directly — by assuming that there is some `n` such that
1356---  `101 = Nat.double n` and then somehow reasoning to a contradiction —
1357---  would be rather complicated.
1358---
1359---  But if we convert it to a claim about the boolean `Nat.even` function,
1360---  we can let Lean do the work for us.
1361-
1362-example : ¬ Nat.Even 101 := by
1363-  intro h; apply (Nat.even_bool_prop 101).mpr at h
1364-  rw [Nat.even] at h; contradiction
1365-
1366---  Conversely, there are situations where it can be easier to work with
1367---  propositions rather than booleans. In particular, knowing that
1368---  `(n == m) = true` is generally of little direct help in the middle of a
1369---  proof involving `n` and `m`. But if we convert the statement to the
1370---  equivalent form `n = m`, then we can easily rewrite with it.
1371-
1372-theorem add_beq_true (n m p : Nat) (h : (n == m) = true) :
1373-    (n + p == m + p) = true := by
1374-  apply (beq_eq_true n m).mp at h
1375-  rw [h, BEq.rfl]
1376-
1377---  We'll come back to reflection and decidable propositions in a later
1378---  chapter, but it serves as a good example showing the different
1379---  strengths of booleans and general propositions. Being able to cross
1380---  back and forth between the boolean and propositional worlds will often
1381---  be convenient in later chapters.

1448---  ## The Logic of Lean
1449-
1450---  Lean's logical core differs in some important ways from other formal
1451---  systems that are used by mathematicians to write down precise and
1452---  rigorous definitions and proofs – in particular from Zermelo–Fraenkel
1453---  Set Theory (ZFC), the most popular foundation for paper-and-pencil
1454---  mathematics.
1455---
1456---  We conclude this chapter with a brief discussion of some of the most
1457---  significant differences between these two worlds.
1458-
1459---  ### Propositional Extensionality
1460-
1461---  Lean's logic is quite minimalistic. This means that one occasionally
1462---  encounters cases where translating standard mathematical reasoning into
1463---  Lean is cumbersome - or even impossible - unless we enrich its core
1464---  logic with additional axioms.
1465-
1466---  For example, the equality assertions that we have seen so far mostly
1467---  have concerned elements of inductive types (`Nat`, `Bool`, etc.). But
1468---  since the equality operator is polymorphic, we can use it at *any* type
1469---
1470---  - in particular, we can write propositions claiming that two
1471---    *propositions* are equal to each other:
1472-
1473-#check (∀ a b : Prop, (a ∧ b) = (b ∧ a) : Prop)
1474-
1475---  This is an equality between two conjunctions, which itself is also a
1476---  proposition. It states that commuted conjunctions are equal
1477---  propositions. However, we cannot prove this equality by reflexivity, as
1478---  the two sides don't compute to the same term, and we cannot proceed by
1479---  cases on `a` or `b`, as they are not inductive.
1480-
1481-sf_expect_failure_in
1482-  example (a b : Prop) : a ∧ b = b ∧ a := by rfl
1483-
1484---  Output:
1485---    Tactic `rfl` failed: The left-hand side
1486---      a
1487---    is not definitionally equal to the right-hand side
1488---      b = b ∧ a
1489---
1490---    a✝ b✝ c : Prop
1491---    n m : Nat
1492---    α✝ : Type
1493---    e1 e2 x✝ y✝ : α✝
1494---    α β : Type
1495---    x x' y : α
1496---    l l' : List α
1497---    f g : α → β
1498---    p : α → Prop
1499---    a b : Prop
1500---    ⊢ a ∧ b = b ∧ a
1501-
1502-sf_expect_failure_in
1503-  example (a b : Prop) : a ∧ b = b ∧ a := by cases a

1507---      Prop

1509---    Explanation: the `cases` tactic is for constructor-based reasoning as well as for applying custom cases principles with a 'using' clause or a registered '@[cases_eliminator]' theorem. The above type neither is an inductive type nor has a registered theorem.
1510---

1524-
1525---  However, we *can* prove that `a ∧ b` implies `b ∧ a`, and vice versa --
1526---  this is the commutativity of conjunction that we have seen earlier.
1527-
1528-#check and_comm
1529-
1530---  Output:
1531---    and_comm {a b : Prop} : a ∧ b ↔ b ∧ a
1532-
1533---  Since it would be convenient to be able to rewrite propositions from
1534---  one side of `↔` to the other, Lean provides an axiom to turn `↔` into
1535---  `=`, which is called *propositional extensionality* (`propext`).
1536-
1537-#print propext
1538-
1539---  Output:
1540---    axiom propext : ∀ {a b : Prop}, (a ↔ b) → a = b
1541-
1542---  (Informally, an *extensional* property is one that pertains to
1543---  observable behavior. Thus, propositional extensionality means that a
1544---  proposition's identity is completely determined by what we can observe
1545---  from it — i.e., whether the proposition holds. We can state this more
1546---  explicitly:)
1547-
1548-theorem prop_true (a : Prop) (h : a) : a = True := by
1549-  apply propext
1550-  constructor
1551-  · intro _
1552-    exact ⟨⟩
1553-  · intro _
1554-    exact h
1555-
1556---  Lean provides an `ext` tactic that applies `propext` for us. We can use
1557---  it to show that commuted conjoined propositions are equal. Similarly,
1558---  we can use it to show that reassociated conjoined propositions are
1559---  equal as well.
1560-
1561-theorem and_comm_eq (a b : Prop) : (a ∧ b) = (b ∧ a) := by
1562-  ext; apply and_comm
1563-
1564-theorem and_assoc_eq (a b c : Prop) : ((a ∧ b) ∧ c) = (a ∧ (b ∧ c)) := by
1565-  ext; apply and_assoc
1566-
1567---  Here is an example of where using `=` instead of `↔` is more
1568---  convenient: we show that it's possible to "flip" three conjoined
1569---  propositions.
1570---
1571---  One way to prove this is to construct the `↔`, destruct the `↔`s
1572---  provided by `and_comm` and `and_assoc`, and apply the resulting
1573---  implications a few times. But this is a lot of hassle, when the proof
1574---  is conceptually simple: we flip `b` and `c`, then we flip that
1575---  conjunction with `a`, and we finish by associativity. By using
1576---  `and_comm_eq`, this is easily done by rewriting equal propositions.
1577-
1578-theorem and_comm_flip (a b c : Prop) : (a ∧ b ∧ c) ↔ (c ∧ b ∧ a) := by
1579-  rw [and_comm_eq b c, and_comm_eq a, and_assoc_eq]
1580-
1581---  The pattern of deriving an equality of propositions out of `↔` then
1582---  rewriting by that equality is so common that Lean will implicitly cast
1583---  `↔` to `=`, allowing you to rewrite on `↔` directly. Notice that `rw`
1584---  is also able to close goals of the form `a ↔ a` by reflexivity.
1585-
1586-theorem and_comm_flip' (a b c : Prop) : (a ∧ b ∧ c) ↔ (c ∧ b ∧ a) := by
1587-  rw [@and_comm b c, @and_comm a, and_assoc]
1588-
1589---  Under the hood, this proof still uses `propext`, which you can check by
1590---  asking for all of the axioms used by a declaration.

1623---  ### Functional Extensionality
1624-
1625---  We can also write propositions claiming that two *functions* are equal
1626---  to each other. In some cases, we can also prove that two functions are
1627---  equal by reflexivity when both reduce to the same expression:
1628-
1629-example : (fun x => x + 2) = (fun x => x + (Nat.pred 3)) := rfl
1630-
1631---  In general, functions can be equal for more interesting reasons. In
1632---  common mathematical practice, two functions `f` and `g` are considered
1633---  equal if they produce the same output on every input:
1634---
1635---      (∀ x, f x = g x) → f = g
1636---
1637---  This is known as *functional extensionality*, which Lean provides as
1638---  `funext`.
1639-
1640-#check (fun f g => funext (f := f) (g := g) :
1641-    ∀ {α β : Type} (f g : α → β), (∀ x, f x = g x) → f = g)
1642-
1643---  Here, functional extensionality means that a function's identity is
1644---  completely determined by what we can observe from it — i.e., the
1645---  results we obtain after applying it. (Its full type is actually
1646---  slightly more general, and is defined in terms of a more fundamental
1647---  concept called *quotients* rather than added directly as an axiom, but
1648---  we will only discuss `funext` here. This is also why, when printing
1649---  axioms for theorems using `funext`, it will instead display a
1650---  `Quot.sound` axiom.)
1651-
1652-#print axioms funext
1653-
1654---  Output:
1655---    'funext' depends on axioms: [Quot.sound]
1656-
1657---  Now we can prove some intuitively obvious equalities about functions
1658---  that would otherwise not be provable without `funext`.
1659-

1707---  One problem with the definition of the list-reversing function
1708---  `List.rev` is that it performs a call to `++` on each step. Running
1709---  `++` takes time asymptotically linear in the size of the list, which
1710---  means that `List.rev` is asymptotically quadratic.
1711---
1712---  We can improve this with the following two-argument definition:
1713-
1714-def revAppend {α} (xs ys : List α) : List α :=
1715-  match xs with
1716-  | [] => ys
1717-  | x :: xs => revAppend xs (x :: ys)
1718-
1719-theorem revAppend_nil {α : Type} {xs : List α} : revAppend [] xs = xs := rfl
1720-
1721-theorem revAppend_cons {α : Type} {x : α} {xs ys : List α} :
1722-    revAppend (x :: xs) ys = revAppend xs (x :: ys) := rfl
1723-
1724-def trRev {α} (xs : List α) : List α := revAppend xs []
1725-

1727---  recursive call to the function is the last operation that needs to be
1728---  performed (i.e., we don't have to execute `++` after the recursive
1729---  call); a decent compiler will generate very efficient code in this
1730---  case.
1731---

1739---  ### Classical vs. Constructive Logic
1740-
1741---  We have seen that it is not possible to test whether or not a
1742---  proposition `a` holds while defining a Lean function. You may be
1743---  surprised to learn that a similar restriction applies in *proofs*! In
1744---  other words, the following intuitive reasoning principle is not
1745---  derivable in Lean with the tools we've seen so far:
1746-
1747-def ExcludedMiddle := ∀ a : Prop, a ∨ ¬ a
1748-
1749---  To understand operationally why this is the case, recall that, to prove
1750---  a statement of the form `a ∨ b`, we use the `left` and `right` tactics,
1751---  which effectively require knowing which side of the disjunction holds.
1752---  But the universally quantified `a` in `ExcludedMiddle` is an
1753---  *arbitrary* proposition, which we know nothing about. We don't have
1754---  enough information to choose which of `left` or `right` to apply.
1755---
1756---  However, in the special case where we happen to know that `a` is
1757---  reflected in some boolean term `b`, knowing whether it holds or not is
1758---  trivial: we just have to check the value of `b`.
1759-
1760-theorem restricted_excluded_middle (a : Prop) (b : Bool) (h : a ↔ b = true) :
1761-    a ∨ ¬ a := by
1762-  cases b with
1763-  | false => right; rw [h]; intro; contradiction
1764-  | true => left; rw [h]
1765-
1766---  In particular, the excluded middle is valid for equations `n = m`
1767---  between natural numbers `n` and `m`.
1768-
1769-theorem excluded_middle_nat_eq (n m : Nat) : n = m ∨ n ≠ m := by
1770-  apply restricted_excluded_middle (n = m) (n == m)
1771-  symm; apply beq_eq_true
1772-
1773---  Sadly, this trick only works for decidable propositions.
1774-
1775---  Logical systems in which excluded middle does not hold are referred to
1776---  as *constructive logics*. They are so called because to prove a
1777---  proposition, we must give a construction for it; for instance, a proof
1778---  of `∃ x, p x` is proven by providing a particular value of `x`.
1779---
1780---  Logical systems in which excluded middle does hold, such as ZFC set
1781---  theory, are referred to as *classical*. Lean provides classical
1782---  reasoning principles in the `Classical` library, including excluded
1783---  middle.
1784-
1785-#check Classical.em
1786-
1787---  Output:
1788---    Classical.em (p : Prop) : p ∨ ¬p
1789-
1790---  All classical reasoning principles in `Classical` are derived from one
1791---  axiom, the axiom of choice. This is the C in ZFC.
1792-
1793-#print Classical.choice
1794-
1795---  Output:
1796---    axiom Classical.choice.{u} : {α : Sort u} → Nonempty α → α
1797-
1798-#print axioms Classical.em
1799-
1800---  Output:
1801---    'Classical.em' depends on axioms: [propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound]
1802-
1803---  Lean also provides a `by_cases` tactic that applies `Classical.em` on a
1804---  given proposition. Theorems proven using this tactic implicitly use
1805---  classical axioms.
1806-
1807-theorem em : ∀ a, a ∨ ¬ a := by
1808-  intro a
1809-  by_cases h : a
1810-  /- h : a -/
1811-  · left; exact h
1812-  /- h : ¬ a -/
1813-  · right; exact h
1814-
1815-#print axioms em
1816-
1817---  Output:
1818---    'em' depends on axioms: [propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound]
1819-
1820---  The following example illustrates why assuming the excluded middle may
1821---  lead to nonconstructive proofs:
1822---
1823---  *Claim*: There exist irrational numbers `n` and `m` such that `n ^ m`
1824---  (`n` to the power `m`) is rational.
1825---
1826---  *Proof*: It is not difficult to show that `sqrt 2` is irrational. So if
1827---  `sqrt 2 ^ sqrt 2` is rational, it suffices to take `n = m = sqrt 2` and
1828---  we are done. Otherwise, `sqrt 2 ^ sqrt 2` is irrational. In this case,
1829---  we can take `a = sqrt 2 ^ sqrt 2` and `b = sqrt 2`, since
1830---  `a ^ b = sqrt 2 ^ (sqrt 2 * sqrt 2) = sqrt 2 ^ 2 = 2`. QED.
1831---
1832---  Do you see what happened here? We used the excluded middle to consider
1833---  separately the cases where `sqrt 2 ^ sqrt 2` is rational and where it
1834---  is not, without knowing which one actually holds! Because of this, we
1835---  finish the proof knowing that such `n` and `m` exist, but not being
1836---  sure of their actual values.
1837---
1838---  As useful as constructive logic is, it does have its limitations: There
1839---  are many statements that can easily be proven in classical logic but
1840---  that have only much more complicated constructive proofs, and there are
1841---  some that are known to have no constructive proof at all! Fortunately,
1842---  like functional extensionality, the excluded middle is known to be
1843---  compatible with Lean's logic, allowing it to be added safely as an
1844---  axiom. However, the results that we cover in Logical Foundations can be
1845---  developed entirely within constructive logic.
1846---
1847---  It takes some practice to understand which proof techniques must be
1848---  avoided in constructive reasoning, but arguments by contradiction, in
1849---  particular, are infamous for leading to nonconstructive proofs. Here's
1850---  a typical example: suppose that we want to show that there exists `x`
1851---  with some property `p`, i.e., such that `p x`. We start by assuming
1852---  that our conclusion is false; that is, `¬ ∃ x, p x`. From this premise,
1853---  it is not hard to derive `∀ x, ¬ p x`. If we manage to show that this
1854---  results in a contradiction, we arrive at an existence proof without
1855---  ever exhibiting a value of `x` for which `p x` holds!
1856---
1857---  The technical flaw here, from a constructive standpoint, is that we
1858---  claimed to prove `∃ x, p x` using a proof of `¬ ¬ ∃ x, p x`. Allowing
1859---  ourselves to remove double negations from arbitrary statements is
1860---  equivalent to assuming the excluded middle law, as shown in one of the
1861---  exercises below.
1862-
1863---  Once again, Lean's `Classical` library provides double negation
1864---  elimination, which relies on the `Classical.choice` axiom.
1865-
1866-#check Classical.not_not
1867-
1868-#print axioms Classical.not_not
1869-
1870---  Output:
1871---    Classical.not_not {a : Prop} : ¬¬a ↔ a
1872-
1873---  Output:
1874---    'Classical.not_not' depends on axioms: [propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound]
1875-
1876---  ### Exercise (3 stars): excluded_middle_irrefutable ⭐⭐⭐
1877-
1878---  The following theorem implies that it is always safe to assume a
1879---  decidability axiom (i.e., an instance of excluded middle) for any
1880---  *particular* proposition `a`. Why? Because the negation of such an
1881---  axiom leads to a contradiction. If `¬ (a ∨ ¬ a)` were provable, then by
1882---  `de_morgan_not_or` as proven above, `a ∧ ¬ a` would be provable, which
1883---  would be a contradiction. So, it is safe to add `a ∨ ¬ a` as an axiom
1884---  for any particular `a`.
1885-
1886-theorem excluded_middle_irrefutable (a : Prop) : ¬ ¬ (a ∨ ¬ a) := by
1887-  sorry
1888-
1889---  ### Exercise (3 stars): not_exists_dist (Advanced) ⭐⭐⭐
1890-
1891---  It is a theorem of classical logic that the following two assertions
1892---  are equivalent:
1893---
1894---      ¬ ∃ x, ¬ p x
1895---      ∀ x, p x
1896---
1897---  The `dist_not_exists` theorem proves one side of this equivalence.
1898---  Interestingly, the other direction cannot be proven in constructive
1899---  logic, but we can prove it here using `by_cases`.
1900-
1901-theorem not_exists_dist (α : Type) (p : α → Prop) :
1902-    (¬ ∃ x : α, ¬ p x) → (∀ x : α, p x) := by

1905---  ### Exercise (5 stars): classical_axioms (Optional) ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐
1906-
1907---  For those who like a challenge, here is an exercise adapted from the
1908---  Coq'Art book by Bertot and Casteran (p. 123). Each of the following
1909---  five statements, together with `ExcludedMiddle`, can be considered as
1910---  characterizing classical logic. We can't prove any one of them in Lean
1911---  without `Classical`, but adding any *one* of them as an axiom allows us
1912---  to work classically.
1913---
1914---  To see this, prove that all six propositions (these five plus
1915---  `ExcludedMiddle`) are equivalent.
1916---
1917---  Hint: Rather than considering all pairs of statements pairwise, prove a
1918---  single circular chain of implications that connects them all. You
1919---  should not use `by_cases`, as this implicitly introduces a dependency
1920---  on `ExcludedMiddle`.
1921-
1922-def Peirce := ∀ a b : Prop, ((a → b) → a) → a
1923-
1924-def NotNot := ∀ a : Prop, ¬ ¬ a → a
1925-
1926-def DeMorganNotAndNot := ∀ a b : Prop, ¬ (¬ a ∧ ¬ b) → a ∨ b
1927-
1928-def ImpOr := ∀ a b : Prop, (a → b) → (¬ a ∨ b)
1929-
1930-def ConsequentiaMirabilis := ∀ a : Prop, (¬ a → a) → a

6---  # Poly: Polymorphism and Higher-Order Functions
7-
8---  ## Polymorphism
9-
10---  In this chapter we continue our development of basic concepts of
11---  functional programming. The critical new ideas are *polymorphism*
12---  (abstracting functions over the types of the data they manipulate) and
13---  *higher-order functions* (treating functions as data). We begin with
14---  polymorphism.
15-
16---  ### Polymorphic Lists
17-
18---  In the last chapter, we worked with lists containing just numbers.
19---  Obviously, interesting programs also need to be able to manipulate
20---  lists with elements from other types — lists of booleans, lists of
21---  lists, etc. We *could* just define a new inductive datatype for each of
22---  these, for example...
23-
24-inductive BoolList : Type where
25-  | nil
26-  | cons (b : Bool) (l : BoolList)
27-
28---  ... but this would quickly become tedious: not only would we have to
29---  make up different constructor names for each datatype, but — even worse
30---  — we would also need to define new versions of all the list
31---  manipulating functions (`length`, `++`, `reverse`, etc.) and all their
32---  properties (`length_reverse`, `append_assoc`, etc.) for each new
33---  definition.
34-
35---  To avoid this repetition, we can make the element type itself an
36---  *argument* to the definition. Lean calls such definitions
37---  *polymorphic*. Here is a polymorphic list type:
38-
39-inductive MyList (α : Type) : Type where
40-  | nil : MyList α
41-  | cons (x : α) (l : MyList α) : MyList α
42-
43---  This is exactly like the definition of `Natlist` from the previous
44---  chapter, except that the `Nat` argument to the `cons` constructor has
45---  been replaced by an arbitrary type `α`, a type parameter `α` has been
46---  added to the header on the first line, and the occurrences of `Natlist`
47---  in the types of the constructors have been replaced by `MyList α`. We
48---  can now write `MyList Nat` instead of a dedicated nat-list type.
49---
50---  What sort of thing is `MyList` itself? A good way to think about it is
51---  as a *type constructor* — that is, a function from `Type`s to `Type`s.
52---  For any particular type `α`, the type `MyList α` is the inductively
53---  defined type of lists whose elements are of type `α`.
54-
55-#check (MyList)
56-
57---  Output:
58---    MyList : Type → Type
59-
60---  The `α` in the definition of `MyList` automatically becomes a parameter
61---  to the constructors `nil` and `cons` — that is, `nil` and `cons` are
62---  now polymorphic constructors. In Lean, the type parameter is *implicit*
63---  by default: Lean will infer it from context. For example, `MyList.nil`
64---  is the empty list, and Lean figures out the element type from how it is
65---  used.
66-
67-#check MyList.nil
68-
69---  Output:
70---    MyList.nil {α : Type} : MyList α
71-
72---  Similarly, `MyList.cons` adds an element of type `Nat` to a list of
73---  type `MyList Nat`. Here is an example of forming a list containing just
74---  the natural number `3`.
75-
76-#check MyList.cons 3 MyList.nil
77-
78---  Output:
79---    MyList.cons 3 MyList.nil : MyList Nat
80-
81---  What is the full type of `MyList.nil`? We can read off the result type
82---  `MyList α` from the definition, but to state the full type we must also
83---  bind `α`. Since the type argument to the constructor is implicit, Lean
84---  writes its type as (the equivalent of) `{α : Type} → MyList α`.
85-
86-#check MyList.nil
87-
88---  Output:
89---    MyList.nil {α : Type} : MyList α
90-
91---  Similarly, the type of `MyList.cons` includes the implicit type
92---  parameter:
93-
94-#check MyList.cons
95-
96---  Output:
97---    MyList.cons {α : Type} (x : α) (l : MyList α) : MyList α
98-
99---  Having to supply a type argument for every single use of a list
100---  constructor would be rather burdensome. Fortunately, the type argument
101---  is implicit, so Lean will normally infer it from context.
102---
103---  We can now go back and make polymorphic versions of all the
104---  list-processing functions that we wrote before. Here is `myRepeat`, for
105---  example:
106-
107-def myRepeat (α : Type) (x : α) (count : Nat) : MyList α :=
108-  match count with
109-  | 0 => .nil
110-  | count' + 1 => .cons x (myRepeat α x count')
111-
112---  Some simple facts about `myRepeat`:
113-
114-theorem myRepeat_zero (α : Type) (v : α) :
115-    myRepeat α v 0 = MyList.nil := rfl
116-
117-theorem myRepeat_succ (α : Type) (v : α) (count : Nat) :
118-    myRepeat α v (count + 1) = MyList.cons v (myRepeat α v count) := rfl
119-
120---  We can use `myRepeat` by applying it first to a type and then to an
121---  element of this type (and a number):
122-
123-example : myRepeat Nat 4 2 = .cons 4 (.cons 4 .nil) := by rfl
124-
125---  To use `myRepeat` to build other kinds of lists, we simply pass a
126---  different type and an element of that type:
127-
128-example : myRepeat Bool false 1 = .cons false .nil := by rfl
129-

174---   ----------------------------------------
175-
176---  From now on, we'll use Lean's built-in `List` type and its associated
177---  notation. The built-in `List` is defined just like our `MyList` above,
178---  but with notation `[]` for `List.nil`, `::` for `List.cons`, and
179---  `[1, 2, 3]` for list literals. The `++` operator is list append. The
180---  type arguments to the list constructors are implicit.
181-
182---  Using Lean's built-in list notations, we can now write lists in the
183---  natural way:
184-
185-example : List Nat := [1, 2, 3]
186-
187---  #### Type Annotation Inference
188-
189---  Let's write the definition of `myRepeat` again, but this time we won't
190---  specify the type of the parameter `α`. Will Lean still accept it?
191-
192-def myRepeat' α (x : α) (count : Nat) : List α :=
193-  match count with
194-  | 0 => .nil
195-  | count' + 1 => .cons x (myRepeat' α x count')
196-
197---  Indeed it will. Lean infers that `α` is a type.
198-
199-#check myRepeat'
200-
201---  Output:
202---    myRepeat'.{u_1} (α : Type u_1) (x : α) (count : Nat) : List α
203-
204---  The generated `u_1` is part of Lean's bookkeeping for treating types
205---  more generally. We will not need to interpret names like this for now —
206---  you can ignore them when they appear in Lean's output unless we
207---  explicitly call attention to them.
208-
209---  Lean was able to use *type inference* to deduce what the type of `α`
210---  must be, based on how it is used. Since `α` is an argument to `List`,
211---  it must be a `Type`, since `List` expects a `Type` as its argument.
212---
213---  This facility means we don't always have to write explicit type
214---  annotations everywhere, although explicit type annotations can still be
215---  quite useful as documentation, so we will continue to use them much of
216---  the time.
217-
218---  #### Type Argument Synthesis
219-
220---  To use a polymorphic function, we need to pass it one or more types in
221---  addition to its other arguments. For example, the recursive call in the
222---  body of the `myRepeat` function above must pass along the type `α`. But
223---  since the second argument to `myRepeat` is an element of `α`, it seems
224---  entirely obvious that the first argument can only be `α` — why should
225---  we have to write it explicitly?
226---
227---  Fortunately, Lean permits us to avoid this kind of redundancy. In place
228---  of any type argument we can write a "hole" `_`, which can be read as
229---  "Please try to figure out for yourself what belongs here." More
230---  precisely, when Lean encounters a `_`, it will attempt to *unify* all
231---  locally available information — the type of the function being applied,
232---  the types of the other arguments, and the type expected by the context
233---  in which the application appears — to determine what concrete type
234---  should replace the `_`.
235---
236---  Using holes, the `myRepeat'` function can be rewritten like this:
237-
238-def myRepeat'' (α : Type) (x : α) (count : Nat) : List α :=
239-  match count with
240-  | 0 => []
241-  | count' + 1 => x :: myRepeat'' _ x count'
242-
243---  Alternatively, we can declare an argument to be implicit when defining
244---  the function itself, by surrounding it in curly braces instead of
245---  parentheses. For example:
246-
247-def myRepeat''' {α : Type} (x : α) (count : Nat) : List α :=
248-  match count with
249-  | 0 => []
250-  | count' + 1 => x :: myRepeat''' x count'
251-
252---  By making the type argument implicit, we no longer need to provide it
253---  to the recursive call to `myRepeat'''`. Indeed, it would be invalid to
254---  provide one, because Lean is not expecting it. For each implicit
255---  parameter, Lean automatically inserts a hidden hole `_` argument for
256---  us, which is then inferred as usual.
257-
258---  #### Supplying Type Arguments Explicitly
259-
260---  One small problem with implicit arguments is that, once in a while,
261---  Lean does not have enough local information to determine a type
262---  argument; in such cases, we need to tell Lean the type explicitly. For
263---  example:
264-
265---  This fails because Lean can't figure out the type of the empty list:
266---  `def mynil := []` — error: type not known We can fix this with an
267---  explicit type annotation:
268---
269---  We can use the `@` prefix to supply the type argument explicitly. The
270---  `@` makes all implicit arguments of a function explicit:
271-
272-#check @List.nil
273-
274-def myNil' := @List.nil Nat
275-
276---  Output:
277---    @List.nil : {α : Type u_1} → List α
278-
279---   ----------------------------------------
280-
281---  _Quiz:_
282-
283---  Which type does Lean assign to the following expression? (The square
284---  brackets in this quiz and the following ones are list brackets.)
285---
286---      [1, 2, 3]
287---
288---  (A) `List Nat`
289---
290---  (B) `List Bool`
291---
292---  (C) `Bool`
293---
294---  (D) No type can be assigned
295-
296---   ----------------------------------------
297-
298---  _Quiz:_
299-
300---  What about this one?
301---
302---      [3 + 4] ++ []
303---

470---  ### Polymorphic Pairs
471-
472---  Like `inductive`s, `structure`s can also be made polymorphic. If we
473---  generalize the definition `NatProd` of pairs of natural numbers from
474---  last chapter, we get polymorphic pairs, often called *products*:
475-
476-structure MyProd (α β : Type) where
477-  fst : α
478-  snd : β
479-
480---  Lean's built-in product type `Prod` provides a `Prod.mk` constructor,
481---  and `Prod.fst` and `Prod.snd` functions for accessing the first and
482---  second components of the pair. It also has special syntax for creating
483---  products:
484-
485-#check (1, true)
486-#eval (1, true).fst
487-#eval (1, true).snd
488-
489---  Output:
490---    (1, true) : Nat × Bool
491-
492---  Output:
493---    1
494-
495---  Output:
496---    true
497-
498---  You can also use `.1` instead of `.fst` and `.2` instead of `.snd`:
499-
500-example : (3, 5).1 = 3 := by rfl
501-example : (3, 5).2 = 5 := by rfl
502-
503---  Lean writes the product type `Prod α β` as `α × β`. In VS Code you can
504---  type `\times` or `\x` to enter the `×` symbol.
505---
506---  The `dsimp only` tactic can be used to simplify `(x, y).fst` into `x`
507---  and `(x, y).snd` into `y`.
508-
509---  It is easy at first to get `(x, y)` and `α × β` confused. Remember that
510---  `(x, y)` is a *value* built from two other values, while `α × β` is a
511---  *type* built from two other types. If `x` has type `α` and `y` has type
512---  `β`, then `(x, y)` has type `α × β`.
513-
514---  The following function takes two lists and combines them into a list of
515---  pairs.
516-
517-def zip {α β : Type} (l₁ : List α) (l₂ : List β) : List (α × β) :=
518-  match l₁, l₂ with
519-  | [], [] => []
520-  | _ :: _, [] => []
521-  | [], _ :: _ => []
522-  | x :: l₁', y :: l₂' => (x, y) :: zip l₁' l₂'
523-
524-theorem zip_nil_left {α β : Type} (l₁ : List α) : zip l₁ [] = ([] : List (α × β)) := by
525-  cases l₁ with
526-  | nil => rfl
527-  | cons h t => rfl
528-
529-theorem zip_nil_right {α β : Type} (l₂ : List β) : zip [] l₂ = ([] : List (α × β)) := by
530-  cases l₂ <;> rfl
531-
532-theorem zip_cons_cons {α β : Type} {x : α} {y : β} {l₁ : List α} {l₂ : List β} :
533-   zip (x :: l₁) (y :: l₂) = (x, y) :: zip l₁ l₂ := by rfl
534-
535---  Notice that the simplification lemmas `zip_nil_left` and
536---  `zip_nil_right` are not proofs by `rfl`. The reason is that `l₁` and
537---  `l₂` are variables, and matching on a variable usually gets stuck, like
538---  we have seen before in Induction when proving the `zero_add` theorem.
539---  To overcome this, we destruct the list so that the `match` knows which
540---  branch to take during the computation done by the `rfl` tactic.
541-

579-

581---  standard library provides `Option α`, with constructors `none` and
582---  `some`. (We already saw `NatOption` in the Lists chapter.) Let's
583---  briefly look at the definition:

588-  | none : Option α
589-  | some (x : α) : Option α

594---  of list.

596-def nth? {α : Type} (l : List α) (n : Nat) : Option α :=
597-  match l with
598-  | [] => none
599-  | x :: l' => match n with
600-    | 0 => some x
601-    | n' + 1 => nth? l' n'

624---  ## Functions as Data
625-
626---  Like most modern programming languages — especially other "functional"
627---  languages, including OCaml, Haskell, Racket, Scala, Clojure, etc. —
628---  Lean treats functions as first-class citizens, allowing them to be
629---  passed as arguments to other functions, returned as results, stored in
630---  data structures, etc.
631-
632---  ### Higher-Order Functions
633-
634---  Functions that manipulate other functions are often called
635---  *higher-order* functions. Here's a simple one:
636-
637-def doIt3Times {α : Type} (f : α → α) (x : α) : α :=
638-  f (f (f x))
639-
640---  The argument `f` here is itself a function (from `α` to `α`); the body
641---  of `doIt3Times` applies `f` three times to some value `x`.
642-
643-#check doIt3Times
644-
645-example : doIt3Times Nat.minusTwo 9 = 3 := by rfl
646-
647-example : doIt3Times not true = false := by rfl
648-
649---  Output:
650---    doIt3Times {α : Type} (f : α → α) (x : α) : α
651-
652---  ### Filter
653-
654---  Here is a more useful higher-order function, taking a list of `α`s and
655---  a *predicate* on `α` (a function from `α` to `Bool`) and "filtering"
656---  the list to yield a new list containing just those elements for which
657---  the predicate returns `true`.
658-
659-def filter {α : Type} (test : α → Bool) (l : List α) : List α :=
660-  match l with
661-  | [] => []
662-  | x :: l' =>
663-    bif test x then x :: filter test l'
664-    else filter test l'
665-
666---  For example, if we apply `filter` to the predicate `Nat.even` and a
667---  list of numbers, it returns a list containing just the even members.
668-
669-example : filter Nat.even [1, 2, 3, 4] = [2, 4] := by rfl
670-
671---  Here are some further examples and properties of `filter`.
672-
673-def isLength1 {α : Type} (l : List α) : Bool :=
674-  l.length == 1
675-
676-example : filter isLength1
677-    [[1, 2], [3], [4], [5, 6, 7], [], [8]]
678-  = [[3], [4], [8]] := by rfl
679-
680-theorem filter_nil {α : Type} {test : α → Bool} : filter test [] = [] := by rfl
681-
682-theorem filter_cons_of_pos {α : Type} {test : α → Bool} {x : α}
683-    {l : List α} (h : test x = true) :
684-    filter test (x :: l) = x :: filter test l := by
685-  rw [filter, h, cond_true]
686-
687-theorem filter_cons_of_neg {α : Type} {test : α → Bool} {x : α}
688-    {l : List α} (h : test x = false) :
689-    filter test (x :: l) = filter test l := by
690-   rw [filter, h, cond_false]
691-
692---  You might have noticed that `filter_cons_of_pos` and
693---  `filter_cons_of_neg` have implicit parameters, such as `head` and
694---  `tail`, that do not have type `Type` like `α` does. As it turns out,
695---  Lean allows *any* parameter to be implicit, not just those of type
696---  `Type`. This is a standard Lean convention for lemmas that are likely
697---  to be used by `rw` when their values can be inferred by unification.
698---
699---  For example, suppose you were using this theorem to rewrite
700---  `filter Nat.even (3 :: rest)`. Matching that expression against the
701---  theorem's left-hand side `filter test (head :: tail)` establishes that
702---  `test = Nat.even`, `head = 3`, `tail = rest`, and `α = Nat`. By making
703---  these arguments implicit, Lean automatically inserts a hole `_` for
704---  each of them when you apply the theorem, just as with implicit
705---  parameters of type `Type`, so they can be inferred from the context.
706---
707---  Note that `h : test head` is not implicit, it's explicit. That's
708---  because it cannot be solved by unification, i.e., Lean can't prove that
709---  `Nat.even 3 = true` that way. It's a general proof obligation.
710---
711---  We'll follow the Lean standard convention from now on.
712-
713---  We can use `filter` to give a concise version of the `countOddMembers`
714---  function from the Lists chapter.
715-
716-def countOddMembers (l : List Nat) : Nat := (filter Nat.odd l).length
717-
718-example : countOddMembers [1, 0, 3, 1, 4, 5] = 4 := by rfl
719-example : countOddMembers [0, 2, 4] = 0 := by rfl
720-example : countOddMembers [] = 0 := by rfl
721-
722---  ### Anonymous Functions
723-
724---  It is arguably a little sad, in the example just above, to be forced to
725---  define the function `isLength1` and give it a name just to be able to
726---  pass it as an argument to `filter`, since we will probably never use it
727---  again. Indeed, when using higher-order functions, we *often* want to
728---  pass as arguments "one-off" functions that we will never use again;
729---  having to give each of these functions a name would be tedious.
730---
731---  Fortunately, there is a better way. We can construct a function "on the
732---  fly" without declaring it at the top level or giving it a name. Lean
733---  provides two syntaxes for anonymous functions:
734---
735---  - `fun n => n * n` — traditional lambda syntax
736---  - `(· * ·)` — "term with holes" syntax, where `·` marks arguments
737-
738-example : doIt3Times (fun n => n * n) 2 = 256 := by rfl
739-
740---  The expression `fun n => n * n` can be read as "the function that,
741---  given a number `n`, yields `n * n`."
742---
743---  Lean also supports a shorter notation using `·` as a placeholder for
744---  the argument:
745-
746-example : doIt3Times (· + 1) 0 = 3 := by rfl
747-
748---  Here is the `filter` example, rewritten to use an anonymous function.
749-
750-example : filter (fun l => l.length == 1)
751-    [[1, 2], [3], [4], [5, 6, 7], [], [8]]
752-  = [[3], [4], [8]] := by rfl
753-
754-example : filter (·.length == 1)
755-    [[1, 2], [3], [4], [5, 6, 7], [], [8]]
756-  = [[3], [4], [8]] := by rfl

773---  `α`, a predicate of type `α → Bool` and a `List α`, should return a

785---  ### Map
786-
787---  Another handy higher-order function is called `map`.
788-
789-def map {α β : Type} (f : α → β) (l : List α) : List β :=
790-  match l with
791-  | [] => []
792-  | head :: tail => f head :: map f tail
793-
794---  It takes a function `f` and a list `l = [n1, n2, n3, ...]` and returns
795---  the list `[f n1, f n2, f n3, ...]`, where `f` has been applied to each
796---  element of `l` in turn. For example:
797-
798-example : map (· + 3) [2, 0, 2] = [5, 3, 5] := by rfl
799-
800---  The element types of the input and output lists need not be the same,
801---  since `map` takes *two* type arguments, `α` and `β`; it can thus be
802---  applied to a list of numbers and a function from numbers to booleans to
803---  yield a list of booleans:
804-
805-example : map Nat.odd [2, 1, 2, 5] = [false, true, false, true] := by rfl
806-
807---  It can even be applied to a list of numbers and a function from numbers
808---  to *lists* of booleans to yield a *list of lists* of booleans:
809-
810-example : map (fun n => [n.even, n.odd]) [2, 1, 2, 5]
811-  = [[true, false], [false, true], [true, false], [false, true]] := by rfl

821-    match l with
822-    | [] => []
823-    | head :: tail => f head :: map f tail

830---

832---

891---  on a *copy* of this file that you can throw away afterwards.)
892-
893---  ### Fold
894-
895---  An even more powerful higher-order function is `fold`. It is the
896---  inspiration for the "reduce" operation that lies at the heart of
897---  Google's map/reduce distributed programming framework.
898-
899-def fold {α : Type} {β : Type} (f : α → β → β) (l : List α) (b : β) : β :=
900-  match l with
901-  | [] => b
902-  | a :: l => f a (fold f l b)
903-
904---  Intuitively, the behavior of the `fold` operation is to insert a given
905---  binary operator `f` between every pair of elements in a given list. For
906---  example, `fold (· + ·) [1, 2, 3, 4]` intuitively means `1 + 2 + 3 + 4`.
907---  To make this precise, we also need a "starting element" that serves as
908---  the initial second input to `f`. So, for example,
909---
910---      fold (· + ·) [1, 2, 3, 4] 0
911---
912---  yields
913---
914---      1 + (2 + (3 + (4 + 0))).
915-
916-example : fold (· && ·) [true, true, false, true] true = false := by rfl
917-
918-example : fold (· * ·) [1, 2, 3, 4] 1 = 24 := by rfl
919-
920-example : fold (· ++ ·) [[1], [], [2, 3], [4]] [] = [1, 2, 3, 4] := by rfl
921-
922-example : fold (fun l n => l.length + n) [[1], [], [2, 3, 2], [4]] 0 = 5 := by rfl
923-
924-theorem fold_nil {α : Type} {β : Type} {f : α → β → β} {b : β} : fold f [] b = b := by rfl
925-
926-theorem fold_cons {α : Type} {β : Type} {f : α → β → β} {a : α} {l : List α} {b : β} :
927-    fold f (a :: l) b = f a (fold f l b) := by rfl
928-
929---   ----------------------------------------
930-
931---  _Quiz:_
932-
933---  Here is the definition of `fold` again:
934-
935-sf_recall
936-  def fold {α β : Type} (f : α → β → β) (l : List α) (b : β) : β :=
937-    match l with
938-    | [] => b
939-    | a :: l => f a (fold f l b)
940-
941---  What is the type of `@fold`?
942---
943---  (A) `{α β : Type} → (α → β → β) → List α → β → β`
944---
945---  (B) `α → β → (α → β → β) → List α → β → β`
946---
947---  (C) `{α β : Type} → α → β → β → List α → β → β`
948---
949---  (D) `α → β → α → β → β → List α → β → β`
950-
951---   ----------------------------------------
952-
953---  _Quiz:_
954-
955---  What does `fold (· + ·) [1, 2, 3, 4] 0` simplify to?
956---
957---  (A) `[1, 2, 3, 4]`
958---
959---  (B) `0`
960---
961---  (C) `10`
962---
963---  (D) `[3, 7, 0]`
964-
965---   ----------------------------------------
966-
967---  ### Exercise (1 star): fold_types_different (Optional, Manually graded) ⭐
968-
969---  Observe that the type of `fold` is parameterized by *two* type
970---  variables, `α` and `β`, and the parameter `f` is a binary operator that
971---  takes an `α` and a `β` and returns a `β`. The examples above show one
972---  instance where it is useful for `α` and `β` to be different. Can you
973---  think of any others?
974-
975---  ### Functions That Construct Functions
976-
977---  Most of the higher-order functions we have talked about so far take
978---  functions as arguments. Let's look at some examples that involve
979---  *returning* functions as the results of other functions. To begin, here
980---  is a function that takes a value `x` (drawn from some type `α`) and
981---  returns a function from `Nat` to `α` that yields `x` whenever it is
982---  called, ignoring its `Nat` argument.
983-
984-def constFun {α : Type} (x : α) : Nat → α :=
985-  fun _ => x
986-
987-def fTrue := constFun true
988-
989-example : fTrue 0 = true := by rfl
990-
991-example : constFun 5 99 = 5 := by rfl
992-
993---  In fact, the multiple-argument functions we have already seen are also
994---  examples of passing functions as data. To see why, recall the type of
995---  addition:
996-
997-#check Nat.add
998-
999---  Output:
1000---    Nat.add : Nat → Nat → Nat
1001-
1002-def plus3 := Nat.add 3
1003-#check plus3
1004-
1005-example : plus3 4 = 7 := by rfl
1006-example : doIt3Times plus3 0 = 9 := by rfl
1007-example : doIt3Times (Nat.add 3) 0 = 9 := by rfl
1008-
1009---  Output:
1010---    plus3 : Nat → Nat
1011-
1012---  Similarly, we can write:
1013-
1014-def fold_plus : List Nat → Nat → Nat :=
1015-  fold (· + ·)
1016-
1017-#check fold_plus
1018-
1019---  Output:
1020---    fold_plus : List Nat → Nat → Nat
1021-
1022---  What's happening here is called *partial application*. In Lean, the
1023---  type constructor `→` is right-associative, meaning a function type like
1024---  `α → β → γ` is parsed like `α → (β → γ)`, or "a function from `α` to a
1025---  function from `β` to `γ`."
1026---
1027---  We can think of `fold` not as a three-argument function, but as a
1028---  one-argument function that:
1029---
1030---  1. Takes an argument `f` of type `α → β → β`
1031---  2. Returns a function of type `List α → β → β` that "remembers" `f`
1032---
1033---  When we write `fold (· + ·)`, we're giving `fold` its first argument,
1034---  `(· + ·)`, and getting back a specialized function that can sum up the
1035---  elements of any list of numbers. This new function still expects two
1036---  more arguments: a list and a starting value.
1037-
1038---  ## Additional Exercises
1039-
1040---  ### Exercise (2 stars): fold_length ⭐⭐
1041-
1042---  Many common functions on lists can be implemented in terms of `fold`.
1043---  For example, here is an alternative definition of `List.length`:
1044-
1045-def foldLength {α : Type} (l : List α) : Nat :=
1046-  fold (fun _ n => n + 1) l 0
1047-
1048-example : foldLength [4, 7, 0] = 3 := by rfl
1049-
1050---  Prove the correctness of `foldLength`.
1051---
1052---  Hint: It may help to use `rw [foldLength, fold]` to unfold the
1053---  definition.
1054-
1055-theorem fold_length_correct {α : Type} {l : List α} :
1056-    foldLength l = l.length := by
1057-  sorry
1058-
1059---  ### Exercise (3 stars): fold_map (Manually graded) ⭐⭐⭐
1060-
1061---  We can also define `map` in terms of `fold`. Finish `foldMap` below.
1062-
1063-def foldMap {α β : Type} (f : α → β) (l : List α) : List β := sorry
1064-
1065---  Write down a theorem `fold_map_correct` stating that `foldMap` is
1066---  correct, and prove it in Lean.
1067-
1068---  FILL IN HERE
1069-
1070---  ### Exercise (2 stars): currying (Advanced) ⭐⭐
1071-
1072---  The type `α → β → γ` can be read as describing functions that take two
1073---  arguments, one of type `α` and another of type `β`, and return an
1074---  output of type `γ`. Recall from our discussion of partial application
1075---  that this type is written `α → (β → γ)` when fully parenthesized. That
1076---  is, if we have `f : α → β → γ`, and we give `f` an input of type `α`,
1077---  it will give us as output a function of type `β → γ`. If we then give
1078---  that function an input of type `β`, it will return an output of type
1079---  `γ`. That is, every function in Lean takes only one input, but some
1080---  functions return a function as output. This is precisely what enables
1081---  partial application, as we saw above with `plus3`.
1082---
1083---  By contrast, functions of type `α × β → γ` — which when fully
1084---  parenthesized is written `(α × β) → γ` — require their single input to
1085---  be a pair. Both arguments must be given at once; there is no
1086---  possibility of partial application.
1087---
1088---  It is possible to convert a function between these two types.
1089---  Converting from `α × β → γ` to `α → β → γ` is called *currying*, in
1090---  honor of the logician Haskell Curry. Converting from `α → β → γ` to
1091---  `α × β → γ` is called *uncurrying*.
1092---
1093---  We can define currying as follows:
1094-
1095-def prodCurry {α β γ : Type} (f : α × β → γ) (x : α) (y : β) : γ := f (x, y)
1096-
1097---  As an exercise, define its inverse, `prodUncurry`. Then prove the
1098---  theorems below to show that the two are really inverses.
1099-
1100-def prodUncurry {α β γ : Type} (f : α → β → γ) (p : α × β) : γ := sorry
1101-
1102---  As a (trivial) example of the usefulness of currying, we can use it to
1103---  shorten one of the examples that we saw above:
1104-
1105-example : map (Nat.add 3) [2, 0, 2] = [5, 3, 5] := by rfl
1106-
1107---  Thought exercise: before looking at the output of the following
1108---  commands, can you calculate the types of `prodCurry` and `prodUncurry`?
1109-
1110-#check @prodCurry
1111-#check @prodUncurry
1112-
1113---  Output:
1114---    @prodCurry : {α β γ : Type} → (α × β → γ) → α → β → γ
1115-
1116---  Output:
1117---    @prodUncurry : {α β γ : Type} → (α → β → γ) → α × β → γ
1118-
1119-theorem uncurry_curry {α β γ : Type} {x : α} {y : β} {f : α → β → γ} :
1120-    prodCurry (prodUncurry f) x y = f x y := by
1121-  sorry
1122-
1123-theorem curry_uncurry {α β γ : Type} {p : α × β} {f : α × β → γ} :
1124-    prodUncurry (prodCurry f) p = f p := by
1125-  sorry
1126-
1127---  ### Exercise (2 stars): nth_error_informal (Advanced, Optional, Manually graded) ⭐⭐
1128-
1129---  Recall the definition of the `nth?` function:
1130-
1131-sf_recall
1132-  def nth? {α : Type} (l : List α) (n : Nat) : Option α :=
1133-    match l with
1134-    | [] => none
1135-    | x :: l' => match n with
1136-      | 0 => some x
1137-      | n' + 1 => nth? l' n'
1138-
1139---  Write a careful informal proof of the following theorem:
1140---
1141---      ∀ (l : List α) (n : Nat), l.length = n → nth? l n = none
1142---
1143---  Make sure to state the induction hypothesis *explicitly*.
1144-
1145---  ### Church Numerals (Advanced)
1146-
1147---  The following exercises explore an alternative way of defining natural
1148---  numbers using the *Church numerals*, which are named after their
1149---  inventor, the mathematician Alonzo Church. We can represent a natural
1150---  number `n` as a function that takes a function `f` as a parameter and
1151---  returns `f` iterated `n` times.
1152-
1153-namespace Church
1154-
1155-def CNat := ∀ (α : Type), (α → α) → α → α
1156-
1157---  Let's see how to write some numbers with this notation. Iterating a
1158---  function once should be the same as just applying it. Thus:
1159-
1160-def one : CNat :=
1161-  fun (α : Type) (f : α → α) (x : α) => f x
1162-
1163---  Similarly, `two` should apply `f` twice to its argument:
1164-
1165-def two : CNat :=
1166-  fun (α : Type) (f : α → α) (x : α) => f (f x)
1167-
1168---  Defining `zero` is somewhat trickier: how can we "apply a function zero
1169---  times"? The answer is actually simple: just return the argument
1170---  untouched.
1171-
1172-def zero : CNat :=
1173-  fun (α : Type) (_ : α → α) (x : α) => x
1174-
1175---  More generally, a number `n` can be written as
1176---  `fun α f x => f (f ... (f x) ...)`, with `n` occurrences of `f`. Let's
1177---  informally notate that as `fun α f x => f^n x`, with the convention
1178---  that `f^0 x` is just `x`. Note how the `doIt3Times` function we've
1179---  defined previously is actually just the Church representation of 3.
1180-
1181-def three : CNat := @doIt3Times
1182-
1183---  So `n α f x` represents "do it `n` times", where `n` is a Church
1184---  numeral and "it" means applying `f` starting with `x`.
1185---
1186---  Another way to think about the Church representation is that function
1187---  `f` represents the successor operation on `α`, and value `x` represents
1188---  the zero element of `α`. We could even rewrite with those names to make
1189---  it clearer:
1190-
1191-def zero' : CNat :=
1192-  fun (α : Type) (_ : α → α) (zero : α) => zero
1193-def one' : CNat :=
1194-  fun (α : Type) (succ : α → α) (zero : α) => succ zero
1195-def two' : CNat :=
1196-  fun (α : Type) (succ : α → α) (zero : α) => succ (succ zero)
1197-
1198---  If we passed in `Nat.succ` as `succ` and `0` as `zero`, we'd even get
1199---  the Peano naturals as a result:
1200-
1201-example : zero Nat Nat.succ 0 = 0 := by rfl
1202-example : one  Nat Nat.succ 0 = 1 := by rfl
1203-example : two  Nat Nat.succ 0 = 2 := by rfl
1204-
1205---  One very interesting implication of the Church numerals is that we
1206---  don't strictly need the natural numbers to be built-in to a functional
1207---  programming language, or even to be definable with an inductive data
1208---  type. It's possible to represent them purely (if not efficiently) with
1209---  functions.
1210---
1211---  Of course, it's not enough just to "represent" numerals; we need to be
1212---  able to do arithmetic with the representation. Show that we can by
1213---  completing the definitions of the following functions. Make sure that
1214---  the corresponding unit tests pass by proving them with `rfl`.
1215-
1216---  ### Exercise (2 stars): church_scc (Advanced) ⭐⭐
1217-
1218---  Define a function that computes the successor of a Church numeral.
1219---  Given a Church numeral `n`, its successor `scc n` should iterate its
1220---  function argument once more than `n`. That is, given
1221---  `fun X f x => f^n x` as input, `scc` should produce
1222---  `fun X f x => f^(n+1) x` as output. In other words, do it `n` times,
1223---  then do it once more.
1224-
1225-def scc (n : CNat) : CNat := sorry
1226-
1227-example : scc zero = one := sorry
1228-theorem scc_2 : scc one = two := sorry
1229-theorem scc_3 : scc two = three := sorry
1230-
1231---  ### Exercise (3 stars): church_plus (Advanced) ⭐⭐⭐
1232-
1233---  Define a function that computes the addition of two Church numerals.
1234---  Given `fun X f x => f^n x` and `fun X f x => f^m x` as input, `plus`
1235---  should produce `fun X f x => f^(n + m) x` as output. In other words, do
1236---  it `n` times, then do it `m` more times.
1237---
1238---  Hint: the "zero" argument to a Church numeral need not be just `x`.
1239-
1240-def plus (n m : CNat) : CNat := sorry
1241-
1242-theorem plus_1 : plus zero one = one := sorry
1243-theorem plus_2 : plus two three = plus three two := sorry
1244-theorem plus_3 : plus (plus two two) three = plus one (plus three three) := sorry
1245-
1246---  ### Exercise (3 stars): church_mult (Advanced) ⭐⭐⭐
1247-
1248---  Define a function that computes the multiplication of two Church
1249---  numerals.
1250---
1251---  Hint: the "successor" argument to a Church numeral need not be just
1252---  `f`.
1253---
1254---  Warning: Lean will not let you pass `CNat` itself as the type `α`
1255---  argument to a Church numeral; you will get a "sort mismatch" error
1256---  between `Type 1` and `Type 2`. Don't worry too much about what this
1257---  means right now, but know that this is Lean's way of preventing a
1258---  paradox in which a type contains itself. So leave the type argument
1259---  unchanged.
1260-
1261-def mult (n m : CNat) : CNat := sorry
1262-
1263-
1264-theorem mult_1 : mult one one = one := sorry
1265-theorem mult_2 : mult zero (plus three three) = zero := sorry
1266-theorem mult_3 : mult two three = plus three three := sorry
1267-
1268---  ### Exercise (3 stars): church_exp (Advanced) ⭐⭐⭐
1269-
1270---  Exponentiation:
1271---
1272---  Define a function that computes the exponentiation of two Church
1273---  numerals.
1274---
1275---  Hint: the type argument to a Church numeral need not just be `α`.
1276---  Finding the right type can be tricky.
1277-
1278-def exp (n m : CNat) : CNat := sorry
1279-
1280-theorem exp_1 : exp two two = plus two two := sorry
1281-theorem exp_2 : exp three zero = one := sorry
1282-theorem exp_3 : exp three two = plus (mult two (mult two two)) one := sorry
1283-
1284-end Church
1285-

4-
5---  Congratulations: We've reached the end of *Logical Foundations*!
6-
7---  ## Looking Back
8-
9---  We've covered quite a bit of ground. Along the way, we developed three
10---  connected themes:
11---
12---  *Functional programming*:
13---
14---  - recursive definitions over immutable data
15---  - higher-order functions
16---  - polymorphism
17---
18---  *Logic*, the mathematical basis for software engineering:
19-
20---  logic                        calculus
21---  --------------------   ~   ----------------------------
22---  software engineering       mechanical/civil engineering
23-
24---  - inductively defined propositions and relations
25---  - inductive proofs
26---  - proof objects
27---
28---  *Lean*, an industrial-strength proof assistant:
29---
30---  - a functional programming language
31---  - tactics for constructing proofs
32---  - proof automation
33-
34---  ## Looking Forward
35-
36---  The next volumes carry these ideas into programming-language theory and
37---  program verification:
38---
39---  - *Type Systems* develops operational semantics and type systems,
40---    including the simply typed lambda calculus and the progress and
41---    preservation theorems.
42---
43---  - *Hoare Logic* introduces imperative programs and Hoare logic, a
44---    framework for stating and proving correctness properties of programs
45---    with mutable state.
46---
47---  Both volumes build directly on the definitions and proof techniques
48---  introduced here.
49-
50---  ## Resources
51-
52---  This volume also contains optional sections and exercises that develop
53---  some topics further.
54---
55---  For questions about Lean, the [Lean community
56---  Zulip](https://leanprover.zulipchat.com/) is an active place to ask
57---  questions and discuss formalization.
58---
59---  The following books continue in several different directions:
60---
61---  - [Functional Programming in
62---    Lean](https://lean-lang.org/functional_programming_in_lean/) explores
63---    Lean as a programming language.
64---
65---  - [Theorem Proving in Lean
66---    4](https://docs.lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/) gives a
67---    systematic introduction to Lean's logic and proof language.
68---
69---  - [Mathematics in
70---    Lean](https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathematics_in_lean/)
71---    develops formalized mathematics using Lean and Mathlib.
