1-import SFLCompat
2-
3---  # Preface
4-
5---  ## Welcome
6-
7---  This is the starting point for a series of electronic textbooks on
8---  *Software Foundations*, the mathematical underpinnings of reliable
9---  software. Topics in the series include basic concepts of logic,
10---  functional programming, computer-assisted theorem proving, operational
11---  semantics, logics and techniques for reasoning about programs, static
12---  type systems, property-based random testing, and verification of
13---  practical C code. The exposition is intended for a broad range of
14---  readers, from advanced undergraduates to PhD students and researchers.
15---  No specific background in logic or programming languages is assumed,
16---  though a degree of mathematical maturity will be helpful.
17---
18---  The principal novelty of the series is that it is one hundred percent
19---  formalized and machine-checked: each chapter of each book is literally
20---  a script for the Lean prover, and the books are intended to be read
21---  alongside (or inside) an interactive session with Lean. All the details
22---  are fully formalized, and almost all of the exercises are designed to
23---  be worked using Lean.
24---
25---  This book, *Logical Foundations in Lean*, lays groundwork for the
26---  others in the series, introducing the reader to the basic ideas of
27---  functional programming, formal logic, and Lean itself.
28-
29---  ## Overview
30-
31---  Building reliable software is hard -- really hard. The scale and
32---  complexity of modern systems, the number of people involved, and the
33---  range of demands placed on them make it challenging to build software
34---  that is even more-or-less correct, much less 100% correct. At the same
35---  time, the increasing degree to which information processing is woven
36---  into every aspect of society greatly amplifies the cost of bugs and
37---  insecurities.
38---
39---  Computer scientists and software engineers have responded to these
40---  challenges with a host of techniques for improving software
41---  reliability, ranging from recommendations about managing software
42---  projects teams (e.g., extreme programming) to design philosophies for
43---  libraries (e.g., model-view-controller, publish-subscribe, etc.) and
44---  whole programming languages (e.g., object-oriented programming,
45---  functional programming, ...) to mathematical techniques for specifying
46---  and reasoning about properties of software and tools for helping
47---  validate these properties. The *Software Foundations* books are focused
48---  on this last set of tools.
49---
50---  The present volume weaves together three conceptual threads:
51---
52---  - basic tools from *logic* for making and justifying precise claims
53---    about programs;
54---
55---  - the use of *provers* (or *proof assistants*) to construct rigorous
56---    logical arguments;
57---
58---  - *functional programming*, both as a programming method that
59---    simplifies reasoning about programs and as a bridge between
60---    programming and logic.
61-
62---  ### Logic
63-
64---  Logic is the field of study whose subject matter is *proofs* --
65---  unassailable arguments for the truth of particular propositions.
66---  Volumes have been written about the central role of logic in computer
67---  science. Manna and Waldinger (1971) called it "the calculus of computer
68---  science," while Halpern *et al.* (2001)'s paper *On the Unusual
69---  Effectiveness of Logic in Computer Science* catalogs scores of ways in
70---  which logic offers critical tools and insights. Indeed, they observe
71---  that, "As a matter of fact, logic has turned out to be significantly
72---  more effective in computer science than it has been in mathematics.
73---  This is quite remarkable, especially since much of the impetus for the
74---  development of logic during the past one hundred years came from
75---  mathematics."
76---
77---  In particular, the fundamental tools of *inductive proof* are
78---  ubiquitous across computer science. You have surely seen them before,
79---  perhaps in a course on discrete math or analysis of algorithms, but in
80---  this book we will examine them more deeply than you have probably done
81---  so far.
82-
83---  ### Proof Assistants
84-
85---  The flow of ideas between logic and computer science over the years has
86---  run in both directions, with CS also making key contributions to logic.
87---  One of these has been the development of software tools for helping
88---  construct and validate proofs of logical statements. These tools fall
89---  into two broad categories:
90---
91---  - *Automated theorem provers* provide "push-button" operation: you give
92---    them a proposition and they return either *true* or *false* (or,
93---    sometimes, *don't know: ran out of time*). Although their reasoning
94---    capabilities are limited, they have matured tremendously in recent
95---    decades and are used now in a multitude of settings. Examples of such
96---    tools include SAT solvers, SMT solvers, and model checkers.
97---
98---  - *Proof assistants* — or just *provers* — are hybrid tools that
99---    automate the more routine aspects of creating proofs while depending
100---    on human guidance for more difficult aspects. Widely used proof
101---    assistants include Isabelle, Agda, Twelf, ACL2, PVS, F*, HOL4, Rocq,
102---    and Lean, among many others.
103---
104---  This course is based around Lean, a prover that has been under
105---  development since 2013 and that has attracted a large and active
106---  community of users in both research and at companies like DeepMind,
107---  OpenAI, Anthropic, MSR, and AWS.
108---
109---  Lean provides a rich environment for interactive development of
110---  machine-checked formal reasoning. The kernel of the Lean system is a
111---  simple proof-checker, which guarantees that only correct deduction
112---  steps are ever performed. On top of this kernel, the Lean environment
113---  provides high-level facilities for proof development, including a large
114---  library of common definitions and lemmas, powerful tactics for
115---  constructing complex proofs semi-automatically, and a highly extensible
116---  system for defining new proof-automation tactics and notations for
117---  specific situations.
118---
119---  Lean and its relatives have become critical enablers for a [huge
120---  variety of work](https://leanprover-community.github.io/papers.html)
121---  across computer science and mathematics:
122---
123---  - As a *platform for modeling programming languages*, proof assistants
124---    have become standard tools for researchers who need to describe and
125---    reason about complex language definitions. They have been used, for
126---    example, to check the security of the JavaCard platform, obtaining
127---    the highest level of common criteria certification, and for formal
128---    specifications of the x86 and LLVM instruction sets and programming
129---    languages such as C.
130---
131---  - As *environments for developing formally certified software and
132---    hardware*, they have been used, for example, to build CompCert (Leroy
133---    *et al.*, 2016), a fully-verified optimizing compiler for C,
134---    [Cedar](https://github.com/cedar-policy/cedar-spec) (Disselkoen *et
135---    al.*, 2024), a formally-specified policy language, and CertiKOS (Gu
136---    *et al.*, 2016), a fully verified hypervisor, and for proving the
137---    correctness of subtle algorithms involving floating point numbers,
138---    and as the basis for CertiCrypt, FCF, and SSProve, which are
139---    frameworks for proving cryptographic algorithms secure. They are also
140---    being used to build verified implementations of the open-source
141---    RISC-V processor architecture.
142---
143---  - As *proof assistants for mathematics*, they have been used to
144---    validate and help develop a number of important results. For example,
145---    the ability to include complex computations inside proofs made it
146---    possible to develop the first formally verified proof of the 4-color
147---    theorem, which had previously been controversial among mathematicians
148---    because the argument required checking a large number of
149---    configurations using a program. More recently, an even more massive
150---    effort led to a formalization of the Feit-Thompson Theorem, the first
151---    major step in the classification of finite simple groups.
152---
153---    Lean, in particular, is now at the core of various formalization
154---    efforts in mathematics, such as the proof of [Fermat's Last
155---    Theorem](https://github.com/ImperialCollegeLondon/FLT), the [Sphere
156---    Packing
157---    Problem](https://github.com/thefundamentaltheor3m/Sphere-Packing-Lean).
158---    and even DeepMind's AI model for International Math Olympiad
159---    problems,
160---    [AlphaProof](https://deepmind.google/blog/ai-solves-imo-problems-at-silver-medal-level/).
161-
162---  ### Functional Programming
163-
164---  *Functional programming* refers both to a collection of powerful coding
165---  idioms that can be used in almost any programming language and to a
166---  family of languages designed to foreground these idioms, including
167---  Haskell, OCaml, Standard ML, F#, Scala, Scheme, Racket, Common Lisp,
168---  Clojure, Erlang, F*, and Lean itself.
169---
170---  Functional programming has been developed over many decades — indeed,
171---  its roots go back to Church's lambda-calculus from the 1930s, well
172---  *before* the first electronic computers! But since the early '90s it
173---  has enjoyed a surge of interest among both software engineers and
174---  language designers.
175---
176---  The basic tenet of functional programming is that, whenever possible,
177---  computation should be *pure*, in the sense that the only effect of
178---  execution should be to produce a result. That is, it should be free
179---  from *side effects* such as I/O, assignments to mutable variables,
180---  redirecting pointers, etc. For example, whereas an *imperative* sorting
181---  function might take a list of numbers and rearrange its pointers to put
182---  the list in order, a pure sorting function would take the original list
183---  and return a fresh list containing the same numbers in sorted order.
184---
185---  A significant benefit of this style of programming is that it makes
186---  programs easier to understand and reason about. If every operation on a
187---  data structure yields a new data structure and leaves the old one
188---  intact, then there is no need to worry about how that structure is
189---  being shared and whether a change by one part of the program might
190---  break an invariant relied on by another part of the program. This is
191---  particularly important when reasoning about concurrent systems, where
192---  every piece of mutable state shared between threads is a potential
193---  source of pernicious bugs.
194---
195---  Another reason for the popularity of functional programming, related to
196---  the first, is that functional programs are often much easier to
197---  parallelize and physically distribute than their imperative
198---  counterparts. If running a computation has no effect other than
199---  producing a result, then it does not matter *where* it is run.
200---  Likewise, if a data structure is never modified destructively, it can
201---  be copied freely, across cores or across the network. Indeed, the
202---  "Map-Reduce" idiom, which lies at the heart of massively distributed
203---  query processors like Hadoop and is used by Google to index the entire
204---  web, is a classic example of functional programming.
205---
206---  For these books, functional programming has yet another significant
207---  attraction: it serves as a bridge between logic and computer science.
208---  Indeed, Lean itself can be viewed as a combination of a small but
209---  extremely expressive functional programming language and a set of tools
210---  for stating and proving logical assertions. Moreover, when we come to
211---  look more closely, we find that these two sides of Lean are actually
212---  aspects of the very same underlying machinery -- i.e., *proofs are
213---  programs*.
214-
215---  ### Further Reading
216-
217---  This text is intended to be self contained, but readers looking for
218---  follow-on textbooks or deeper treatments of particular topics will find
219---  some suggestions for further reading in the Postscript chapter.
220-
221---  ## Practicalities
222-
223---  ### System Requirements
224-
225---  Lean runs on Linux, MacOS, and Windows. The files in this book have
226---  been tested with Lean version `4.34.0-rc2`.
227-
228---  ### Installation
229-
230---  The Visual Studio Code IDE is the recommended platform for using Lean.
231---  To get set up, follow these steps:
232---
233---  - Install VS Code if needed.
234---
235---  - From the Extensions tab of VS Code, install the Lean 4 extension.
236---
237---  - Download the book, build it if necessary — more below.
238---
239---  - Open the built book directory in a VS Code window.
240---
241---  - Open a Lean file; the extension will offer to install Lean; accept,
242---    and it will fetch the version this book needs.
243---
244---  - Wait for Lean to build the project (it takes a few minutes).
245-
246---  #### Downloading and using the book for a class
247-
248---  If you are **using this book as part of a class**, your instructor will
249---  have created a "student" release for you. Download the `.zip` file for
250---  that release, unzip it, and then open the resulting directory in VS
251---  Code. Open any `.lean` file (e.g., `LF/Basics.lean`) to get started.
252---
253---  If you would like to read the HTML version of the book, it should be
254---  hosted on your course website (you may be reading it now!).
255---
256---  Note that, as the book is changing while you are taking your class, you
257---  should download a fresh `.zip` for each homework you do, opening it in
258---  a fresh directory. This way you will have access to prior solutions,
259---  and you will automatically get any Lean updates. More on exercises
260---  below.
261-
262---  #### Downloading and building the book from Git, for self study
263-
264---  If you are **reading Software Foundations on your own**, you can get
265---  the most up-to-date version from the
266---  [SF-in-Lean](https://github.com/plclub/sf-in-lean) GitHub repository.
267---  Clone that repository and then build it by typing `make lf-student`
268---  from the root directory. Doing so will construct the student version
269---  (full prose, with solutions elided) of the *Logical Foundations* book.
270---
271---  Building the book requires that you have Lean installed. If you do not,
272---  follow the instructions [here](https://lean-lang.org/install/manual/)
273---  to install the Lean toolchain manager `elan` which will then manage
274---  your Lean installation. Alternatively, once you have added the Lean 4
275---  extension to VS Code, you can open a Lean file in the repository (for
276---  example, `LF.lean` from the top level directory) and it will install
277---  `elan` and Lean automatically. Both installation methods have the same
278---  effect, putting the Lean toolchain in the same place on your
279---  filesystem.
280---
281---  With Lean installed, `make lf-student` writes two things to
282---  `_out/lf/student/`:
283---
284---  - `html/`, an HTML-formatted version of the whole book; and
285---
286---  - `lean/`, a standalone Lean project holding the same chapters as
287---    `.lean` files, with solutions to exercises omitted.
288---
289---  Use `make student` instead if you also want *Type Systems* (`ts`) and
290---  *Hoare Logic* (`hl`). The first build compiles the whole dependency
291---  tree and takes a while; later builds are incremental.
292---
293---  Now you can open the generated Lean project as its own folder — not as
294---  a file inside your clone:
295---
296---      code _out/lf/student/lean
297---
298---  or
299---
300---      cd _out/lf/student/lean
301---      code .
302---
303---  You can also use File → Open Folder.
304---
305---  Treat this as a scratch copy: **every `make` regenerates it from the
306---  Verso sources, overwriting whatever is there.** Work on your proofs
307---  here, but keep anything you want to survive somewhere else.
308---
309---  If you would like to read the book HTML, start a local HTTP server and
310---  point it at the generated HTML files:
311---
312---      python3 -m http.server 8000 -d _out/lf/student/html
313---
314---  Then visit `http://localhost:8000` and start reading.
315---
316---  If you want to build everything — student version, "terse" instructor
317---  version, solutions, and grading versions — type `make`, `make lf`, etc.
318-
319---  ### Exercises
320-
321---  Each chapter includes numerous exercises. Each is marked with a "star
322---  rating," which can be interpreted as follows:
323---
324---  - One star: easy exercises that underscore points in the text and that,
325---    for most readers, should take only a minute or two. Get in the habit
326---    of working these as you reach them.
327---
328---  - Two stars: straightforward exercises (five or ten minutes).
329---
330---  - Three stars: exercises requiring a bit of thought (ten minutes to
331---    half an hour).
332---
333---  - Four and five stars: more difficult exercises (half an hour and up).
334---
335---  Those using SF in a classroom setting should note that the autograder
336---  assigns extra points to harder exercises:
337-
338---  1 star  = 1 point
339---  2 stars = 2 points
340---  3 stars = 3 points
341---  4 stars = 6 points
342---  5 stars = 10 points
343-
344---  Some exercises are marked "advanced," and some are marked "optional."
345---  Optional exercises provide a bit of extra practice with key concepts
346---  and introduce secondary themes that may be of interest to some readers.
347---  Advanced exercises offer an extra challenge and a deeper cut at the
348---  ideas. Doing just the non-optional, non-advanced exercises should
349---  provide good coverage of the core material.
350-

365-
366---  ## For Potential Contributors
367-
368---  If you find things you'd like to help add or improve, your
369---  contributions are welcome! To get started, clone the [SF-in-Lean git
370---  repo](https://github.com/plclub/sf-in-lean) and have a look at
371---  `ALPHA-TESTERS.md`.
372-

5-
6---  # Tactics: More Basic Tactics
7-
8---  This chapter introduces several additional proof strategies and tactics
9---  that allow us to begin proving more interesting properties of
10---  functional programs.
11---
12---  We will see:
13---
14---  - how to use auxiliary lemmas in both "forward-" and "backward-style"
15---    proofs;
16---
17---  - how to reason about data constructors -- in particular, how to use
18---    the fact that they are injective and disjoint;
19---
20---  - how to strengthen an induction hypothesis, and when such
21---    strengthening is required; and
22---
23---  - more details on how to reason by case analysis.
24-
25---  ## The `apply` Tactic
26-
27---  We often encounter situations where the goal to be proved is *exactly*
28---  the same as some hypothesis in the context or some previously proved
29---  lemma.
30-
31---  The `apply` tactic is useful when the goal is instead the conclusion of
32---  an implication.
33-
34---  For example, suppose we have a hypothesis `h : p → q` and our goal is
35---  `q`. We can use `apply h` to replace the goal `q` with the premise `p`:
36-
37-example (p q : Prop) (h : p → q) (hp : p) : q := by
38-  apply h
39-  exact hp
40-
41---  The `apply` tactic also works with hypotheses and lemmas whose types
42---  are implications. If the conclusion of the implication matches the
43---  current goal, its premises become new subgoals to be proved.
44-
45-example (n m o p : Nat) (hnm : n = m) (h : n = m → [n, o] = [m, p]) :
46-    [n, o] = [m, p] := by
47-  apply h
48-  exact hnm
49-
50---  When we use `apply h`, Lean tries to match the conclusion of the type
51---  of `h` with the current goal. Here `h : n = m → [n, o] = [m, p]` has
52---  conclusion `[n, o] = [m, p]`, which matches the current goal. Lean then
53---  replaces the goal with the premise that is still needed, `n = m`. Then
54---  we close the goal with `exact hnm`.
55---
56---  More generally, the type of a theorem or hypothesis used with `apply`
57---  may have universally quantified variables and premises. Lean tries to
58---  match its conclusion with the current goal to determine appropriate
59---  values for the quantified variables.
60-
61-example (n m : Nat) (h₁ : (n, n) = (m, m))
62-    (h₂ : ∀ (q r : Nat), (q, q) = (r, r) → [q] = [r]) :
63-    [n] = [m] := by
64-  apply h₂
65-  exact h₁
66-
67---  ### Exercise (2 stars): apply_exercise (Optional) ⭐⭐
68-
69---  Complete the following proof using only `apply`.
70-
71-theorem apply_exercise (m : Nat)
72-    (h₁ : ∀ (n : Nat), n.even = true → (n + 1).even = false)
73-    (h₂ : ∀ (n : Nat), n.even = false → n.odd = true)
74-    (hEven : m.even = true) :
75-    (m + 1).odd = true := by
76-  sorry
77-
78---  To use the `apply` tactic, the conclusion of the fact being applied
79---  must match the goal. For example, `apply` will not work if the left and
80---  right sides of the equality are swapped.
81-
82-example (n m : Nat) (h : n = 0 → n = m) (hn : n = 0) : m = n := by
83-  /- Here we cannot use `apply` directly...
84-    ...but we can use the `symm` tactic, which switches the left
85-    and right sides of an equality in the goal. -/
86-  symm
87-  apply h
88-  exact hn
89-
90---  ### Exercise (2 stars): apply_exercise1 ⭐⭐
91-
92---  You can use `apply` with previously defined theorems, not just
93---  hypotheses in the context. Use a previously-defined theorem about `rev`
94---  from Poly. Use that theorem as part of your (relatively short) solution
95---  to this exercise. You do not need `induction`.
96-
97-theorem rev_exercise1 {α : Type} (l l' : List α) (h : l = l'.rev) :
98-    l' = l.rev := by

101---  ### Exercise (1 star): apply_rewrite (Optional, Manually graded) ⭐
102-
103---  Briefly explain the difference between the tactics `apply` and `rw`.
104---  What are the situations where both can usefully be applied?
105-
106---  ### Supplying arguments to `apply`
107-
108---  The following silly example uses two rewrites in a row to get from
109---  `[a, b]` to `[e, f]`.
110-
111-example (a b c d e f : Nat)
112-    (h₁ : [a, b] = [c, d])
113-    (h₂ : [c, d] = [e, f]) :
114-    [a, b] = [e, f] := by
115-  rw [h₁, h₂]
116-
117---  Since this is a common pattern, we might like to pull it out as a lemma
118---  that records, once and for all, the fact that equality is *transitive*.
119-
120-theorem trans_eq {α : Type} (x y z : α) :
121-    x = y → y = z → x = z := by
122-  intro h₁ h₂
123-  rw [h₁, h₂]
124-
125---  Lean already provides exactly this theorem as `Eq.trans`:
126-
127-#check Eq.trans
128-
129---  Output:
130---    Eq.trans.{u} {α : Sort u} {a b c : α} (h₁ : a = b) (h₂ : b = c) : a = c
131-
132---  In Lean's version, the arguments corresponding to `x`, `y`, and `z` are
133---  implicit, since they can usually be inferred from the equality
134---  hypotheses and the goal.
135---
136---  Now let's use our `trans_eq` to prove the example above.
137-
138---  If we simply write `apply trans_eq`, Lean can infer some arguments from
139---  the goal, but not the intermediate list or the hypotheses needed for
140---  the lemma's premises. If you inspect the proof state after `apply`, you
141---  will see that Lean has created three goals:
142---
143---  1. `[a, b] = ?y`
144---  2. `?y = [e, f]`
145---  3. `List Nat`
146---
147---  Recall that `trans_eq` has five arguments. From the goal, Lean can
148---  infer the endpoints `x` and `z`, namely `[a, b]` and `[e, f]`. But it
149---  still needs an intermediate term `y`.
150---
151---  We want to prove `[a, b] = [e, f]`. By transitivity, it's enough to
152---  prove `[a, b] = ?y` and `?y = [e, f]`, for some intermidiate list `?y`.
153---  Here `?y` is a *metavariable*: a place holder for a value Lean has not
154---  yet determined. Before we provide the hypothesis `h₂`, Lean doesn't
155---  know that this intermediate list shoud be `[c, d]`.
156-
157-sf_expect_failure_in
158-  example (a b c d e f : Nat)
159-      (h₁ : [a, b] = [c, d])
160-      (h₂ : [c, d] = [e, f]) :
161-      [a, b] = [e, f] := by
162-    apply trans_eq
163-
164---  Output:
165---    unsolved goals
166---    case a
167---    a b c d e f : Nat
168---    h₁ : [a, b] = [c, d]
169---    h₂ : [c, d] = [e, f]
170---    ⊢ [a, b] = ?y
171---
172---    case a
173---    a b c d e f : Nat
174---    h₁ : [a, b] = [c, d]
175---    h₂ : [c, d] = [e, f]
176---    ⊢ ?y = [e, f]
177---
178---    case y
179---    a b c d e f : Nat
180---    h₁ : [a, b] = [c, d]
181---    h₂ : [c, d] = [e, f]
182---    ⊢ List Nat
183-
184---  One way to resolve this is to supply all the arguments and hypotheses
185---  explicity:
186-
187-example (a b c d e f : Nat)
188-    (h₁ : [a, b] = [c, d])
189-    (h₂ : [c, d] = [e, f]) :
190-    [a, b] = [e, f] := by
191-  apply trans_eq [a, b] [c, d] [e, f] h₁ h₂
192-
193---  In the previous example, we had to specify the `x` and `z` arguments to
194---  `trans_eq` before we could supply `[c, d]` for `y` or `eq1` and `eq2`
195---  for the premises. However, we just said that Lean was able to infer
196---  these arguments, so it's a bit redundant (and wordy) for us to do it.
197-
198---  Thankfully, Lean allows us to use `_`s for positional arguments that it
199---  can infer.
200-
201-example (a b c d e f : Nat)
202-    (h₁ : [a, b] = [c, d])
203-    (h₂ : [c, d] = [e, f]) :
204-    [a, b] = [e, f] := by
205-  apply trans_eq _ _ _ h₁ h₂
206-
207---  If we know the name of the argument we are supplying (in this case
208---  `y`), we can name it directly and avoid typing any `_`s. This feature
209---  is called *named arguments*. Named arguments can be used in function
210---  applications generally, not just with `apply`.
211-
212-example (a b c d e f : Nat)
213-    (h₁ : [a, b] = [c, d])
214-    (h₂ : [c, d] = [e, f]) :
215-    [a, b] = [e, f] := by
216-  apply trans_eq (y := [c, d])
217-  apply h₁
218-  apply h₂
219-
220---  Like any other kind of software, there are conventions and best
221---  practices associated with writing proofs in Lean. One of these
222---  conventions concerns the use of the `exact` tactic. When fully applying
223---  another theorem like in the previous examples, it is considered good
224---  practice to use the `exact` tactic instead of `apply`.This signals to a
225---  reader of the proof that the proof is "exactly" an instance of another
226---  lemma, and that nothing of particular interest is happening here. This
227---  achieves a similar goal as when a mathematician says that one result is
228---  "just" an instance of another.
229-
230-example (a b c d e f : Nat)
231-    (h₁ : [a, b] = [c, d])
232-    (h₂ : [c, d] = [e, f]) :
233-    [a, b] = [e, f] := by
234-  exact trans_eq _ _ _ h₁ h₂
235-
236---  Recall the `calc` we have learned in the UsingLean chapter. It works by
237---  chaining equalities together using transitivity, serving the same
238---  purpose here as applying `trans_eq`.
239-
240-example (a b c d e f : Nat)
241-    (h₁ : [a, b] = [c, d])
242-    (h₂ : [c, d] = [e, f]) :
243-    [a, b] = [e, f] := by
244-  calc
245-  [a, b] = [c, d] := by rw [h₁]
246-  [c, d] = [e, f] := by rw [h₂]
247-

250-theorem trans_eq_exercise (n m o p : Nat)
251-    (h₁ : m = o.minusTwo)
252-    (h₂ : (n + p) = m) :
253-    (n + p) = o.minusTwo := by

256---  ## The `injection` and `contradiction` Tactics
257-
258---  Recall the definition of natural numbers:
259-
260-sf_recall
261-  inductive Nat : Type where
262-    | zero
263-    | succ (n : Nat)
264-
265---  It is obvious from this definition that every number has one of two
266---  forms: either it is the constructor `0` or it is built by applying the
267---  constructor `.succ` to another number. But there is more here than
268---  meets the eye: implicit in the definition are two additional facts:
269---
270---  - The constructor `.succ` is *injective* (or *one-to-one*). That is, if
271---    `n + 1 = m + 1`, it must also be that `n = m`.
272---
273---  - The constructors `0` and `.succ` are *disjoint*. That is, `0` is not
274---    equal to `n + 1` for any `n`.
275---
276---  Similar principles apply to every inductively defined type: all
277---  constructors are injective, and the values built from distinct
278---  constructors are never equal. For lists, the `List.cons` constructor is
279---  injective and the empty list `List.nil` is different from every
280---  non-empty list. For booleans, `true` and `false` are different. (Since
281---  `true` and `false` take no arguments, their injectivity is neither here
282---  nor there.) And so on.
283-
284---  ### Injectivity
285-
286---  We can *prove* the injectivity of `Nat.succ` by using the `Nat.pred`
287---  function:
288-
289-example (n m : Nat)
290-    (h : n + 1 = m + 1) :
291-    n = m := by
292-  have : n = Nat.pred (n + 1) := by rfl
293-  /- The hypothesis name defaults to `this` when unspecified. -/
294-  rewrite [this, h]
295-  rw [Nat.pred_succ]
296-
297---  This technique for injectivity can be generalized to any constructor by
298---  writing the equivalent of `pred` — i.e., writing a function that
299---  "undoes" one application of the constructor.
300---
301---  As a convenient alternative, Lean provides a tactic called `injection`
302---  that allows us to exploit the injectivity of any constructor. Here is
303---  an alternate proof of the above theorem using `injection`:
304-
305-example (n m : Nat)
306-    (h : n + 1 = m + 1) :
307-    n = m := by
308-  injection h with hmn
309-
310---  By writing `injection h with hmn` at this point, we are asking Lean to
311---  generate all equations that it can infer from `h` using the injectivity
312---  of constructors (in the present example, the equation `n = m`). This
313---  equation is added as a hypothesis (called `hmn` in this case) into the
314---  context. Because this equation is exactly our goal, in this case the
315---  `injection` tactic is able to automatically close the goal.
316-
317---  `with ...` can be omitted if the generated equations are not used.
318-
319-example (n m : Nat)
320-    (h : n + 1 = m + 1) :
321-    n = m := by
322-  injection h
323-
324---  Here's a more interesting example that shows how `injection` can derive
325---  multiple equations at once.
326-
327-example (n m o : Nat)
328-    (h : [n, m] = [o, o]) :
329-    n = m := by
330-  injection h with h₁ h₂
331-  injection h₂ with h₃
332-  rw [h₁, h₃]
333-
334---  There is also a related tactic, `injections`, that applies the
335---  `injection` tactic to all your hypotheses at once, as many times in a
336---  row as it can. Using this tactic can avoid needing to repeatedly use
337---  `injection` on lists. For example:
338-
339-example (n m o : Nat)
340-    (h : [n, m] = [o, o]) :
341-    n = m := by
342-  injections h₁ _ h₃
343-  rw [h₁, h₃]
344-
345---  ### Exercise (3 stars): injection_ex3 ⭐⭐⭐
346-
347-theorem injection_ex3 {α : Type} (x y z : α) (l j : List α)
348-    (h₁ : x :: y :: l = z :: j)
349-    (h₂ : j = z :: l) :
350-    x = y := by
351-  sorry
352-
353---  So much for injectivity of constructors. What about disjointness?
354-
355---  The principle of disjointness says that two terms beginning with
356---  different constructors (like `0` and `Nat.succ`, or `true` and `false`)
357---  can never be equal. This means that, any time we find ourselves in a
358---  context where we've *assumed* that two such terms are equal, we are
359---  justified in concluding anything we want, since the assumption is
360---  nonsensical.
361-
362---  The `contradiction` tactic, which we've already seen for handling cases
363---  where we have assumed `False`, also embodies this principle: if we have
364---  a a hypothesis involving an equality between different constructors
365---  (e.g., `false = true`), `contradiction` solves the current goal
366---  immediately. Some examples:
367-
368-example (n m : Nat)
369-    (h : false = true) :
370-    n = m := by
371-  contradiction
372-
373-example (n : Nat)
374-    (h : n + 1 = 0) :
375-    2 + 2 = 5 := by
376-  contradiction
377-
378---  These examples are instances of a logical principle known as the
379---  *principle of explosion*, which asserts that a contradictory hypothesis
380---  entails anything (even manifestly false things!).
381---
382---  Notice that due to the way addition on naturals is defined, deriving a
383---  contradiction from `1 + n = 0` is not as trivial as it seems.
384-
385-sf_expect_failure_in
386-  example (n : Nat)
387-      (h : 1 + n = 0) :
388-      2 + 2 = 5 := by
389-    contradiction -- doesn't work because `1 + n` doesn't reduce to `n.succ`.
390-
391---  To fix it, rewriting with `Nat.one_add` changes the hypothesis from
392---  `1 + n = 0` to `n.succ = 0`. Then Lean can immediately recognize this
393---  as impossible.
394-
395-example (n : Nat)
396-    (h : 1 + n = 0) :
397-    2 + 2 = 5 := by
398-  rw [Nat.one_add] at h
399-  contradiction
400-
401---  If you find the principle of explosion confusing, remember that these
402---  proofs are *not* simply showing that the conclusion of the statement
403---  holds. Rather, they are showing that, *if* the nonsensical situation
404---  described by the premise did somehow hold, *then* the nonsensical
405---  conclusion would hold too (because we'd be living in an inconsistent
406---  universe where every statement is true).
407---
408---  We'll explore the principle of explosion in more detail in the next
409---  chapter.
410-
411---  ### Exercise (1 star): disjoint_ex3 ⭐
412-
413-theorem disjoint_ex3 {α : Type} (x y z : α) (l : List α)
414-    (h : x :: y :: l = []) :
415-    x = z := by
416-  sorry

419-

425-    | green
426-    | blue
427-

429-  inductive Color : Type where
430-    | black
431-    | white
432-    | primary (p: RGB)

435-

440---      x : RGB
441---      y : RGB

443---      ------------------------------
444---      ⊢ y = x

449---

465---      --------------

467---

487---      -------------------

489---
490---  and we apply the tactic `injection h with hxy`. What will happen?

492---  (A) "No more goals."

501-
502---  _Quiz:_
503-
504---  Finally, suppose Lean's proof state looks like
505---
506---      x : Nat
507---      y : Nat
508---      h : 1 + x = 1 + y
509---      -------------------
510---      ⊢ y = x
511---
512---  and we apply the tactic `injection h with hxy`. What will happen?
513---
514---  (A) "No more goals."
515---
516---  (B) The tactic fails.
517---
518---  (C) Hypothesis `h` becomes `hxy : x = y`.

522---   ----------------------------------------
523-
524---  The injectivity of constructors allows us to reason that
525---  `∀ (n m : Nat), n + 1 = m + 1 → n = m`. The converse of this
526---  implication is an instance of a more general fact about both
527---  constructors and functions:
528-
529-example {α β : Type} (f : α → β) (x y : α)
530-    (h : x = y) : f x = f y := by
531-  rw [h]
532-
533-example (n m : Nat) (h : n = m) :
534-    n + 1 = m + 1 := by
535-  rw [h]
536-
537---  Indeed, there is also a tactic named `congr` that can prove such goals
538---  directly. Given a goal of the form `f a₁ ... aₙ = g b₁ ... bₙ`, the
539---  tactic `congr` will produce subgoals of the form `f = g`, `a₁ = b₁`,
540---  ..., `aₙ = bₙ`. At the same time, any of these subgoals that are simple
541---  enough (e.g., immediately provable by `rfl`) will be automatically
542---  discharged.
543-
544-example (n m : Nat) (h : n = m) :
545-    n + 1 = m + 1 := by
546-  congr
547-
548---  The `congr` tactic also accepts a numerical argument, which tells Lean
549---  how deeply to decompose the goal. So, given a goal like
550---  `((a, b), (c, d)) = ((e, f), (g, h))`, `congr 1` only applies `congr`
551---  once to the goal, and would produce two subgoals: `(a, b) = (e, f)` and
552---  `(c, d) = (g, h)`. `congr 2`, meanwhile, would apply `congr` again to
553---  both these subgoals, and produce four subgoals: `a = e`, `b = f`,
554---  `c = g` and `d = h`. Using `congr` without an argument always
555---  decomposes the goal as deeply as possible.
556---
557---  Why does Lean provide this level of flexibility? Depending on what we
558---  are trying to prove, deeper applications of `congr` may make our goal
559---  unprovable. Consider this example:
560-
561-sf_expect_failure_in
562-  example (a b c d : Nat) (hab : a = b) (hcd : c = d) :
563-      (a, c + 1) = (b, 1 + d) := by
564-    congr
565-
566---  We now have three goals: `c = 1`, `1 = d`, and `1 = d`, but these are
567---  not provable from our hypotheses! `congr` has gone too deep.
568-
569---  Output:
570---    unsolved goals
571---    case e_snd.e_a
572---    a b c d : Nat
573---    hab : a = b
574---    hcd : c = d
575---    ⊢ c = 1
576---
577---    case e_snd.e_a.e_2
578---    a b c d : Nat
579---    hab : a = b
580---    hcd : c = d
581---    ⊢ 1 = d
582---
583---    case e_snd.e_a.e_3
584---    a b c d : Nat
585---    hab : a = b
586---    hcd : c = d
587---    ⊢ 1 = d
588-
589-example (a b c d : Nat) (hab : a = b) (hcd : c = d) :
590-    (a, c + 1) = (b, 1 + d) := by
591-  /- Only shallowly using `congr` here allows us to complete the proof -/
592-  congr 1
593-  rw [Nat.add_comm]
594-  congr
595-
596---  ## Using `apply` on Hypotheses
597-
598---  The tactic `apply t at h` matches an implication `t` (say, of the form
599---  `a → b`) against a hypothesis `h` in the local context. Unlike ordinary
600---  `apply`, which matches the goal against `b` and replaces it with the
601---  subgoal `a`), `apply t at h` matches the type of `h` against `a` and,
602---  if successful, replaces `h` with a hypothesis of type `b`.
603---
604---  In other words, `apply t at h` gives us a form of "forward reasoning":
605---  given `t : a → b` and `h : a`, it replaces `h` with a proof of `b`.
606---
607---  By contrast, ordinary `apply t` is "backward reasoning": given
608---  `t : a → b` and a goal `⊢ b`, it replaces the goal with `⊢ a`.
609---
610---  Here is a proof that uses forward reasoning rather than backward
611---  reasoning:
612-
613-example (n m p q : Nat)
614-    (h : n = m → p = q)
615-    (hnm : n = m) :
616-    p = q := by
617-  apply h at hnm
618-  exact hnm
619-
620---  Forward reasoning begins with what is already known — premises and
621---  previously proven theorems — and derives new facts from them until the
622---  goal is reached. Backward reasoning begins with the *goal* and works
623---  backward through implications that would prove it, until remaining
624---  goals are facts that are already known.
625---
626---  The informal proofs in mathematics and computer science often use
627---  forward reasoning. In Lean, however, backward reasoning is often more
628---  idiomatic, though forward reasoning can sometimes be easier to follow
629---  or more natural for particular proofs.
630---
631---  You may be interested to know that the `apply ... at ...` tactic is not
632---  part of Lean's core set of tactics. However, Lean makes it very easy
633---  for users to define new tactics that suit their particular proof style,
634---  and so the developers of the
635---  [Mathlib](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4) library
636---  defined the `apply ... at ...` tactic to better support forward
637---  reasoning. Mathlib is a very large development, so we will not import
638---  the whole thing here, but we have made `apply ... at ...` available
639---  because it is quite useful.
640-
641---  To apply a tactic in multiple places at the same time, you can list
642---  multiple hypotheses in a row after the `at`. You can also explicitly
643---  use a tactic on the goal (usually because you are applying the tactic
644---  to both a hypothesis and the goal) by including it after the `at` with
645---  the turnstile symbol `⊢`, written `\|-`, `\goal` or `\vdash`.
646-
647-example (n m : Nat) (h : n + 0 = m) : n = m + 0 := by
648-  rw [Nat.add_zero] at h ⊢
649-  assumption
650-
651---  ## Specializing Hypotheses
652-
653---  We've already seen how we can use `have` to do forward reasoning, by
654---  letting us state and prove useful facts that get us closer to the main
655---  goal we're trying to prove. Often, though, these facts are just special
656---  cases of more general hypotheses we already have.
657---
658---  If `h` is a quantified hypothesis in the current context — i.e.,
659---  `h : ∀ (x : α), P x` — then we can use `have` to obtain a special case
660---  of `h` by supplying a value for `x`. For example, `have h := h e`
661---  introduces a new `h` which `x` has been instantiated with `e`.
662---
663---  For example:
664-
665-example (m : Nat) (h : ∀ n, m * n = 0) : m = 0 := by
666-  have h := h 1
667-  rw [Nat.mul_one] at h
668-  exact h
669-
670---  You may notice that, in the above proof, the original `h` is still
671---  present in the context, although it is shadowed by the new `h`. Often
672---  we don't care to keep this old hypothesis around, and so we can use the
673---  `replace` tactic instead. It behaves like `have`, except that it gets
674---  rid of the old hypothesis afterwards when possible:
675-
676-example (m : Nat) (h : ∀ n, m * n = 0) : m = 0 := by
677-  replace h := h 1
678-  rw [Nat.mul_one] at h
679-  exact h
680-
681---  Specializing a hypothesis in this way is common enough that Lean
682---  provides the `specialize` tactic for it. For example, `specialize h 1`
683---  is a more concise way of writing `replace h := h 1`:
684-
685-example (m : Nat) (h : ∀ n, m * n = 0) : m = 0 := by
686-  specialize h 1
687-  rw [Nat.mul_one] at h
688-  exact h
689-
690---  ### Exercise (3 stars): nth?_always_none ⭐⭐⭐
691-
692---  Use `have`, `replace`, or `specialize` to prove the the following
693---  lemma, following the model of the examples above. Do not use
694---  `induction`.
695-
696-theorem nth?_always_none (l : List Nat) (h : ∀ i, nth? l i = none) :
697-    l = [] := by
698-  sorry
699-
700---  Tactics like `have` and `replace` can also be used with lemmas and
701---  theorems we've already proven, not just things in our context. Using
702---  these tactis before `apply` gives us yet another way to control where
703---  `apply` does its work.
704-
705-example (a b c d e f : Nat)
706-    (h₁ : [a, b] = [c, d])
707-    (h₂ : [c, d] = [e, f]) :
708-    [a, b] = [e, f] := by
709-  have h := trans_eq (y := [c, d])
710-  apply h
711-  /- This tactic closes a goal if it appears anywhere in the context.
712-     In this case we could also write `exact h₁` ... -/
713-  assumption
714-  /- .. and here we could also write `exact h₂` -/
715-  assumption
716-
717---  ## Generalizing the Induction Hypothesis
718-
719---  Recall this function for doubling a natural number from the Induction
720---  chapter:
721-
722-sf_recall
723-  def Nat.double (n : Nat) : Nat :=
724-    match n with
725-    | 0 => 0
726-    | n' + 1 => double n' + 2
727-
728---  Sometimes `induction` gives us an an induction hypothesis too specific
729---  to be useful. This can happen when another varaible in the theorem is
730---  fixed during the induction, even though the induction step might need
731---  to use it with different values of that variables.
732---
733---  For example, suppose we want to show that `Nat.double` is injective —
734---  i.e., that it maps different arguments to different results:
735-
736-sf_experiment
737-  theorem double_injective (n m : Nat) (h : n.double = m.double) : n = m := sorry
738-
739---  The way we start this proof is a bit delicate: if we begin it with
740-
741-sf_expect_failure_in
742-  theorem double_injective (n m : Nat) (h : n.double = m.double) : n = m := by
743-    induction n with
744-    | zero =>
745-      cases m with
746-      | zero => rfl
747-      | succ m' =>
748-        rw [Nat.double_zero, Nat.double_succ] at h
749-        contradiction
750-    | succ n' ih =>
751-      cases m with
752-      | zero =>
753-        rw [Nat.double_zero, Nat.double_succ] at h
754-        contradiction
755-      | succ m' =>
756-        congr
757-
758---  Output:
759---    unsolved goals
760---    case succ.succ.e_a
761---    n' m' : Nat
762---    ih : n'.double = (m' + 1).double → n' = m' + 1
763---    h : (n' + 1).double = (m' + 1).double
764---    ⊢ n' = m'
765-
766---  We get stuck — `m` is fixed during the induction, so in the successor
767---  case the induction hypothesis `ih` is specialized to the current value
768---  of `m`. After the case split, that value is `m' + 1`, and the induction
769---  hypothesis has the form:
770---
771---      ih : n'.double = (m' + 1).double → n' = m' + 1
772---
773---  From `h`, using the definition of `Nat.double` we can obtain
774-
775---  n'.double = m'.double
776-
777---  and to prove the goal we would like to apply an induction hypothesis at
778---  `m'`. Nevertheless, `ih` is specialized to `m' + 1` — it would require
779-
780---  n'.double = (m' + 1).double
781-
782---  and would conclude
783-
784---  n' = m' + 1
785-
786---  which is not what we need. Instead, we need an induction hypothesis
787---  that is general in `m`:
788---
789---      ih : ∀ m, n'.double = m.double → n' = m
790---
791---  Then in this branch we can instantiate it with `m'`.
792-
793---  We can obtain a more generalized induction hypothesis by writing
794---
795---      induction n generalizing m with
796---
797---  What went wrong?
798-
799---  The problem is that `m` is already in the context when we invoke
800---  `induction n`. Since `m` is an ordinary argument of the theorem, this
801---  is exactly what we normally want — we are considering some particular
802---  `n` and `m`, together with the hypothesis `n.double = m.double` and
803---  trying to prove `n = m`.
804---
805---  The claim itself makes perfect sense, but for the induction, however,
806---  keeping `m` fixed causes the trouble: we are proving, for *all* `n`,
807---  the proposition
808---
809---  - `P n` = "if `n.double = m.double`, then `n = m`"
810---
811---  by showing
812---
813---  - `P 0`
814---
815---    (i.e., "if `Nat.double 0 = m.double` then `0 = m`") and
816---
817---  - `P n → P (n + 1)`
818---
819---    (i.e., "if `n.double = m.double` then `n = m`" implies "if
820---    `(n + 1).double = m.double` then `n + 1 = m`").
821---
822---  If we look closely at the inductive step, it is saying something rather
823---  strange: that, for a *particular* `m`, if we know
824---
825---  - "if `n.double = m.double` then `n = m`"
826---
827---  then we can prove
828---
829---  - "if `(n + 1).double = m.double` then `n + 1 = m`".
830---
831---  To see why this is strange, let's choose of a particular `m` — say,
832---  `5`. The statement is then saying that, if we know
833---
834---  - `Q` = "if `n.double = 10` then `n = 5`"
835---
836---  then we can prove
837---
838---  - `R` = "if `(n + 1).double = 10` then `n + 1 = 5`".
839---
840---  But knowing `Q` doesn't give us any help at all with proving `R`. If we
841---  tried to prove `R` from `Q`, we would start with something like
842---  "Suppose `(n + 1).double = 10`..." but then we would be stuck: the
843---  induction hypothesis `Q` only tells us what happens if `n.double = 10`,
844---  whereas our assumption says `(n + 1).double = 10`, so `Q` is useless
845---  here.
846---
847---  This is exactly what we saw in the proof state.
848-
849---  Trying to carry out this proof by induction on `n` with `m` fixed
850---  doesn't work, because we are then trying to prove a statement involving
851---  *every* `n` but just a *particular* `m`.
852---
853---  A successful proof of `double_injective` *generalizes* `m` when
854---  carrying out the induction on `n`, so that the induction hypothesis
855---  holds for every `m`, rather than for just the particular `m` in the
856---  context.
857-
858-theorem double_injective (n m : Nat) (h : n.double = m.double) : n = m := by
859-  induction n generalizing m with
860-  | zero =>
861-    cases m with
862-    | zero => rfl
863-    | succ m' => contradiction
864-  | succ n' ih =>
865-    cases m with
866-    | zero => contradiction
867-    | succ m' =>
868-      congr
869-      apply ih -- now works
870-      rw [Nat.double_succ, Nat.double_succ] at h
871-      injections
872-
873---  Let's look at an informal proof of this theorem. Notice that the
874---  induction hypothesis is generalized over `m`, corresponding to the use
875---  of `generalizing m`.
876---
877---  *Theorem*: For any natural numbers `n` and `m`, if
878---  `n.double = m.double`, then `n = m`.
879---
880---  *Proof*: We prove by induction on `n` that, for *any* `m`, if
881---  `n.double = m.double` then `n = m`.
882---
883---  - First, suppose `n = 0`. We must show that, for any `m`, if
884---    `Nat.double 0 = m.double`, then `0 = m`.
885---
886---    There are two cases to consider for `m`:
887---
888---    1. If `m = 0`, we are done.
889---
890---    2. Otherwise if `m = m' + 1` for some `m'`, then by definition of
891---       `Nat.double` we have `Nat.double 0 = 0` and
892---       `(m' + 1).double = m'.double + 2`. Clearly `0` cannot equal
893---       `m'.double + 2`, so this case is impossible.
894---
895---  - Second, suppose `n = n' + 1`. The induction hypothesis says that, for
896---    every `m`, if `(n' + 1).double = m.double` then `n' + 1 = m`. Again
897---    there are two cases to consider for `m`:
898---
899---    1. If `m = 0`, then by the definition of `Nat.double` our assumption
900---       says `n'.double + 2 = 0`, which is impossible.
901---
902---    2. Otherwise suppose `m = m' + 1`. Our assumption is then that
903---       `(n' + 1).double = (m' + 1).double`. By the definition of
904---       `Nat.double`, this gives `n'.double + 2 = m'.double + 2`. By
905---       injectivity of `Nat.succ`, we obtain `n'.double = m'.double`. We
906---       can now instantiate the induction hypothesis with `m'`, obtaining
907---       `n' = m'`. Now we can conclude `n' + 1 = m' + 1`, which is exactly
908---       what we wanted to show.
909---
910---  *Qed*.
911-
912---  The thing to take away from all this is that you need to be careful,
913---  when using induction, that your induction hypothesis is not too
914---  specific. When proving a proposition quantified over variables `n` and
915---  `m` by induction on `n`, it is sometimes crucial to *generalize* `m`,
916---  so that the induction hypothesis applies to every `m` rather than just
917---  the particular `m` in the context.
918-

934---  ## Rewriting with Conditional Statements
935-
936---  Suppose that we know two numbers have the same double, and we want to
937---  use this fact to rewrite one of them into the other. Recall the theorem
938---  `double_injective` from the previous section:
939-
940-#check double_injective
941-
942---  Output:
943---    double_injective (n m : Nat) (h : n.double = m.double) : n = m
944-
945---  For example, we can prove:
946-
947-example (n m p q : Nat)
948-    (h : n.double = m.double)
949-    (hm : m + p = q) :
950-    n + p = q := by
951-  rw [double_injective n m]
952-  · assumption
953-  · assumption
954-
955---  The use of `rw` here is a little different from the examples we have
956---  seen so far. The theorem `double_injective` says `n = m` *provided
957---  that* `n.double = m.double`, not just `n = m`. When we write
958---  `rw [double_injective n m]`, Lean uses the conclusion `n = m` to
959---  rewrite the goal, and then asks us to prove the hypothesis needed by
960---  `double_injective`. Thus we get two goals: the updated main goal,
961---  `m + p = q`, which follows from `hm`, and the condition from
962---  `double_injective`, `n.double = m.double`, whicch follows from `h`.
963-
964---  If we rewrite with a conditional statement of the form `P → a = b`,
965---  then Lean tries to rewrite with `a = b`, and then asks us to prove `P`
966---  in a new subgoal. If the statement has more than one assumption, then
967---  we get one subgoal for each assumption.

1017---  ## Using `cases` on Expressions
1018-
1019---  We have seen many examples where `cases` is used to perform case
1020---  analysis of the value of some variable. Sometimes we need to reason by
1021---  cases on the result of some *expression*. We can also do this with
1022---  `cases`.
1023---
1024---  Here are some examples:
1025-
1026-def chooseIf {α : Type} (test : α → Bool) (x y : α) : α :=
1027-  if test x then x else y
1028-
1029-theorem chooseIf_self {α : Type} (test : α → Bool) (x : α) :
1030-    chooseIf test x x = x := by
1031-  rw [chooseIf]
1032-  cases test x <;> rfl
1033-
1034---  After *unfolding* `chooseIf` in the above proof, we find that we are
1035---  stuck on `(if test x = true then x else x) = x`. But either `test x` is
1036---  `true` or it isn't, so we can use `cases (test x)` to let us reason
1037---  about the two cases.
1038---
1039---  In general, the `cases` tactic can be used to perform case analysis of
1040---  the results of arbitrary computations. If `e` is an expression whose
1041---  type is some inductively defined type `T`, then, for each constructor
1042---  `c` of `T`, `cases e` generates a subgoal in which all occurrences of
1043---  `e` (in the goal and in the context) are replaced by `c`.
1044-
1045---  ### Destructing Tuples
1046-
1047---  `cases` is useful when we are dealing with inductively defined types
1048---  that can be one thing or another; a `Bool` is either a `false` or a
1049---  `true`, and a `Nat` is either `0` or `succ n`. When we want more
1050---  information about inductively defined types that are products of
1051---  multiple things, we instead want a way to get the pieces of that value
1052---  out from it.
1053---
1054---  When we have a value `v : α × β` in our context, we can get the first
1055---  and second projections of `v` using this tactic:
1056---
1057---      let ⟨a, β⟩ := v
1058-

1076---  ### Splitting with Equations
1077-
1078---  When using `cases`, we can specify to Lean that it should remember an
1079---  equality between a compound expression and what we are decomposing it
1080---  into, using `cases h : ...` syntax. This information can actually be
1081---  critical, and, if we leave it out, we might lack information we need to
1082---  complete a proof.
1083-
1084---  For example, suppose we define a function `keepIf` like this:
1085-
1086-def keepIf {α : Type} (test : α → Bool) (x : α) : Option α :=
1087-  if test x then some x else none
1088-
1089---  Now suppose that we want to prove `keepIf_some`. If we start the proof
1090---  like this (with no `h : ⋯` on the `cases`)...
1091-
1092-sf_expect_failure_in
1093-  theorem keepIf_some {α : Type} (test : α → Bool) (x y : α)
1094-      (h : keepIf test x = some y) :
1095-      x = y := by
1096-    rw [keepIf] at h
1097-    cases (test x)
1098-
1099---  Output:
1100---    unsolved goals
1101---    case false
1102---    α : Type
1103---    test : α → Bool
1104---    x y : α
1105---    h : (if test x = true then some x else none) = some y
1106---    ⊢ x = y
1107---
1108---    case true
1109---    α : Type
1110---    test : α → Bool
1111---    x y : α
1112---    h : (if test x = true then some x else none) = some y
1113---    ⊢ x = y
1114-
1115---  ... then we are stuck at this point because the context does not
1116---  contain enough information to prove the goal. Because `test x` appears
1117---  in our hypothesis, rather than in our goal, `cases (test x)` does not
1118---  automatically replace the expression with `false` or `true` like it did
1119---  during the proof of `chooseIf`. We want to add an equation to the
1120---  context that records which case we are in. This is precisely what the
1121---  `h : ⋯` qualifier does.
1122-
1123-theorem keepIf_some {α : Type} (test : α → Bool) (x y : α)
1124-    (h : keepIf test x = some y) :
1125-    x = y := by
1126-  rw [keepIf] at h
1127-  cases hTest : test x
1128-  -- Now we have the same state as at the point where we got stuck
1129-  -- above, except that the context contains an extra equality
1130-  -- assumption, which is exactly what we need to make progress.
1131-  · rw [hTest] at h
1132-    contradiction
1133-  · rw [hTest] at h
1134-    injections

1142---  ## Review
1143-
1144---  We've now talked about many of Lean's most fundamental tactics. We'll
1145---  introduce a few more in the coming chapters, and later on we'll see
1146---  some more powerful *automation* tactics that make Lean help us with
1147---  low-level details. But basically we've got what we need to get work
1148---  done.
1149---
1150---  Here are the ones we've seen so far.
1151---
1152---  Managing goals and hypotheses:
1153---
1154---  - `intro h`: move an assumption/quantified variable from the goal into
1155---    the local context
1156---
1157---  - `apply thm`: use a theorem, hypothesis, or constructor whose
1158---    conclusion matches the goal; its premises become new goals
1159---
1160---  - `apply thm at h`: use a theorem on a hypothesis in the context,
1161---    replacing `h` by the resulting
1162---
1163---    fact (forward reasoning)
1164---
1165---  - `specialize h ...`: instantiate quantified variables in a hypothesis,
1166---    modifying `h` in place
1167---
1168---  - `replace h := ...`: replace a hypothesis with a newly proved fact
1169---
1170---  - `have h : P := ...`: prove a local fact `P` and add it to the context
1171---    with the name `h`
1172---
1173---  - `contradiction`: close the current goal when the context contains
1174---    contradictory assumptions
1175---
1176---  Equality, rewriting, and unfolding:
1177---
1178---  - `rfl`: close an equality that holds by reflexivity (possibly after
1179---    computation)
1180---
1181---  - `rw [h]`: rewrite the goal using an equality hypothesis or theorem
1182---
1183---  - `rw [d]`: unfold a definition in the goal
1184---
1185---  - `rw [h] at h'`: rewrite a hypothesis using an equality hypothesis or
1186---    theorem
1187---
1188---  - `rw [d] at h'`: unfold a definition in a hypothesis
1189---
1190---  - `symm`: reverse an equality goal, changing `t = u` to `u = t`
1191---
1192---  - `symm at h`: reverse an equality hypothesis
1193---
1194---  - `calc`: prove a goal about equality or another transitive relation by
1195---    giving a sequence of intermediate steps
1196---
1197---  - `congr`: use congruence to reduce an equality between expressions
1198---    with the same outer form; for example, a goal `f x = f y` may be
1199---    reduced to `x = y`
1200---
1201---  - `injection h with ...`: use injectivity of constructors to extract
1202---    equalities from constructor applications equations
1203---
1204---  - `injections`: repeatedly use constructor injectivity on suitable
1205---    equalities in the context
1206---
1207---  Case analysis:
1208---
1209---  - `cases x`: reason separately about the possible constructors of an
1210---    inductively defined value
1211---
1212---  - `cases h : e`: perform case analysis on an expression `e` and add an
1213---    equation named `h` recording the result of the case analysis
1214---
1215---  Induction:
1216---
1217---  - `induction x`: prove the goal by induction on an inductively defined
1218---    value
1219---
1220---  - `induction x generalizing y`: induction on `x` while generalizing the
1221---    listed local variables, giving a more general induction hypothesis
1222-
